title: Reference trajectory generation for 3-Dimensional walking of a humanoid robot
abstract: Humanoid walking planning is a complicated task because of the high number of degrees of freedom (DOFs) and the variable mechanical structure during walking. In this paper, a planning method for 3-dimensional (3-D) walking movements was developed based on a model of a typical humanoid robot with 12 DOFs on the lower body. The planning process includes trajectory generation for the hip, ankle, and knee joints in the Cartesian space. The balance of the robot was ensured by adjusting the hip motion. The angles for each DOF were obtained from 3-D kinematics calculation. The calculation gave reference trajectories of all the DOFs on the humanoid robot which were used to control the real robot. The simulation results show that the method is effective.

title: Review of Bioinspired Vision-Tactile Fusion Perception (VTFP): From Humans to Humanoids
abstract: Humanoid robots are designed and expected to resemble humans in structure and behavior, showing increasing application potentials in various fields. Like their biological counterparts, their environmental perception ability is fundamental. In particular, the visual and tactile perception are the two main sensory modes that humanoids use to understand and interact with the environment. Vision-Tactile Fusion Perception (VTFP) has shown multiple possibilities for better sensing understanding in challenging conditions, causing new research interests and questions. The overlap between visual and tactile perception in humanoids is continually growing. This work has reviewed the current state of the art of VTFP. It starts with the physiological basis of biological vision and tactile systems as well as the VTFP mechanisms as inspirations for humanoid perception. Then, the bioinspired visual-tactile fusion systems for humanoids are reviewed as the emphasis. After the survey on the vision and tactile sensors of robots, seven currently publicly available VTFP datasets are introduced. They are the data sources for several studies on neural network-inspired fusion algorithms. Furthermore, the applications of VTFP on humanoids are summarized. Finally, the challenges and future work are discussed. This review aims to provide several references for further exploitation of VTFP and its applications on humanoids.

title: ADHERENT: Learning Human-like Trajectory Generators for Whole-body Control of Humanoid Robots
abstract: Human-like trajectory generation and footstep planning represent challenging problems in humanoid robotics. Recently, research in computer graphics investigated machine-learning methods for character animation based on training human-like models directly on motion capture data. Such methods proved effective in virtual environments, mainly focusing on trajectory visualization. This letter presents ADHERENT, a system architecture integrating machine-learning methods used in computer graphics with whole-body control methods employed in robotics to generate and stabilize human-like trajectories for humanoid robots. Leveraging human motion capture locomotion data, ADHERENT yields a general footstep planner, including forward, sideways, and backward walking trajectories that blend smoothly from one to another. Furthermore, at the joint configuration level, ADHERENT computes data-driven whole-body postural reference trajectories coherent with the generated footsteps, thus increasing the human likeness of the resulting robot motion. Extensive validations of the proposed architecture are presented with both simulations and real experiments on the iCub humanoid robot, thus demonstrating ADHERENT to be robust to varying step sizes and walking speeds.

title: Miha: An Affordable Humanoid Platform for Research and Development
abstract: The current paper introduces Miha, an affordable yet highly performant humanoid platform for research and development. The motivation behind the platform is to significantly lower the costs compared to similar offerings, democratizing access to humanoid robotics research and helping in the standardization of common control functions. The platform offers 22 degrees of freedom smart actuators, pressure sensors, inertial measurement units, stereo cameras, multiple microphones, speakers, and a convenient 2.4-inch liquid crystal display for the on-device user interface. It includes a unique dual hot-swap battery design that allows continuous operation in the field with best-in-class 3-hours autonomy on one charge. The presented version uses a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 as the main controller and uses ROS Noetic. We demonstrate several control functions, including walking. The vast majority of hardware and software components are either off-the-shelf or provided as open-source.

The motivation behind the platform is to significantly lower the costs compared to similar offerings, democratizing access to humanoid robotics research and helping in the standardization of common control functions. The platform offers 22 degrees of freedom smart actuators, pressure sensors, inertial measurement units, stereo cameras, multiple microphones, speakers, and a convenient 2.4-inch liquid crystal display for the on-device user interface. It includes a unique dual hot-swap battery design that allows continuous operation in the field with best-in-class 3-hours autonomy on one charge. The presented version uses a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 as the main controller and uses ROS Noetic. We demonstrate several control functions, including walking. The vast majority of hardware and software components are either off-the-shelf or provided as open-source.<Introduction>Humanoid robots have captured the imagination of scientists and the public alike. As Isaac Asimov posited over 70 years ago, the human form is the most successful generalized form in nature, making it a prime candidate for robotic design[1]. Despite the clear economic and functional advantages, progress in humanoid robotics has been slow[2]. First, humanoid robotics control is a very tough problem. In engineering we resort to simplifying complex problems in order to produce robust and controllable mechanisms. In the case of humanoid robotics, complexity and the resulting emergent behavior are of interest. Second, humanoid robotics research needs physical platforms to operate and experiment. Historically, the focus was on replicating the human form at scale, which inevitably led to very expensive and difficult-to-use platforms. The cost of these platforms tends to increase exponentially with their size, and as a result, only a very limited number of universities and research institutions can afford to invest in this domain[3]. Despite these challenges, improvements in materials science have led to lighter and stronger robot structures[4]. Nevertheless, advances in battery technology have extended operational periods[5]. Furthermore, the integration of machine learning and artificial intelligence has enhanced the capabilities of control systems, enabling more adaptive movements. Modern humanoid robots contain advanced control systems that utilize machine learning techniques to manage balance, locomotion, and manipulation tasks. Reinforcement learning and neural networks are increasingly employed to enable robots to learn from their environments and improve their performance over time. For example, Boston Dynamics’ Atlas robot uses algorithms to perform tasks such as parkour and backflips, demonstrating advancements in dynamic stability and control[6]. The sensory systems of humanoid robots have also seen considerable advancements. High-resolution cameras, LiDAR, and inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide comprehensive environmental feedback and proprioception[7]. These sensors enable robots to navigate complex environments, recognize objects, and interact with humans more naturally. The incorporation of tactile sensors in robotic hands has improved the precision of object manipulation, allowing robots to perform delicate tasks that were previously unachievable, as in the case of the Minsight robotic fingertip that includes the usage of machine learning methods[8]. A notable trend in humanoid robotics is the development of collaborative robots, or cobots, designed to work alongside humans in shared environments, such as in the case of the Robonaut for space missions[9]. These robots are equipped with advanced safety features and intuitive interfaces that facilitate human-robot collaboration. For instance, SoftBank Robotics’ Pepper robot is widely used in customer service and educational settings, where it interacts with people in a friendly and engaging manner[10]. To address the high costs associated with humanoid robots, researchers are exploring modular and cost-effective designs. Modular robots consist of interchangeable components that can be easily upgraded or replaced, reducing maintenance costs and extending the lifespan of the platform. Such an example is the Connect-R modular robotic system which can operate in extreme environments, such as for oil and gas production, nuclear maintenance, along with space and underwater explorations[11]. Additionally, the use of 3D printing has made it more feasible to produce humanoid robots at a lower cost[12]. Based on Markets and Markets, 3D printing for construction processes reduces construction waste by up to 60%, labor cost up to 80% and construction time up to 70%[13]. Based on these observations, we propose an affordable, yet performant humanoid platform that would energize and democratize the research in this area. Through careful design, we have reduced the mass of the robot (2.1Kg vs., for example, 5.6Kg for NAO), therefore reducing the torque requirements for actuators. This has a profound impact on cost, with our offer being about a third of that of similar robots on the market (NAO[14], ROBOTIS OP3[15]). To the best of our knowledge, based on the technical choices that we made, our robot is the most affordable among all robots with similar performances. We also employ an original power distribution model, unique for humanoid robots, with two batteries located in the soles, providing more extended autonomy (approximately 3 hours - almost double the autonomy of the previously mentioned platforms) with hot-swapping capability for an uninterrupted operation in the field. By choosing to use readily available components, we allow the users to service the robot on their own and avoid costly and lengthy repair time. The open-source nature of the robot’s structure allows researchers to freely adapt the robot for particular research. The few custom-designed electronic parts have a clear purpose and are unique offerings on the market: a Raspberry Pi HAT that packs high-performance dual Dynamixel buses, IMU, audio codec and power management and an original pressure sensor array that doubles as a battery power management. To our knowledge, this pressure sensor is the only one available for Dynamixel protocol, and from all comparable platforms, only NAO offers this type of sensors. To improve user experience, Miha includes a2.4′′TFT screen that can display status information and, using a common Bluetooth mini-keyboard, researchers can control the robot without using an external computer. To our knowledge Miha is the only robot on the market offering this kind of convenience. In contrast with other robots Miha is a native robotic operating system (ROS) and not an afterthought. This allows researchers to benefit from the entire ROS ecosystem (visualization, simulation, control, monitoring) and creates a common reference platform for ROS community to develop generic control models for humanoid robots. This article is structured to provide a comprehensive overview of the development and performance of the Miha humanoid robot. The introduction offers an overview of humanoid robotics, highlighting their significance, the challenges faced, and the motivation for this research. In the related work section, existing research in humanoid robotics is reviewed, discussing previous advancements and challenges, and positioning the current research within this context. The materials and methods section is divided into four subsections: design principles, which outline the fundamental principles guiding the robot’s design such as modularity, cost-efficiency, and robustness; specifications, detailing the technical aspects; hardware implementation, which provides an overview of the physical construction, materials used, and mechanical design aspects; and software, describing the control algorithms, software architecture, and the machine learning techniques used for control and adaptation. The results section presents experimental setups and test scenarios. Finally, the conclusion and future work section summarizes the research outcomes and contributions, discusses the implications for the field of humanoid robotics, addresses the limitations of the current study, and outlines potential areas for future research and development.<Related Work>Humanoid robotics is a domain that is not as young as many would think. Without a doubt, the pioneers in the field have been the Japanese universities and companies, and the beginnings can be traced back to Waseda University and Prof. Ichiro Kato, who in 1973 developed WABOT-1, the world’s first full-scale humanoid robot. After many iterations of their WL series, the University introduced WABIAN in 1996 and WABIAN-R in the following year[16], two robots with a large number of Degrees of Freedom (DoF) (35 for WABIAN and 43 for WABIAN-R) and adult human proportions. In 1996, Honda presented P2[17]the result of 10 years of secret research. The robot demonstrated stair climbing and performed simple manipulation tasks. The following year, it presented P3, a slightly smaller (at 1.6m) and lighter (160kg) version. The trend continued in 2000 when the company presented Asimo[18]a significantly lighter (52 kg) and shorter (1.2 m) robot. Instead, the focus was on operation safety and more advanced forms of human interaction. An interesting feature introduced by Asimo was the distribution of computational functions over almost 20 CPUs. In Japan, the strategic importance of humanoid research crystallized in the creation of the Humanoid Robotics Project (HRP), funded by the Japanese Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) with Kawada Industries at the forefront. Under this project, a series of full-sized humanoid robots were introduced starting in 2002 with HRP-2[19], a robot that was capable of standing up from laying flat on the floor, followed in 2007 by HRP-3[20]a dust-proof construction, and in 2010 with HRP-4[21]and HRP-4C[22]. As the robots progressed, the focus was on reducing their weight as a way to reduce the risk of operating in a human environment. At ATR Computational Neuroscience Laboratories in Japan, the focus was on producing robots with high capabilities to study the underlying mechanisms of the brain. The resulting robot, CB (Computational Brain)[23], had 50 DoF and a very sophisticated plethora of sensors, remarkable at the time: position and velocity sensors for all joints, torque sensors for main joints in arms, legs, torso and neck, foot force sensors and two inertial measurement units (IMU). Walking and balancing were controlled by an onboard computer while an external cluster of PCs handled vision tasks (too complex for the hardware at that time). At the University of Tokyo, in the development of Kojiro[24],[25]the effort was placed in replicating the complex musculoskeletal human structure, especially the multi-articulated spine structure. This impressive robot provides an excellent opportunity for the development of very complex control models as stated in[25]. At the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, similar full-size robots KHR-1, KHR-2, HUBO[26]and HUBO-2[27]have been designed and built with the purpose of studying complex bipedal walking and robot-human interaction. Importantly, this project aimed at reducing the costs of the platform by using, when possible, readily available parts like motors and harmonic gears and through lightweight design. In Europe, we can note the work at the Technische Universität München where the very ambitious robot Johnnie[28]was developed in early 2001, and later in 2010, LOLA[29]. Both robots were full-size and included custom-designed frames. Moreover, LOLA’s complexity lies in its specialized 8-bit CPU designed for the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, utilizing modern, radiation-hardened technology and undergoing verification processes to ensure reliable operation under varying conditions such as supply voltage, ambient temperature, and in the harsh environment of lunar orbit[30]. In Italy at Instituto Italiano di Tecnologia (IIT) iCub[31], a very ambitious project started in 2008, aimed to push the technological boundaries of complexity to provide researchers with a platform that supports a very high number of degrees of freedom (53 in the latest version) including highly actuated five fingered hands. The robot, while not fully autonomous (it requires an “umbilical cord” for communication and power supply), is equipped with cameras, IMUs, microphones, and speakers, as well as pressure-sensitive skin. The design also includes expressive facial expressions that mimic human emotions. This allows the robot to be used in research beyond “classical” walking and manipulating skills. It should be noted that the robot hardware, software, and documentation are open-source. At the same institute, a full-sized humanoid WALK-MAN[32]was presented in 2017 for participation in the DARPA’s disaster response challenge. The robots mentioned above have rarely been produced beyond a few prototypes and, in general, have been used for research within the labs where they were built. There has been an increasing interest in the last 10-15 years from private enterprises in developing such robots for commercial purposes. One such company is PAL Technologies, based in Spain, which produced a series of full-sized humanoid robots available for purchase. They include REEM-B[33]and REEM-C, focused on human interaction and the study of safe operation in a human environment. Another model, Talos[34], is focused on industrial applications, like those imposed by the DARPA Robotics Challenge. In 2013, NASA introduced a full-sized humanoid robot, Valkyrie[35], that went through a significant number of updates and improvements. In partnership with the Florida Institute for Human and Machine Cognition (IHMC), the robot included advanced walking and control algorithms. Almost all robots mentioned earlier were full-sized or close (1.8m or about). The reasons behind this were multiple: they were mandated by requirements (like in the case of DARPA challenges or when the robot was specifically intended to perform human tasks in a real environment), or the technology available at the time made smaller or lighter designs impossible (ex. computing capabilities, power density, communication) or simply to push the boundaries of engineering and control. The byproduct of this approach was that these platforms were costly, unsuitable for extensive adoption, and severely restricted the ability to study and innovate in this domain. Almost all papers mentioned above raise the point about reducing costs and aim to provide solutions while staying true to the original requirements. At the end of 2000, Sony introduced SDR-3X (Sony Dream Robot)[36]followed in 2003 by SDR-4X (nicknamed QRIO)[37]. These robots aimed at providing a more accessible platform to study locomotion and complex behavior by reducing their size and the mass. These robots have a more limited practicability but represent an excellent tool for a wider community of researchers. Probably the most widely used and recognizable humanoid robot in research is NAO[14], now in the 6th generation. This robot despite its smaller stature (57 cm height and 5.5 kg), managed to pack an impressive 21 or 25 DoF, IMU, four ultrasonic sensors, force-sensing resistors, four directional microphones and speakers, two HD cameras. The robot is supported by a suite of custom software that makes it easier to program custom movements and runs NAOqi, a Linux derivative that includes an easy-to-use Application Store. The robot is a main platform used in the Robocup[38]annual competitions. The robot DARwIn-OP[15], the result of collaboration between Virginia Tech and the Korean company Robotis, added an extra dimension in the pursuit for wide adoption: the whole robot is open-sourced, both hardware and software, and customers can choose to buy or make the robot on their own. The last iteration ROBOTIS OP3 includes 20 DoF, IMU, an HD camera and has only 3.5Kg and 51cm. A very interesting characteristic of this robot is the use of ROS (Robot Operating System)[39]. In recent years, a very important technology has emerged and found its way into robot development: 3D printing. The robot Poppy[40], introduced in 2014, took advantage of this technology to produce the first fully 3D printed open source and open hardware humanoid robot. Despite its rather tall stature (84 cm), it only weighed 3.5 kg thanks to the 3D printed frames and used 25 DoF provided by off-the-shelf actuators supplied by Robotis. This experience is now rolled into the Reachy[41]platform that is available as an highly performant and affordable torso close to the human parameters that provide exciting experimentation in remote manipulation using VR technology. For an overview covering some of these robots, together with some more in-depth technical details was done by[42]. Following the observation that size has an exponential impact on costs, and taking advantage of the advances in embedded systems and 3D printing, our platform, Miha, pushes the envelope further with a design that provides a rich set of capabilities in a very tight budget, without compromising functionality. As a significant difference to previous designs, Miha is intended to be easily produced, even allowing for self-build and customizing.<Materials and Methods>This section will start with an overview of the design principles employed in the build of Miha (Fig. 1), followed by a detailed presentation of the hardware and software capabilities.<Results>To demonstrate the capabilities of our robot, we have implemented some simple walking routines. We should note that the purpose of this paper is to focus on the platform and we do not introduce any novel concepts in bipedal walking. We are planning to leverage the platform for such work in the future, and we hope those interested in humanoid behavior will, too. Miha includes a simple walking controller5based on ZMP[46],[47]. The desired trajectory of the torso is used to calculate the trajectories for legs and arms using the KDL library (see III-D2) and then passed to the direct position controller (see III-D1). For the moment, the controller does not integrate pressure readings or balance adjustments based on the IMU readings. These capabilities will be added in an updated release soon. A video of the robot performing this walking routine can be seen athttps://youtube.com/shorts/TdH9DUi6K8c. Figure 9illustrates an early walking example, showcasing joint trajectories that have not yet been corrected for errors in positioning or distortion in the frames. Despite these initial imperfections, the primary objective of this test was to evaluate the platform’s capability to effectively control the actuators and acquire sensory information at a high frequency. This preliminary demonstration serves as a crucial step in the development process, allowing us to identify areas for improvement and refine our control algorithms. As we continue to iterate and optimize the walking routines, we anticipate achieving smoother and more coordinated locomotion, ultimately enhancing the overall performance and stability of the robot platform. For scripted movements, themh5_behaviourpackage includes aDirectornode that allows experimenters to define movement routines conveniently in XACRO (an XML extension format widely used in ROS) supporting macros and parameters. An example of such a routine (including visualization of robot in RViz) is available athttps://youtu.be/q_ET4ftx0Qk. In addition to the outlined capabilities of our robot platform and the implemented walking routines, several noteworthy observations further highlight its potential and versatility. One of the inherent strengths of our robot platform lies in its modularity and expandability. The design allows for easy integration of additional sensors, actuators, and peripherals, enabling researchers to tailor the platform to suit specific experimental needs. This modularity lays the groundwork for future enhancements and adaptations, facilitating advancements in various domains beyond bipedal locomotion. The incorporation of “near” real-time control mechanisms as provided by the decoupling inros_controlof time-critical operations, like communication with servomotors, as high-priority threads, empowers researchers to interact with the robot dynamically and receive instantaneous feedback. With the current hardware optimization and the choice of SoC we have achieved communication frequencies of 250Hz, resulting in delays of 4ms when processing sensory information or commands. This capability opens avenues for exploring advanced control strategies, adaptive behaviors, and human-robot interaction paradigms. By harnessing “near” real-time data processing and sensor fusion techniques, we can fine-tune the robot’s responses and refine its performance across diverse tasks and environments. Our robot platform serves as an interdisciplinary collaboration, bridging the gap between robotics, computer science, biomechanics, and cognitive science. Its multifaceted nature encourages researchers from various disciplines to converge their expertise and perspectives, fostering innovation and cross-pollination of ideas. Through collaborative efforts, we envision unlocking new insights into humanoid behavior, cognition, and embodiment, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries and technological advancements. Beyond its research-oriented applications, our robot platform holds significant potential for educational initiatives and outreach programs. Its intuitive interface, coupled with educational resources and tutorials, makes it accessible to students, educators, and enthusiasts alike. By engaging learners in hands-on robotics projects and experiential learning experiences, we can inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and innovators, nurturing a passion for robotics and fostering robotics literacy across diverse communities. While our current focus remains on laying the groundwork and establishing foundational capabilities, we remain committed to exploring and harnessing the full spectrum of possibilities that our robot, Miha, affords. To compare the Miha robot to existing literature, we examine several key aspects: affordability, modularity, sensory systems, and control capabilities. O’Hara’s work discusses the advancements in AI integration within humanoid robots, emphasizing the need for platforms to test and develop these technologies[1]. Miha, with its integration of the Robot Operating System (ROS), stands out by providing an ecosystem for AI development. Unlike other platforms, Miha is designed to leverage ROS, offering access to its simulation, visualization, and control tools, which is needed for advancing AI research. In the study by Xiloyannis et al. on soft robotic suits, the focus is on core technologies and challenges in achieving flexible and adaptive movements[2]. Miha’s design incorporates these principles through the use of lightweight materials and advanced actuation, but it also addresses the challenge of cost, making humanoid robotics accessible to a broader range of researchers. By reducing the mass and torque requirements, Miha achieves significant cost savings compared to other robots like NAO and ROBOTIS OP3, positioning itself as a more accessible alternative for academic and industrial research. Gold highlights the importance of open science and the democratization of innovation[3]. Miha aligns with this vision by employing open-source hardware and software, allowing researchers to modify and improve the platform collaboratively. This approach not only reduces costs but also accelerates innovation by fostering a community-driven development model, contrasting with more proprietary systems that can be restrictive and expensive. The work of Hartmann et al. on sustainable robotics emphasizes the importance of environmental considerations in robot design[4]. Miha’s use of readily available components and its power-efficient design contribute to its sustainability. The inclusion of features like hot-swappable batteries and a pressure sensor array that doubles as battery management highlights Miha’s commitment to extending operational life and reducing electronic waste, setting it apart from other platforms that might not prioritize sustainability as highly. In terms of sensory systems, the advancements discussed by Balestrieri et al.[7]and Andrussow et al.[8]are reflected in Miha’s comprehensive sensor suite, which includes high-performance IMUs and pressure sensors. Miha’s sensors enable feedback for locomotion and manipulation tasks, aligning with the latest trends in enhancing robot-environment interactions. Miha’s pressure sensor array, designed specifically for the Dynamixel protocol, offers capabilities comparable to those found in high-end robots like NAO, but at a fraction of the cost. Collaborative robotics, as reviewed by Patil et al.[9], focuses on robots working alongside humans in shared environments. Miha’s modular design and intuitive control interface facilitate such interactions, allowing it to be easily adapted for various collaborative tasks. Its open-source nature and use of ROS also ensure that it can be integrated into existing research frameworks and industrial applications, promoting wider adoption and versatility. Finally, Kantaros et al.[12]and Hossain et al.[13]discuss the impact of 3D printing on reducing costs and making robotics more accessible. Miha leverages this by incorporating 3D-printed components, which not only reduce manufacturing costs but also allow for rapid prototyping and customization. This approach supports the broader trend towards more affordable and customizable robotic platforms, enabling researchers and developers to experiment and iterate more freely. In summary, Miha compares favorably to the literature by addressing key challenges in humanoid robotics through affordability, modularity, advanced sensory systems, and sustainable design. Its integration of ROS, open-source framework, and power management solutions position it as a versatile and accessible platform for advancing research and development in humanoid robotics.<Conclusion>In closing, our paper introduces Miha, an innovative and cost-effective humanoid platform designed to revolutionize research and development in robotics. The inspiration behind Miha’s development was to break down barriers by significantly reducing costs compared to existing solutions, thereby democratizing access to humanoid robotics and standardizing essential control functions. Packed with advanced features including 22 degrees of freedom smart actuators, pressure sensors, inertial measurement units, stereo cameras, multiple microphones, speakers, and a user-friendly 2.4-inch liquid crystal display, Miha embodies versatility for researchers. Its unique dual hot-swap battery design ensures uninterrupted field operation, boasting an impressive 3-hour autonomy on a single charge. Powered by a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 and running the Noetic robot operating system, Miha effortlessly demonstrates various control functions, including walking. Notably, the majority of Miha’s components are off-the-shelf or open-source, fostering accessibility and stimulating collaborative innovation. Looking ahead, our focus shifts towards refining control algorithms, enhancing locomotion capabilities, and integrating cutting-edge sensing and perception technologies. By tackling these challenges head-on, we aim to unleash Miha’s full potential and propel the field of humanoid robotics forward. While our paper primarily highlights Miha’s platform without introducing novel bipedal walking concepts, we envision a future where Miha plays a pivotal role in advancing humanoid behavior studies.Miha’s walking controller, rooted in ZMP principles, leverages torso trajectory to compute leg and arm movements through the KDL library. While our current controller doesn’t yet integrate pressure readings or IMU-based balance adjustments, these enhancements which will be performed in the future are poised to elevate Miha’s versatility and adaptability. As support for real-time improves (both at OS and ROS level) we look at evaluating the implications and possible benefits they might offer for controlling complex humanoid robots.
authors: A. Sonea; N. Goga; R. Cristina Popa; I. Marin; I. Petre; C. Gheorghe; G. Suciu; V. Suciu

title: A biped gait learning algorithm for humanoid robots based on environmental impact assessed artificial bee colony
abstract: Gait pattern performance is a very important issue in the field of humanoid robots, and more and more researchers are now engaged in such studies. However, the tuning processes of the parameters or postures are very tedious and time-consuming. In order to solve this problem, an artificial bee colony (ABC) learning algorithm for a central pattern generator (CPG) gait produce method is proposed in this paper. Furthermore, the fitness of the bee colony is considered through environmental impact assessment, and it is also estimated from the cause of colony collapse disorder from the results of recent investigations in areas, such as pesticides, electromagnetic waves, viruses, and the timing confusion of the bee colony caused by climate change. Each environmental disaster can be considered by its adjustable weighting values. In addition, the developed biped gait learning method is called the ABC-CPG algorithm, and it was verified in a self-developed high-integration simulator. The strategy systems, motion control system, and gait learning system of the humanoid robot are also integrated through the proposed 3-D simulator. Finally, the experimental results show that the proposed environmental-impact-assessed ABC-CPG gait learning algorithm is feasible and can also successfully achieve the best gait pattern in the humanoid robot.
text: <title>A biped gait learning algorithm for humanoid robots based on environmental impact assessed artificial bee colony<abstract>Abstract:Gait pattern performance is a very important issue in the field of humanoid robots, and more and more researchers are now engaged in such studies. However, the tuning processes of the parameters or postures are very tedious and time-consuming. In order to solve this problem, an artificial bee colony (ABC) learning algorithm for a central pattern generator (CPG) gait produce method is proposed in this paper. Furthermore, the fitness of the bee colony is considered through environmental impact assessment, and it is also estimated from the cause of colony collapse disorder from the results of recent investigations in areas, such as pesticides, electromagnetic waves, viruses, and the timing confusion of the bee colony caused by climate change. Each environmental disaster can be considered by its adjustable weighting values. In addition, the developed biped gait learning method is called the ABC-CPG algorithm, and it was verified in a self-developed high-integration simulator. The strategy systems, motion control system, and gait learning system of the humanoid robot are also integrated through the proposed 3-D simulator. Finally, the experimental results show that the proposed environmental-impact-assessed ABC-CPG gait learning algorithm is feasible and can also successfully achieve the best gait pattern in the humanoid robot.<Introduction>Robots have become irreplaceable assistants ever since automatic production became widespread throughout the world. By taking advantage of mechanical techniques and control theories, robots can accomplish heavy or complicated work easily. Creatures demonstrate excellent abilities worth imitating because of undergoing biological evolution over thousands of years, so biomimetic robots are one of the most essential projects in this field. Humanoid robots in particular are the most interesting subject among biomimetic robots. Based on medicine and biology, the development of humanoid robots and artificial intelligence helps people further understand how human beings think and how they react to their environment. Compared with multi-legged animals, creatures that walk on two legs have more difficulty keeping balance. How to make robots walk fast and steadily is the essential issue in developing humanoid robots. Many methods have been proposed to solve this tough problem, including center of pressure (COP)[1], zero moment point (ZMP)[2]–​[11], dynamic walking control[12]–​[14], gait reference generation[15]–​[17], biological inspiration[18],[19], and others. In this paper, the neural oscillator, which is also called the central pattern generator (CPG), is adopted to produce a legged locomotion. The basic idea of CPG comes from observation of animal rhythmic activities and experimentation[20],[21]. Based on reference[22], which applies the neural oscillator model to simulate the walking pattern of biped robots, CPG has become a powerful tool for generating a gait pattern for humanoid robots. The literature[23]presents a center of gravity (CoG) based CPG gait pattern generator; however, the real CoG of the robot cannot be obtained precisely, and the walking speed is slow. Reference[24]also presents a CPG based solution for passive dynamic models. However, this solution is hard to apply to a server motor based humanoid robot. CPG-inspired workspace trajectory generation for quadruped robots is also present in[25]. This approach can accomplish locomotion control in four-legged robots, but it is hard to implement in biped robots. In previous research, particle swarm optimization (PSO)[26]and fuzzy policy gradient learning (FPGL)[27],[28]have been used in robots for them to learn a walking pattern. FPGL is characterized by its quick convergence with a small number of experiences, but it gets trapped in a local minima result easily. In addition, the initial motion critically affects the learning result of FPGL, and so this is not close to becoming a general method depending on the experience of the operator. On the other hand, swarm intelligence as PSO is a good way to search for a global optimal solution. However, it is shown in[29]that the convergence rate of PSO is lower than that of ABC. Therefore, we introduce the artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm[29]–​[31]to search for the best parameters for CPG. In this paper, an environmental impact assessed ABC-CPG biped gait learning algorithm is proposed to solve this problem. In recent years, a strange phenomenon has spread around the world, which is that the collectives of bees are suddenly and mysteriously disappearing. Bee experts call this phenomenon, colony collapse disorder (CCD)[32]. Benjamin and McCallum wrote a book,A World Without Bees[33], to explore such issues. Moreover, Einstein predicted, “If the bee disappeared off the surface of the globe, then man would only have four years of life left[33].” This issue also appeared on the cover of Time Magazine on August 19, 2013[34]. However, the cause of CCD has still not been fully determined; experts generally agree that this phenomenon is caused by a number of factors such as pesticides, electromagnetic waves, viruses, and the timing confusion of the bee colony caused by climate change. This ecological catastrophe shows that the living requirements of bees are not only defined by the source of their food; the more important condition is environmental pollution. Therefore, the environmental impact should be considered if we want to apply the ABC algorithm to solve some problems. In this paper, the ABC-CPG gait learning algorithm will take into consideration the impact of food, environmental pollution, and time sequence on the living environment of bees. All the fitness functions can basically be defined by these impacts, where the degree of timing confusion is calculated by the waveform alignment technique, called dynamic time warping (DTW)[35]. It is worth mentioning that the gait of the robot can become more stable using the DTW method. Robots can search appropriate CPG parameters according to the weighting values of these fitness functions. On the other hand, if one wants to design an adult-sized humanoid robot to attend a robot competition, for example, the FIRA RoboWorld Cup[36]or RoboCup[37], this team usually has only one robot, which mainly leads to two problems. One is that a new technique is not easily tried on the robot and the team members have to assess the risk of the robot getting damaged; the other is that the robot must accomplish many tasks but team members cannot conduct different testing at the same time. Both problems slow down the research and development, so a simulator plays a role in offering a good and convenient testing environment, where various methods can be evaluated and examined. In the end, only the methods which can be successfully implemented in the simulator are worth applying to real applications. The simulator developed in this paper is constructed with Open Graph Library (OpenGL)[38]and Open Dynamic Engine (ODE)[39]. We focus on the application of biped gait learning, human-machine systems, and simulating the strategies of FIRA RoboWorld Cup and RoboCup competitions. By utilizing this 3D simulator, our robot, David II, won the championship in the technical challenge competition in the 2013 RoboCup Japan Open; the championship in the all-round competition in the 2013 FIRA RoboWorld Cup held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; and the high technology robot competition at the 2013 International Robot Contest held in Seoul, South Korea. The major contributions of this paper are 1) proposing a novel environmental impact assessed concept to determine the fitness functions of the gait learning algorithm; 2) using the ABC algorithm to figure out the best parameters of CPG for the humanoid robot; 3) developing an integrated 3D simulator to verify the gait learning algorithm and strategy systems of the robot soccer competitions; and 4) presenting the feasibility and practicality of the proposed 3D simulator and ABC-CPG gait learning method. This paper is organized as follows. InSection II, the CPG method and inverse kinematics of the robot are introduced. The overview of the ABC algorithm, DTW, and environmental impact assessment method are described inSection III. The humanoid robot simulation system is depicted inSection IV. InSection V, the experimental results of ABC-CPG gait learning are presented to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed learning method.Section VIconcludes the paper.<CPG Based Gait Locomotion>The locomotion of animals is executed by serial signals from the cerebellum and vertebrae. Based on this concept, in robotic research, CPG is used to create the gait pattern. Thus, CPG is also one kind of neural systems, and it is a feasible way to make robots move with a stable locomotion. The inverse kinematics of the robot and CPG method are addressed as follows.<ABC-CPG Gait Learning>Because of the fast convergence speed, the ABC algorithm is applied in this paper to gait learning to find the best parameters of CPG. Also, the overview of the ABC algorithm and the proposed concept of the environmental impact assessment are introduced in the following subsections.<Humanoid Robot Simulation System>In this section, the entire architecture and function of the simulator are introduced. Open Dynamic Engine (ODE) is a powerful free library, and it is usually used to simulate a collision event in academic research. In order to make the simulation system more elastic and efficient, it is separated into two processing systems, simulating and rendering. Also, according to the user’s preference in the “.NET” framework environment, the operation interface can be modified easily. Therefore, the developmental scalability of the simulator can be much more promoted. In addition, developers could show simulating information on the interface. And the work of rendering is implemented by OpenGL.Fig. 8shows that it would be very convenient to directly combine the simulator with other software which has been built, such as competition strategy system or human-machine interface (HMI), and it is not necessary to rewrite any program again.<Experimental Results>In this section, two parts of the experiments are illustrated briefly. Part A is the results for ABC-CPG gait learning, and Part B is the demonstration for the RoboCup soccer game. Finally, other competition configurations of the proposed simulator are also addressed.<Conclusions>Since the ZMP method needs a lot of highly accurate sensor information, CPG is chosen as a more practical way to generate biped leg locomotion. By setting two coupled oscillators, three dimensional outputs of CPG, which are decided on the position of the robot’s ankles and the angular position of each leg joint, can be figured out with inverse kinematics. In terms of learning, ABC is a good way to find an optimal solution for obtaining the best CPG parameters. In fact, the learning method is one of the keys, and the determination of the fitness functions is especially significant because all the results evolve by these fitness values. Therefore, in order to determine the appropriate fitness functions and make the gait pattern more stable, a novel environmental impact assessed method is proposed in this paper; its concept is inspired by the cause of CCD. The experimental results have demonstrated that the ABC-CPG gait learning method is feasible and effective. In addition, a highly integrated 3D simulator for the humanoid robot has been developed and applied to the biped gait learning system, human-machine interface, and strategy system in this paper. The developed simulator has strong practicability and operability for robotics research and preparation for robot competitions. Also, the practicality and performance of the developed simulator has received good validations at the 2013 RoboCup Japan Open Tokyo, the 2013 FIRA RoboWorld Cup, and the 2013 International Robot title: Experimental Evaluation of the Impact of Physical Space Information on Wireless Link Quality Estimation
abstract: Predicting wireless link quality (LQ) is a promising approach to enhancing Quality of Experience (QoE). This paper examines the impact of physical space on LQ; it uses machine learning to predict RSSI and throughput from physical space information. Experiments show that the position/orientation of user equipment (UE) are crucial, with orientation affecting RSSI, and velocity significantly impacting throughput. It is revealed that these LQ parameters have different spatial factor dependencies. An experiment is conducted in a static indoor environment with clear line of sight to simplify the problem. We focus on deriving LQ from current physical space information rather than forecasting future quality.
text: <title>Experimental Evaluation of the Impact of Physical Space Information on Wireless Link Quality Estimation<abstract>Abstract:Predicting wireless link quality (LQ) is a promising approach to enhancing Quality of Experience (QoE). This paper examines the impact of physical space on LQ; it uses machine learning to predict RSSI and throughput from physical space information. Experiments show that the position/orientation of user equipment (UE) are crucial, with orientation affecting RSSI, and velocity significantly impacting throughput. It is revealed that these LQ parameters have different spatial factor dependencies. An experiment is conducted in a static indoor environment with clear line of sight to simplify the problem. We focus on deriving LQ from current physical space information rather than forecasting future quality.<Introduction>The rapid advances in mobile devices have driven a signifi-cant increase in demand for new mobile multimedia services, such as video games, ultra-high-definition video, and aug-mented reality (AR). These services, which offer immersive and interactive experiences, necessitate high communication quality to achieve the desired Quality of Experience (QoE) as perceived by users[1]. However, maintaining sta-ble communication quality in wireless environments can be challenging, with issues like signal interruptions and latency frequently. Various technical measures have been developed to address these challenges and prevent degradation in communication quality. Traditional techniques to mitigating communication qual-ity degradation, such as handover, beam forming, fast session transfer, and Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS), primarily focus on the reactive approach. These techniques control communication after the link quality has already begun to deteriorate, which can be insufficient in scenarios where timely intervention is crucial. As a result, there is a growing need for proactive measures that anticipate and address potential issues before they affect communication quality. Predicting future link quality and implementing preemptive controls based on these predictions are therefore essential for ensuring reliable wireless communication. In this context, the use of machine learning (ML) for predicting wireless communication quality, or Link Quality (LQ), has gained considerable attention[2]. Machine learning models excel at identifying patterns and trends within large datasets, enabling accurate predictions and informed decision-making. However, the collection and management of big data incur significant costs, underscoring the impor-tance of efficient data collection strategies. It is crucial to define which types of data should be collected to maximize the effectiveness of machine learning models while mini-mizing resource expenditure. Existing research has focused on the impact of various physical spatial factors-such as the position, velocity, and orientation of mobile terminals or surrounding objects-on communication quality[3],[4]. Furthermore, when a mobile terminal is carried by a user, it has been demonstrated that the presence and behavior of the user can also affect LQ[4]. These studies have provided valuable insights, yet several important questions remain unanswered. Specifically, it is not fully understood which physical spatial factors are most critical in influencing communication quality variations, nor is it clear whether different types of communication quality parameters require different kinds of spatial information for accurate prediction. The present study aims to address these gaps by investigating the specific impact of various physical spatial factors on the accuracy of LQ predictions in a single-terminal wire-less communication environment. To simplify the problem, the study assumes a controlled environment with a clear line of sight between the base station and the device, with no other moving objects other than the wireless device itself. The focus of this research is on predicting LQ based on current physical space information rather than forecasting future quality. This study emphasizes two key indicators of wireless communication quality: Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) and throughput. RSSI is widely recognized in communication quality research for its relevance to signal strength, while throughput is closely related to QoE, making it a critical parameter for assessing the user experience in real-world applications. The rest of this paper is organized as follows.Section 2describes the overall architecture of the system and the data being utilized.Section 3introduces the experimental setup.Section 4discusses the performance evaluation results, andSection 5concludes this paper.<Experimental Setup>We developed a Humanoid model with dielectric constant equivalent to that of the human body to reproduce the im- pact of the human body holding a user equipment (UE) on LQ (Fig. 3(a)). It had a PC as a terminal in a back-pack that measures LQ L[t] at time t. The humanoid stood on a two-wheeled robot and movement control was imple-mented using the Robot Operating System (ROS)[6]. The position and angular information within the terminal states information were calculated using Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization (AMCL) based on point clouds acquired from the Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) unit mounted on the humanoid. Figure 3(b) shows the map of the indoor experimental environment. The humanoid conducted random walk; when the robot reached the current goal position, the next goal position was randomly selected from among the 7 other goal points. Table Ilists the experimental parameters. The experi-ment was conducted in an IEEE 802.11ac Wi-Fi environ-ment using the 5 GHz band[7]. Both LQ information and physical space information were collected at the rate of 10 samples/sec. Data acquisition was performed over a duration of 6 hours, with 80% of the data used for training the LQ estimation model, 2% for validation, and 18% for testing.<Experimental Results and Discussion>Six features of the UE's own physical space information, namely position coordinates{x[t], y[t]}, orientation{kz[t],w[t]}, and velocity{v[t],w[t]}, were divided into three categories, position coordinates, velocity, and orien-tation, and their effects on the performance of estimating wireless communication quality were evaluated. We compared the estimation accuracy when position coordinates, velocity, and orientation information were input, and when only position coordinates and orientation, position and ve-locity, and position were input.Figures 4(a)and 4(b) show cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the absolute er-ror between the predicted and measured values when RSSI and Throughput were used as the estimation targets, respec-tively. in the case of RSSI, the 50% CDF value was 0.461 dB when the estimation was made with information on position coordinates, orientation, and speed, and 0.468 dB when po-sition and orientation were used; the accuracy was basically the same. For Throughput, on the other hand, the CDF 50% value was 4.68 Mbps when predictions used position coordi-nates, orientation, and velocity information, and 8.54 Mbps when position and orientation were used. Adding veloc-ity information to the input values improved the CDF 50% value (absolute error) by 3.86 Mbps. This indicates that throughput is influenced by velocity and angular velocity. Additionally, when comparing the reduction in absolute error between estimations made using only position infor-mation, position and orientation information, and position and velocity information, the improvement forRSSIestimation was 0.16 dB in the former case and 0.09 dB in the latter. This indicates that changes in orientation have a greater impact on RSSI variation than changes in the device's speed. In contrast, for throughput estimation, the absolute error de-creased by 3.88 Mbps when using position and orientation information, while it decreased by 6.52 Mbps when using position and velocity information. This demonstrates that the device's speed has a stronger influence on throughput variation than orientation. Figures 4(c) and 4(d) show IF for each feature when all category information is input. The results show that for both RSSI and Throughput, the position coordinates are most im-portant, followed by orientation. However, the importance of the velocity category{v[t],w[t]}was found to be more important in the case of Throughput than RSSI. These re-sults, as in the previous paragraph, indicate that RSSI is mainly determined by the physical location of the terminal, and is less influenced by velocity and angular velocity, while Throughput is more more dependent on velocity and angular velocity parameters. The results indicate that the terminal's position information was the most critical factor, contributing significantly to the accuracy of LQ estimation. Additionally, orientation was identified as a valuable parameter for enhancing estimation accuracy, as it influenced shielding and other propagation conditions. This is especially important when the UE is held by a human, as channel blockage caused by the user's body can occur, making orientation information crucial for accurate LQ estimation. In contrast to the findings observed in the RSSI estimations, the greater influence of speed on throughput estimation can be attributed to factors such as Doppler shift and fading. Since RSSI is primarily determined by the positional relationship between the device and the base station, the effect of speed on RSSI was relatively small. However, in the case of throughput, as the device's speed increases, the channel con-ditions fluctuate rapidly, potentially causing adaptive modu-lation and coding to function sub optimally, which could lead to the selection of lower modulation schemes. As a result, it can be inferred that the device's speed has a significant impact on throughput variation.<Conclusion>In this study, the physical space information of the UE was decomposed into three categories with six features: position coordinates, orientation, and speed; their effects on the per-formance of LQ estimation were evaluated. The evaluation focused on scenarios where the UE was possessed by a hu-man in an indoor environment. As for the LQ, RSSI, which indicates the radio wave status, and throughput, which deter-mines the application experience quality, were selected. The experiment was conducted in a Wi-Fi environment using the 5 GHz band. The results showed how each feature category affects the estimation of RSSI and throughput. Location was shown to be the most IF, contributing the most to the accuracy ofLQestimation. Orientation was also identified as a beneficial parameter for improving estimation accuracy, as it is determinative of shielding and other prop-agation conditions. On the other hand, terminal movement speed and angular velocity were found to have no direct impact on RSSI estimation quality, but they were found to have an important impact on Throughput.

title: Foot Placement Compensator Design for Humanoid Walking Based on Discrete Control Lyapunov Function
abstract: In this paper, an online foot position compensator (FPC) is proposed for improving the robustness of humanoid walking based on orbital energy conservation and discrete control Lyapunov function (DCLF), with which the asymptotic stability of the humanoid system can be maintained and, thus, the foot placement control is achieved. The online FPC is developed based on linear model predictive control (MPC) by replanning the trajectories of the center of mass (CoM) and properly placing the footsteps to resist external disturbances and recover the walking posture. To further improve the robustness of the humanoid robots to suppress strong external disturbance, a strategy of upper body posture control is proposed. The presented controller stabilizes the humanoid robot by utilizing hip joints to modulate the upper body posture online. Webots simulations and real experiments on a full-body NAO humanoid robot verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

title: Time-Varying Foot Placement Control for Humanoid Walking on Swaying Rigid Surface
abstract: Locomotion on dynamic rigid surface (i.e., rigid surface accelerating in an inertial frame) presents complex challenges for controller design, which are essential to address for deploying humanoid robots in dynamic real-world environments such as moving trains, ships, and airplanes. This article introduces a real-time, provably stabilizing control approach for humanoid walking on periodically swaying rigid surface. The first key contribution is an analytical extension of the classical angular momentum-based linear inverted pendulum model from static to swaying grounds whose motion period may be different than the robot’s gait period. This extension results in a time-varying, nonhomogeneous robot model, which is fundamentally different from the existing pendulum models. We synthesize a discrete footstep control law for the model and derive a new set of sufficient stability conditions that verify the controller’s stabilizing effect. Finally, experiments conducted on a Digit humanoid robot, both in simulations and on hardware, demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in addressing bipedal locomotion on swaying ground, even under uncertain surface motions and unknown external pushes.
text: <title>Time-Varying Foot Placement Control for Humanoid Walking on Swaying Rigid Surface<abstract>Abstract:Locomotion on dynamic rigid surface (i.e., rigid surface accelerating in an inertial frame) presents complex challenges for controller design, which are essential to address for deploying humanoid robots in dynamic real-world environments such as moving trains, ships, and airplanes. This article introduces a real-time, provably stabilizing control approach for humanoid walking on periodically swaying rigid surface. The first key contribution is an analytical extension of the classical angular momentum-based linear inverted pendulum model from static to swaying grounds whose motion period may be different than the robot’s gait period. This extension results in a time-varying, nonhomogeneous robot model, which is fundamentally different from the existing pendulum models. We synthesize a discrete footstep control law for the model and derive a new set of sufficient stability conditions that verify the controller’s stabilizing effect. Finally, experiments conducted on a Digit humanoid robot, both in simulations and on hardware, demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in addressing bipedal locomotion on swaying ground, even under uncertain surface motions and unknown external pushes.<Introduction>Locomotion is a fundamental capability of legged robots, enabling them to navigate diverse environments to perform various real-world tasks, such as warehouse automation, home assistance, package delivery, and search and rescue. Although robust walking on complex yet static terrains such as slopes[1], stairs[2], and gravel[3]has been extensively studied, the focus has primarily been on overcoming significant challenges in controller design due to the inherently unstable, hybrid, nonlinear dynamics of legged robots, compounded by uncertainties such as terrain irregularities. Conversely, bipedal locomotion on dynamic rigid surface (DRS)—rigid surface that moves within an inertial frame, such as those on buses, vessels, and airplanes—remains relatively underexplored. This is despite the critical importance of such capabilities in scenarios involving firefighting, inspection, maintenance, disinfection, and emergency response on container ships, naval vessels, moving transportation vehicles, airplanes, and oil platforms. Current robust controllers designed for static terrains may only handle mild DRS motions and are prone to failure under more intense or prolonged DRS movements. For instance, as depicted in Fig.1, the proprietary controller of the Digit humanoid robot fails to maintain stable locomotion under moderate DRS sway. The primary issue is that omitting explicit consideration of surface motion results in the motion acting as a temporally persistent disturbance, giving the robot insufficient recovery time. This may induce excessive control actions that exceed the robot’s actuator capabilities, leading to potential instability and safety risks. As one of the earliest attempts to solve these open control problems of humanoid locomotion on DRS, this article introduces a control framework that explicitly incorporates DRS motion into the dynamic modeling and controller design of the robot. Our approach not only aims to enable stable locomotion on DRS for legged robots but also seeks to offer performance guarantees through provable stabilization of the walking dynamics associated with DRS locomotion.<ALIP-DRS Model>This section describes the derivation of the proposed ALIP-DRS model for bipedal walking on swaying DRS. The key to the derivation is the analytical extension of the classical ALIP model[15]from static to dynamic terrain, achieved by explicitly incorporating the DRS sway in the model. This incorporation leads to the distinct time-varying and nonhomogeneous nature of the ALIP-DRS. Also, we explicitly consider the discrete robot dynamics at foot-landing events, which allows us to exploit foot placement in the controller design to ensure ALIP-DRS’s stability. This consideration results in the hybrid nature of the ALIP-DRS. Fig.2illustrates the 3-D ALIP-DRS.<ALIP-DRS Footstep Control and Stability Analysis>This section introduces the discrete footstep control and stability analysis for the ALIP-DRS. The controller serves as the higher layer planner of a hierarchical control framework, which indirectly stabilizes the unactuated dynamics of a walking robot, as detailed in SectionIV. The design of this controller builds upon the existing footstep controller[15], adapting it from the classical ALIP model to the proposed ALIP-DRS model, as discussed in SectionIII-A. Given that the previous stability conditions of LIP models are not suitable for ALIP-DRS (Remark2), new conditions are introduced in SectionsIII-B.<Hierarchical Control Framework>This section explains the proposed hierarchical control framework designed to achieve stable humanoid walking during DRS sway. While the three-layer structure of this framework is standard[15], the key novelty of the framework lies in its utilization of the proposed ALIP-DRS footstep control law as a higher layer footstep planner. As shown in Fig.6, the framework is structured into three layers to ensure the computational efficiency for real-time motion generation while guaranteeing stability for the complex full-order robot dynamics associated with humanoid walking on DRS. Its higher layer footstep planner uses the proposed ALIP-DRS footstep controller in(20)to generate the desired footstep locations in real-time. The middle layer produces the task-space reference trajectories for the full-order robot model that agree with the desired footstep positions supplied by the higher layer. These trajectories also conform to the simplifying assumptions of the ALIP-DRS, such as the constant CoM height, which minimizes discrepancies between the reduced-order ALIP-DRS and the full-order robot model. This alignment ensures that the desired footstep positions provided by the higher layer are physically feasible for the actual robot to follow, indirectly supporting the stabilization of the full-order robot model, as detailed in the next section. The lower layer controller ensures that the actual robot faithfully executes the planned full-body trajectories. The stability of the complete full-order system under this hierarchical control framework is analyzed in SectionV.<Stability Analysis for Full-Order Model>This section introduces the stability analysis for the hybrid closed-loop full-order system under the proposed framework. The stability of the closed-loop full-order system needs to be analyzed, as it is not automatically guaranteed by the proposed control framework. This necessity arises because the framework does not explicitly treat the inevitable inaccuracy in the ALIP-DRS model. While the higher layer planner of the framework stabilizes the ALIP-DRS model, which approximates the unactuated dynamics, the planner does not directly stabilize the complete nonlinear model of the unactuated subsystem. Meanwhile, the lower layer controller regulates the fully actuated output-function dynamics but does not directly influence the unactuated subsystem. Given the nonlinear and hybrid nature of the full-order robot model, the proposed stability analysis employs Lyapunov functions[46]. Without loss of generality, this analysis considers the IO-QP controller(33)as the framework’s lower layer. The analysis also considers the general case where$N_{1}T_{\text{step}}=N_{2}T_{x,\text{DRS}}=T_{\text{sys}}$.<Simulation Validation>This section reports simulations performed on a Digit robot inmatlab, validating the proposed approach under various surface motions and uncertainties. Simulation validation is necessary as it enables us to evaluate the proposed framework beyond the physical limitations of hardware experiments, such as the frequency and magnitude constraints of the DRS movement.<Hardware Experiment Validation>This section presents the hardware experiment results that validate the stability, tracking performance, and robustness of humanoid walking under the proposed framework. Due to hardware constraints, such as the limited surface area and motion capabilities of the physical DRS, the locomotion tasks and DRS motions implemented in the experiments differ from those in the simulation cases. Still, the framework is tested under different DRS motion frequencies and directions, and is also evaluated in the presence of various uncertainties, including sudden pushes and uncertain surface motions. A video of the experiments is available online.1<Discussion>This section discusses the capabilities and limitations of the proposed control approach, as well as potential directions for future research. To control bipedal walking on swaying DRS, this study introduces a new reduced-order robot model, ALIP-DRS, to approximate the associated hybrid, nonlinear, time-varying, nonhomogeneous unactuated robot dynamics. The key novelty of this model lies in its explicit consideration of the DRS sway motion. Due to the DRS sway, the ALIP-DRS is time-varying and nonhomogeneous, fundamentally different from the classical LIP and its variations (see Remark2). The close alignment between Digit’s unactuated movement variables and the ALIP-DRS’s trajectories is confirmed through both simulations (see Figs.8,9,11, and12) and hardware experiments (see Figs.15–​17and19), highlighting the reasonable accuracy of the ALIP-DRS. Also, thanks to its generality, this model can be readily generalized to other legged robot platforms beyond humanoids. In addition, the stability for the closed-loop ALIP-DRS model under discrete footstep control is provably verified based on the stability of its homogeneous portion. The previously developed stability conditions for existing LIP models, which are time-invariant or homogeneous, are not directly applicable to the time-varying and nonhomogeneous ALIP-DRS. The proposed stability analysis, based on the general stability theory of linear impulsive nonhomogeneous systems, can be generalized to continuous control of pendulum models and to alternative state variables beyond those considered in this study. The study also introduces a hierarchical control framework that incorporates the ALIP-DRS’s foot placement controller as its higher layer footstep planner. By stabilizing the ALIP-DRS, the discrete controller indirectly stabilizes the actual unactuated dynamics of the robot during walking. The stability conditions for the complete full-order system under the control framework are also provided. Due to their general applicability, these conditions can be extended to prior LIP-based hierarchical approaches[15]. Experimental results confirm that the proposed framework achieves stable walking under various DRS sway motions and uncertainties. Building on these theoretical findings, future work will extend the stability conditions of the ALIP-DRS model to accommodate DRS motions in both vertical and horizontal directions. In the presence of vertical and horizontal surface motions, the hybrid ALIP-DRS model(13)will be updated with a time-varying matrix$\mathbf {A}_{x}$, whose explicit time dependence is induced by vertical surface motion[34],[49]. The stability conditions for this generalized ALIP-DRS model will be developed by integrating the stability analysis from this study with that for locomotion control on vertical surface motions. This future research will address the observed deviation between the actual robot state and the ideal ALIP-DRS model during unknown DRS pitching motions (see Fig.19). Moreover, future efforts will explore real-time surface motion estimation using onboard robot sensors, so as to enable the proposed hierarchical control framework to adapt more effectively to unknown surface motions and further enhance locomotion robustness. Finally, since real-world dynamic ground motions (e.g., ship movement[34]) can usually be approximated as piecewise periodic time functions, we can apply the proposed hierarchical control framework to each periodic segment of the ground motion based on the specific profile of each segment. To provide theoretical guarantee for this gait composition approach, we can theoretically extend the proposed footstep planner and its underlying stability conditions by drawing on existing stability analysis for walking on static terrains, such as the analysis based on composite limit cycles[23].<Conclusion>This article has introduced a real-time, provably stabilizing control approach that employs a novel reduced-order robot model to enable bipedal walking on a swaying DRS. Specifically, the classical ALIP model was analytically extended to explicitly account for time-varying DRS motion, whose frequency may differ from the robot’s gait frequency. A discrete-time footstep control strategy was constructed, which was proven to be exponentially stabilizing for the ALIP-DRS model. With the ALIP-DRS footstep controller serving as a motion planner that generates the desired swing-foot landing positions in real-time, a hierarchical control framework was developed for the full-order robot model. The closed-loop stability conditions for the hybrid full-order control system were constructed by analyzing both the unactuated and fully actuated subsystems under the proposed control framework. Both numerical simulations and hardware experiments on a Digit humanoid robot confirmed that the proposed ALIP-DRS model is reasonably accurate in describing the unactuated dynamics of the actual robot. Further, the proposed framework achieved stable walking under various DRS sway motions, and demonstrated high robustness under different uncertainties including sudden pushes and inaccurately known or unknown DRS motions in different directions.
authors: Y. Gao; V. Paredes; Y. Gong; Z. He; A. Hereid; Y. Gu

title: Repeatable Folding Task by Humanoid Robot Worker Using Deep Learning
abstract: We propose a practical state-of-the-art method to develop a machine-learning-based humanoid robot that can work as a production line worker. The proposed approach provides an intuitive way to collect data and exhibits the following characteristics: task performing capability, task reiteration ability, generalizability, and easy applicability. The proposed approach utilizes a real-time user interface with a monitor and provides a first-person perspective using a head-mounted display. Through this interface, teleoperation is used for collecting task operating data, especially for tasks that are difficult to be applied with a conventional method. A two-phase deep learning model is also utilized in the proposed approach. A deep convolutional autoencoder extracts images features and reconstructs images, and a fully connected deep time delay neural network learns the dynamics of a robot task process from the extracted image features and motion angle signals. The “Nextage Open” humanoid robot is used as an experimental platform to evaluate the proposed model. The object folding task utilizing with 35 trained and 5 untrained sensory motor sequences for test. Testing the trained model with online generation demonstrates a 77.8% success rate for the object folding task.
