title: Development and Investigation of Vision System for a Small-Sized Mobile Humanoid Robot in a Smart Environment
abstract: The conducted research aims to develop a computer vision system for a small-sized mobile humanoid robot. The decentralization of the servomotor control and the computer vision systems is investigated based on the hardware solution point of view, moreover, the required software level to achieve an efficient matched design is obtained. A computer vision system using the upgraded tiny-You Only Look Once (YOLO) network model is developed to allow recognizing and identifying objects and making decisions on interacting with them, which is recommended for crowd environment. During the research, a concept of a computer vision system was developed, which describes the interaction between the main elements, on the basis of which hardware modules were selected to implement the task. A structure of information interaction between hardware modules is proposed, and a connection scheme is developed, on the basis of which a model of a computer vision system is assembled for research, with the required algorithmic and software for solving the problem. To ensure the high speed of the computer vision system based on the ESP32-CAM module, the neural network was improved by replacing the Visual Geometry Group 16 (VGG-16) network as the base network for extracting the functions of the Single Shot Detector (SSD) network model with the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model, which made it possible to preserve the multidimensional structure of the network model feature graph, resulting in increasing the detection accuracy, while significantly reducing the amount of calculations generated by the network operation, thereby significantly increasing the detection speed, due to a limited set of objects. Finally, a number of experiments were carried out, both in static and dynamic environments, which showed a high accuracy of identifications.
text: <title>Development and Investigation of Vision System for a Small-Sized Mobile Humanoid Robot in a Smart Environment<abstract>Abstract:The conducted research aims to develop a computer vision system for a small-sized mobile humanoid robot. The decentralization of the servomotor control and the computer vision systems is investigated based on the hardware solution point of view, moreover, the required software level to achieve an efficient matched design is obtained. A computer vision system using the upgraded tiny-You Only Look Once (YOLO) network model is developed to allow recognizing and identifying objects and making decisions on interacting with them, which is recommended for crowd environment. During the research, a concept of a computer vision system was developed, which describes the interaction between the main elements, on the basis of which hardware modules were selected to implement the task. A structure of information interaction between hardware modules is proposed, and a connection scheme is developed, on the basis of which a model of a computer vision system is assembled for research, with the required algorithmic and software for solving the problem. To ensure the high speed of the computer vision system based on the ESP32-CAM module, the neural network was improved by replacing the Visual Geometry Group 16 (VGG-16) network as the base network for extracting the functions of the Single Shot Detector (SSD) network model with the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model, which made it possible to preserve the multidimensional structure of the network model feature graph, resulting in increasing the detection accuracy, while significantly reducing the amount of calculations generated by the network operation, thereby significantly increasing the detection speed, due to a limited set of objects. Finally, a number of experiments were carried out, both in static and dynamic environments, which showed a high accuracy of identifications.<General Concept of Mobile Robot Computer Vision Control System>Analyzing the specifics and complexity of the developed mobile humanoid robot, the authors decided to apply a decentralized approach to the control system by dividing the humanoid robot motion control system and the computer vision system into separate modules. Grounding for this decision was next: the bandwidth of the video channel increases, which reduces the signal delay time in the computer vision system; and the load on the resolution capabilities of the microcontroller module of the servomotor control system is reduced, which speeds up the execution of commands. All actions for recognition and identification using AI, as well as algorithms for making decisions and interacting with the outside world and objects, are implemented on a personal computer (notebook). At the first step in solving the problem, it is necessary to develop a general concept for the control system implementation, which should include a computer vision module and will be used to transfer the video stream to the laptop and return commands to interact with objects (ball).Figure 1shows the general concept for the control system implementation for a mobile humanoid robot. The basic idea of this concept is the development of a decentralized control system, that is, its division into two subsystems. Very strong restrictions on the overall dimensions of the humanoid robot became grounding for this decision. As a result, four main modules will be placed on the basis of the humanoid robot: wireless communication module; camera module; control module; and power module. Wireless communication module allows to exchange data between a humanoid robot and a control system, decision-making using wireless Local Area Network (LAN) technologies[17]. Camera module will perform the function of broadcasting the mobile robot environment using wireless network technologies. Control module is designed to execute commands that the module receives from the control and decision-making system, which is located on a personal computer (notebook). An additional task of the control module is to implement the ability to connect servomotors, which will provide freedom of action for the humanoid robot to perform the tasks. Power module provides a small-sized battery assembly, which will be used to power a humanoid robot. On the basis of a personal computer (notebook), it is proposed to create a control and decision-making system, and this decision is justified by the fact that the development of an object recognition and identification system, as well as a decision-making system, requires “serious” computing power that cannot be placed on the basis of a humanoid robot. As a result, this subsystem consists of the following modules: wireless communication module; streaming video processing module; image recognition module; object identification module; and decision module. Streaming video processing module is designed for primary processing of streaming video received from a humanoid robot and preparing it for the recognition module. Image recognition module processes the received streaming video, divides it into frames, and recognizes the presence of objects in the frame. The object identification module uses the neural networks to identify the robot's nearby objectives, i.e., the objectives located in the robot's working zone. Consequently, the object identification module gives the suggested name of the identified object and the accuracy of the suggestion. Decision module analyzes the results obtained with the object identification module and, depending on the underlying algorithm, performs interaction actions with the object.<Selection of Hardware Modules for the Robot's Computer Vision Control System>The humanoid mobile robot “Vivi” by Doctors of Intelligence and Technology LTD is used as a model for conducting research. Overall dimensions are: height is 200 mm; width is 72.2 mm; arm length (from shoulder to hand) is 105 mm; movement provides 18 servomotors model EMax ES08MAII. Based on the concept proposed above for a computer vision system for a humanoid robot (Fig. 1), at the beginning of development, it is necessary to discuss the restrictions that are imposed when choosing hardware modules, on the basis of which the camera module and control module will be implemented. Dimension: Camera module is no more than$30\ \text{mm} \times 45\ \text{mm} \times 15\ \text{mm} (\text{width}\times \text{length} \times \text{height})$. Control module is no more than$54\ \text{mm} \times 51\ \text{mm} \times 7\ \text{mm} (\text{width}\times \text{length} \times \text{height})$. Power: Camera module working voltage is 5 V, and average current is 180 mA (max); Control module working voltage is 4.5-6.4 V, and average current is 80 mA (min). Wireless communication module: WiFi 802.11 b/g/n support for camera module and control module. Required camera module features are as follows: Connection of a camera with the ability to transmit streaming video with a minimum resolution of$800\ \text{pixel}\ \times 600\ \text{pixel}$30 frames per second (fps); The ability to create an access point to a wireless network based on the module. Required control module functions are as follows: Power supply support for up to 18 Emax ES08MA II servomotors[18]; The maximum average current (when 18 servomotors are working) can reach 2800 mA. The rationale for the selected restrictions and their values are the overall dimensions of the humanoid robot: total$72\ \text{mm} \times 200\ \text{mm} \times 80\ \text{mm}. (\text{width}\times \text{length} \times \text{height})$and body dimensions$40\ \text{mm} \times 55\ \text{mm} \times 80\ \text{mm} (\text{width}\times\ \text{length} \times \text{height})$I, which should accommodate control module, camera module, and power module. As a result, the developed solution has a rigid framework for the analysis and selection of hardware modules. First, we will analyze and select a hardware module for the implementation of the camera module, and based on the above limitations, the following modules were selected, which are shown inFig. 2, and their parameters are presented inTable 2. Having carried out a comparative analysis of the parameters of hardware modules (Table 2) for the implementation of a computer vision system for a humanoid robot, we can identify the following advantages and disadvantages for solving the problem. The OV7670 VGA hardware module fits the overall dimensions and has an attractive price (5 US dollar). However, it has a number of disadvantages, such as the absence of a wireless network module and a microcontroller-based module for primary processing of the video stream; and to use this module, you need to purchase separately a Wi-Fi module and a control module (Arduino Min, STM32), which accordingly increases not only the cost but also the complexity of the design, as well as overall dimensions. At the same time, the speed of the microcontroller will be significantly lower (16–32 MHz) than that of the pyAI-K210 and ESP32 modules. Comparing the pyAI-K210 and ESP32 hardware modules, it can be seen that these two modules have similar parameters in terms of microcontroller speed and camera characteristics. The main differences between such modules are the overall dimensions and weight of the hardware module, but the price of ESP32-Cam is about 4.5-5.0 times lower than pyAI-K210 and has a wider distribution and software support for libraries for working with modules and sensors. Based on this comparison, an ESP32-Cam will be used to implement the camera module onboard a humanoid robot. The next step is to select a hardware module for the implementation of the control module by a humanoid robot. Based on the above restrictions, the following hardware modules fell into the analysis area, which are presented inFig. 3, and their parameters are presented inTable 3. Analyzing the main parameters of the control system hardware modules, it can be seen that the 16 road steering gear control board servo and neue version 32 Kanal roboter servo control board modules are based on the STM 32 bit microcontroller. At the same time, the neue version 32 Kanal roboter servo control board has a module for wireless data transmission via Wi-Fi and bluetooth, which fits certain restrictions, but these modules do not fit in terms of overall dimensions, as well as the number of servomotors that can be connected to the board management. On the other hand, the control system hardware of neue version 32 Kanal roboter servo control board, 32-Emax ES08MA II servomotor, and 16-road steering gear control board servo, will not allow to realize all degrees of freedom for a humanoid robot. Considering the parameters of the humanoiden roboter control board, it can be seen that it not only is suitable in terms of overall dimensions, but also is determined by the presence of a Wi-Fi module onboard a control system based on the ESP8266MOD microcontroller. This will make it possible to create an access point on its basis and simplify the process of transmitting commands to a humanoid robot from a control and decision-making system; as a result, to implement a control system for a humanoid robot, the authors suggest using the humanoiden roboter control board for 15 US dollar.<Structural Diagram of Interaction Between Main Elements of Mobile Robot Computer Vision Control System>After choosing the hardware modules, it is necessary to develop a general structure for the information interaction of the camera module and control module with the system of management and decision making to control the humanoid robot. This structure is shown inFig. 4. Based on the developed structure of information interaction between software and hardware modules, taking into account the specifics of developing programs for a microcontroller, to implement a computer vision system for a mobile humanoid robot based on ESP32-Cam and a neural network for object recognition and identification, it is proposed to use the following set of libraries supported in the environment Arduino IDE development[28]: WebServer makes it possible to implement a simple web server with support for only one client at a time, which allows to process requests using the Get and Post methods. The built-in I0T Development Framework from Espressif Systems (ESP-IDF) web server will be used. This web server is based on the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) stack and allows developers to create and conFig. web interfaces to manage and interact with the ESP32-CAM[29]. Wi-Fi will allow to connect to an existing local network, using authentication tools, via SSID and password. ESP32-Cam is a driver library for working with the OV2640 camera for the ESP32-Cam hardware module. For control based on the humanoiden roboter control board hardware module, it is proposed to use the following libraries: WebServer and Wi-Fi will perform similar functions as on a computer vision system. HTTP server node JS is a library that makes it possible to receive and process commands to control a humanoid robot from a personal computer. Servo is a library that allows to control the rotation angles of Emax ES08MA II servomotors. Battery is modular assembly of batteries with minimum parameters: 5 V and 3000 mA. HC-SR04 is a hardware module that is an ultrasonic sensor for calculating the distance to an object in the working area of a computer vision system[30]. On the side of a personal computer (notebook), the humanoid robot control and decision-making system is implemented based on the Python 3.10 language[31]in the PyCharm development environment[32]using the following libraries: OpenCV is a computer vision library that is designed to analyze, classify, and process the received image from ESP32-Cam. NumPy is a library for processing large multidimensional arrays and matrices with the ability to structure them. Urllib, HTTP client support library, makes it possible to obtain a URL address for transmitting a video stream from the ESP32-Cam. TensorFlow is a machine learning library designed to solve the problems of building and training a neural network in order to automatically find and classify patterns found in the working environment of a humanoid robot. YOLO v.3 is a neural network library (script) for object recognition and identification. CUDA 10.1.105 is Nvideo's technology library that uses the GPU to accelerate parallel computing in object recognition and identification. In the developed computer vision system, the choice of the CUDA 10.1.105 library is due to the following reasons: parallel computing on the GPU and convenience and compatibility with machine learning and computer vision frameworks such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, and OpenCV. The use of CUDA allows to parallelize the execution of algorithms and data processing, which can lead to a significant acceleration of the process. A feature of the ESP32 microcontroller is the use of a special ESP AsyncWebServer library, which provides the functionality of a web server, and it supports one access point, that is, one operator. Based on this limitation, one point transmits the streaming video to the computer vision system, and the second one, which is implemented on the humanoiden roboter control board, controls the robot. It is also necessary to implement the computational functions “Calculating the Distance to an Object”, which will allow calculating the distance to the detected object based on the ultrasonic method, and the “Decision Selection Algorithm” block contains behavioral actions, depending on the name of the identified object, distance, and objective functions and tasks of their interaction. The results of the selected interaction with the object are transferred to the “Sending commands by protocol HTPS” block, in which a sequence of commands is formed and transmitted via the HTPS using the Post and Get methods to the humanoid robot control board hardware module. For the convenience of visualization and understanding the type of signal transmitted to the circuit, it was decided to designate them in the following colors: green-digital signal for data transmission; black-power circuit “ground” or “gnd”; red-power supply + 5V or “vcc”. The electrical circuit diagram for connecting the ESP32-Cam module using the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is shown inFig. 5. The assembled test layout of the computer vision system with the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected is shown inFig. 6afront view andFig. 6bback view.Figure 6cis a front view of humanoid robot body; andFig. 6dis the location of the modules inside the case.<Development of Computer Vision System Algorithm for Mobile Humanoid Robot and Its Software Implementation>The next step in the development of a computer vision system for a humanoid robot is the development of an algorithm and a set of programs for interaction between the ESP32-Cam microcontroller and the HC-SR04 sensor on one hand and for system of management and decision making (notebook) on the other hand. An enlarged algorithm for the operation of a computer vision system is shown inFig. 7. Let us briefly describe the purpose of the main blocks of the algorithm (Fig. 7), which are implemented on the basis of the ESP32-Cam hardware module using the HC-SR04 sensor (Fig. 6). When power is connected to the ESP32-Cam module, the libraries are initialized (Fig. 4), after which the local wireless network is searched using authentication data (SSID and password). If the connection fails, then an error message is displayed in the port monitor (Arduino IDE during settings), and upon successful connection, the local network access point (router) allocates a local dynamic IP address of the ESP32-Cam. The video stream and data from the sensor will be transmitted to the system of management and decision making (notebook) at this address. After receiving the local IP address, we activate the 2Mp camera OV2640. Taking into account the peculiarities of the operation of microcontrollers, until the power is turned off on the ESP32-Cam, the video stream from the OV2640 camera, as well as the results of calculating the distance values from the ultrasonic sensor HC-SR04, will be continuously transmitted through the received IP address in a cycle. It is worth noting that all calculations of the distance to the object using the sensor will be carried out on the basis of the ESP32-Cam module, and the calculation results in centimeters will be transmitted to the system of management and decision making. The operation algorithm of the system of management and decision making (notebook) is built according to the following principle, after starting the program, at the first stage, the libraries are initialized (Fig. 4). After that, it checks for the presence of an IP address assigned to the ESP32-Cam in the local network. If the given IP address is not found, the user is given an error message. If the connection is successful, the program starts receiving the video stream and distance calculation results from the HC-SR04 sensor. The next step of the program is to solve the problem of recognizing the presence of an object in the working area of a humanoid robot. If an object is in the working area, it is identified with the display of the name of the object, the value of the probability of matching and recognition time, as well as the distance to it. Based on the received data (object name and distance), it is possible to implement a decision making mechanism to interact with the object in accordance with the tasks, as a result, the humanoid robot control board module receives commands for execution. At the same time, in real time, all the necessary information (name of the object, probability of coincidence, and distance to it) is visualized to the user in the Human-Machine Interface (HMI) window. The program will function until the user completes work with it or the power is turned off on the ESP32-Cam module. When creating a program for the ESP32-Cam module, we will use the Arduino IDE 1.8.19 development environment with the obligatory connection of the following libraries in the boards manager: Arduino AVR Boards ver. 1.8.5 and ESP32 ver.2.0.4 by Espressif System. At the first step, write a program for broadcasting a video stream from ESP32-Cam, connecting libraries: #include <WebServer.h>; #include <WiFi.h>; #include <esp32cam.h>. Let us write the constants that will contain the login and password for ESP32-Cam authentication in the local network (set by the developer): const char* WIFI_SSID = “Crow”; const char* WIFI_PASS = “notebookpuk100”. Let us write the port for connecting to the web server. WebServer server(80); We indicate the pins to which the HC-SR04 sensor is connected to the ESP32-Cam: #define trigPin 13; #define echoPin 15. For the convenience of computer vision system testing with different types of resolution obtained from a 2Mp OV2640 camera, we indicate the following working resolutions: static auto IoRes = esp32cam::Resolution::find(320, 240); static auto midRes = esp32cam::Resolution::find(350,530); static auto ords = esp32cam::Resolution::find(800, 600). That is, it will make it possible, when testing a computer vision system, to change the image quality in the program on the system of management and decision making side. In the future, it will be possible to select only one quality of streaming video for the tasks, which will make it possible to reduce the load on the microcontroller. Let us create a serveJpg() function to receive a streaming video as a jpg sequence and an error handler in the form of a 503 code for the server[33]. {auto frame = esp32cam::capture(); if (frame == nullptr) { Serial.println(«CAPTURE FAIL»); server.send(503, «», «»}; // means that right now the server is not ready to process the request, because it is overloaded or technical work is being carried out on it Return;} Serial.printf(“CAPTURE OK %dx%d %db\n”, frame-> getwidth(), frame->getlIeight(), static_cast<int> (frame->size())); server.setContentLength(frame->size()); server.send(200,“image/jpeg”), // successful request, server is running, information is being transmitted. WiFiClient client = server.client(); frame->writeTo(client);} Let us create the functions void handleJpgLo(), void handleJpgHi(), and void handleJpgMid() to check the possibility of streaming video at three resolutions: IoRes, midRes, and hires. An example of such an implementation of the void handleJpgLo() function is presented below: {if (!esp32cam::Camera.changeResolution(IoRes)) { Serial.println(“SET-LO-RES FAIL”);} serveJpg();} It is similarly implemented for the functions void handleJpgHi() and void handleJpgMid(). The next step is to describe the necessary data in the void setup() function, skip the description of the standard port settings, and present the most interesting points: Set the signal levels on the pins to which the HC-SR04 sensor is connected: pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT); pinMode(echoPin, INPUT); Set up the OV2640 camera parameters and check its performance: {using namespace esp32cam; Config cfg; cfg.setPins(pins::AiThinker); cfg.setResolution(ords); cfg.setBufferCount(2); cfg.setJpeg(80); bool ok = Camera.begin(cfg); Serial.println(ok? “CAMERA OK”: “CAMERA FAIL”);} It is worth paying attention to the last line, which allows to display technical information in the port monitor in the Arduino IDE development environment when it is configured. Connect to a local wireless network using the data entered in WIFI_SSID and WIFI_PASS: WiFi.persistent(false); WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA); WiFi.begin(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASS); while (WiFi.status()!= WL_CONNECTED). Upon successful connection, the received local IP address of the ESP32-Cam module is displayed in the Arduino IDE port monitor, which will be needed to broadcast the video stream in system of management and decision making: Serial.print(«http://»); Serial.println(WiFi.localIP()). Let us activate three servers, with the help of which streaming video is transmitted in the form of a sequence of jpg files with different resolutions and turn on the server: server.on(“/cam-lo.jpg”, handleJpgLo); server.on(“/cam-hi.jpg”, handleJpgHi); server.on(“/cam-mid.jpg”, handleJpgMid); server.begin(). The last step is to write the void loop(), which is executed in a cyclic mode and is a feature of working with microcontrollers: Prescribe the program code for the operation and calculation of the distance for the HC-SR04 sensor: {digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW); // we apply a low level signal to pin 13; delay(200); // make a delay of 200 ms; digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH); // we apply a high level signal to pin 13; This allows to create a sequence of ultrasonic sequences on trigPin, which will then be captured as a reflected signal from objects on the echoPin; delay(200); digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW); duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH); distance = (duration/2)/29.1; // distance calculation (in centimeters) Serial.print(distance); Serial.println(«cm») // information output to the port monitor (for testing) server.handleClient();}//launch Web Server Now it is necessary to develop software for recognition and identification of objects and its visualization in the system of management and decision making block. To do this, we will use the PyCharm[33]development environment and the Python 3.10 programming language[32]. In the first step, we include the following libraries: import cv2 import numpy as np import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import time import sys import os Set the following weight configuration for object detection: CONF = 0.6 SCORE = 0.3 IOU = 0.7 Object detection weights such as Confidence Threshold (CONF), Evaluation Threshold (SCORE), and Overlap Threshold (IOU) are typically chosen based on the experience and requirements of a particular computer vision task. The definition of these weights depends on the specific task and can be selected based on the requirements for the accuracy and completeness of object detection. Optimal values can be determined by experimenting and tuning the model on the training dataset. Write the path to the neural network configuration file: config = “D:\Yv3\darknetmaster\cfg\yolov3.cfg” Connect the neural network weight file: weights = “D:\Yv3\darknetmaster\yolov3.weights” $\text{font}_{-} \text{scale}=1$ $\text{thickness} =1$ Connect the library of all object labels: labels = open(“D:\Yv3\darknetmaster\data\coco.names”).read().strip().split(“\n”) Write a color generator for each recognized object: colors = np.random.randint(0, 255, size=(len(labels), 3), dtype=”uint8”) Load the neural network YOLO: net = cv2.dnn.readNetFromDarknet(config, weights) The next step is to connect to receive a fragment of streaming video in the form of a sequence of jpg files from the ESP32-Cam module, with the following lines: url =http://192.168.1.12/cam-hi.jpg// local IP address of the ESP32-Cam module on the network cam = cv2.VideoCapture(url) We start working with layers in accordance with the technology incorporated in the YOLO library: Iterate over all detected objects; For detection in output We extract the class identifier (label) and the reliability (as a probability) of detecting the current object; scr = detection[5:] class_id = np.argmax(scr) confidence = scr[class_id] Determine the class of the object and evaluate the reliability of the found object; If confidence>CONF: Scale the coordinates of the bounding box relative to the size of the image, given that YOLO actually returns the center coordinates$(x, y)$of the bounding box, followed by the width and height of the boxes; box = detection[:4] * np.array$([w,h,\ w,h])$ (centerX, centerY, width, height) = box.astype(“int”) Use center coordinates$(x, y)$to get vertex and left corner of bounding box; $x$= int(centerX - (width/2)). $y$= int(centerY - (height / 2)). Depending on the number of stored object labels, it makes it possible to increase the number of simultaneously identified objects in the working area of a humanoid robot, and the developer can create his own label library, which will increase the quality of identification and reduce time. To successfully flash the microcontroller based on the ESP32-Cam module, we need to select the following configuration setting in the Arduino IDE development environment[28]in the Tools menu, as shown inFig. 8. After successful installation of the required firmware, the ESP32-Cam should be restarted through the tools menu of the serial monitor, which includes mainly setting the dynamic IP address of the module in the local network, the Joint Photographic Expert Group (jpg) sequence and resolution, and other features. An example of information displayed in the serial monitor is shown inFig. 9. An example of the HMI of the developed computer vision system for a humanoid robot is shown inFig. 10. As you can see inFig. 10, a standard set of configuration files and label files was used, and the developed computer vision system for a humanoid robot identifies objects. Now you can develop your own library assembly to solve the identification of the “ball” object, and in the future this library can be expanded depending on requirements.<Experiment>Let us conduct a series of natural experiments with the developed computer vision system for a humanoid robot to assess its performance. To do this, we will assemble a layout that will simulate the location of the computer vision system inside a humanoid robot, taking into account the vertical height of its location from the floor, which will make it possible to check the performance of the HC-SR04 sensor in real conditions of its operation. An example of a layout for conducting experiments is shown inFig. 11. At the first stage, the research on the recognition and identification of a statistical object of the form of a ball with the label “robo ball” is conducted, and in this case, the classic coco.names library is used. To do this, we place a static object “robo ball” at different distances from the computer vision system and measure the following characteristics: the probability of coincidence and recognition time, under the general condition that the illumination is 497 Lux (standard office and natural). The results of the first experiment are shown inTable 4. An obtained result can be explained by the peculiarity of the architecture of the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). In this case, when recognizing an object, “robo ball” is applied once to the entire image at once. The network divides the image into a kind of grid and predicts the bounding boxes and the probability that there is the desired object for each area, which affects the large spread, where the range of object identification accuracy changes from 0.37 (for objects that strongly affect the accuracy) to 0.94 (for objects with have a minor effect). From this we can conclude that the use of CNN to solve the problem is not effective, due to the high divergence of identification accuracy at different distances from a mobile humanoid robot. As a result, there is no point in conducting an experiment for the dynamic object “robo ball” with this library. We will improve the neural network, due to the idea of improvement, which is that S-SSD[34]replaces the VGG-16 network[35]as the basic network for extracting features of the Single Shot Detector (SSD) network model with a tiny-YOLO lightweight network model[36]. This will make it possible to preserve the multidimensional structure of the network model feature graph, which will increase the detection accuracy, while significantly reducing the amount of calculations generated by the network operation, thereby significantly increasing the detection speed, due to a limited set of objects (in the “robo ball” experiment). It will also remove time delays when working in a dynamic environment. Let us repeat the conditions of the first experiment based on the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model for recognizing and identifying the “robo ball” object in room conditions. The results of the second experiment are presented inTable 5. For the convenience of analyzing the data obtained in the two experiments described above, we present them in the form of a dependence graph: recognition accuracy and time on distance, for the classic coco.names library and the lightweight tiny-YOLO network model. The resulting graphs are shown inFigs. 12and13, respectively. As can be seen fromFig. 12, the computer vision system based on the coco.names standard library for the “robo ball” object has an identification accuracy of 0.59-0.94, while the identification time is in the intervals from 0.373-0.410 s and the graph has a difficultly unpredictable shape that does not depend on distance to the object. In contrast to the graph of the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model (Fig. 13), it can be seen that the identification accuracy depends on the distance, that is, the farther the “robo ball” object is from the humanoid robot, the probability of belonging to this label decreases, while it is worth noting that to solve the problem in this study, the distance of 200 cm is large enough and will not be used. The created dataset for the task of detecting and recognizing objects of a mobile humanoid robot is built on the basis of the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model, surpasses the SSD network model in terms of detection accuracy and detection speed, and can simultaneously meet the requirements of detection accuracy and real-time performance (in dynamics) when performing indoor tasks. These conclusions are confirmed by comparative experiments on the accuracy and speed of object detection, as well as on the detection and recognition of objects in real time by a mobile robot in a real indoor environment. The next experiment is the recognition and identification of an object with the label “robo ball” in dynamics, that is, the essence of the experiment is to identify a dynamically receding object, and in fact, this is a simulation of a humanoid robot playing football. The results of such an experiment are shown inFig. 14. Analyzing the obtained results of identifying the “robo ball” object in dynamics, it can be seen that the recognition accuracy of the improved neural network at a distance of 100 cm and 150 cm (Figs. 14band14c) was affected by the presence of the object in direct sunlight, which gave the appearance of lightening of the contours of the object, and as a result, it led to a decrease in the recognition accuracy, in contrast to the results obtained at distances of 200 cm (Fig. 14d), in which the object left the clarification zone, which accordingly increased the recognition accuracy to 0.97. Despite the obtained results, it can be concluded that the neural network improvements based on the tiny-YOLO lightweight network model provide high speed and accuracy of object recognition with a low camera resolution on the ESP32-Cam (2Mp) module for small-sized mobile humanoid robots. Let us compare the developed computer vision system with a control system for a humanoid robot, with similar solutions. The comparison results are presented inTable 6. Let us buildTable 7to compare the identification time of the “ball” object from distance for the developed computer vision system based on ESP32-Cam with a computer vision system based on NVIDIA Jetson Nano[38] Let us present the comparison results obtained fromTable 7in the form of a graph, which is shown inFig. 15.<Conclusion>The developed computer vision system for small-sized mobile humanoid robots was implemented on the basis of ESP32-Cam using an ultrasonic sensor HC-SRO. To speed up the process of recognition and identification of the “robo ball” object, the authors proposed a tiny-YOLO lightweight network model. This solution allowed us to preserve the multidimensional structure of the feature graph of the network model, and therefore increase the detection accuracy, while significantly reducing the amount of calculations generated by the network operation, thereby significantly increasing the detection speed when using microcontroller systems. As can be seen from the results of the experiments, the improved neural network made it possible to obtain an average time for identifying the object “robo ball” 0.028 in natural conditions, with a high probability from 0.99 at a distance of 50 cm to 0.80 at 200 cm, while it is worth noting that a camera is used OV2640 2MP/FOV70. In the future, it is planned to develop a target detection system and implement mechanisms for interacting with “objects”, as well as consider the possibility of implementing movement trajectory prediction to predict actions. The experimental results obtained show that the developed computer vision system has a number of significant advantages, such as high recognition speed comparable to the expensive NVIDIA Jetson Nano and improved AI YOLO v.3 algorithm implemented for ESP32-Cam, which gives a minimal identification error for a dynamic object and has minimal requirements for the power module, moreover, the price of the developed computer vision module does not exceed 8 US dollar, compared to analogues of 180 US dollar. However, the developed solution is not without drawbacks. Restrictions on overall dimensions have significantly reduced the computing power of the module, as a result of which the solution of some recognition and identification problems must be solved on a separate device. Thus, this problem and its solution is the next direction of possible research.

title: Forming the Concept of Direction Developmentally
abstract: The concept of direction is critical for a robot to establish its abilities in spatial perception. This article addresses the issue of how a robot developmentally forms the concept of direction. We propose a novel framework, based on the related mechanisms of humans, in which motion cues are employed instead of other commonly used sensing means like vision or audition. Using motion cues is actually one of the most important ways for humans to acquire concepts. This leads to advantages in two ways: 1) models based on motion cues are usually more convenient for a robot's control of motion and 2) multimodal perceptual cues can complement each other and result in improved robustness. The framework behind our methodology lies in developmentally forming the concept of direction in two successive phases: 1) the robot acquires the perceptual representation of its motion by motor babbling and 2) the corresponding higher level features are gradually captured, based on which the conceptual representation is obtained and then the concept of direction is formed. The proposed framework and the corresponding models are evaluated with a PKU-HR5.0II humanoid robot. The results show that the robot can successfully form the concept of direction in a manner similar to that of humans.

title: In-Robot Network Architectures for Humanoid Robots With Human Sensor and Motor Functions
abstract: The design concepts of the in-robot network (IRN) architectures of humanoid robots are proposed in this paper. First, this paper reveals the network requirements for humanoid robots to realize perception abilities and action execution abilities near those of human beings. Humanoid robots need to be equipped with many sensors to collect surrounding environmental information. It is also necessary to use many motion actuators to enhance the degree of freedom to achieve the smooth motion abilities of humans. To maintain reliable data transmission between a number of nodes, an efficient and reliable IRN architecture is needed. This paper first discusses the limitations of existing humanoid robots in the number of sensors and degrees of freedom and points out that one of the reasons for this limitation is the lack of reliable network architectures. In-vehicle networks (IVNs) and various network technologies are used. These include time-sensitive networks and control area networks (CANs) to name a few. Additionally, heterogeneous network protocols are used. IRNs also include networks of sensors and actuators with different performance parameters such as bandwidth, delay, and transmission speed. IRNs may adopt design ideas similar to those of IVNs to satisfy the network requirements for humanoids. To accomplish this, three feasible IRN architectures are proposed and analyzed. Finally, to compare and analyze the three proposed IRN architectures, this paper uses OMNeT++ simulation software.

In-vehicle networks (IVNs) and various network technologies are used. These include time-sensitive networks and control area networks (CANs) to name a few. Additionally, heterogeneous network protocols are used. IRNs also include networks of sensors and actuators with different performance parameters such as bandwidth, delay, and transmission speed. IRNs may adopt design ideas similar to those of IVNs to satisfy the network requirements for humanoids. To accomplish this, three feasible IRN architectures are proposed and analyzed. Finally, to compare and analyze the three proposed IRN architectures, this paper uses OMNeT++ simulation software.<Introduction>Humanoids are intelligent robots with appearances and functions similar to those of humans. This kind of robots pursues the high fidelity of human beings. Not only the facial and limb features but also the movement abilities and shapes of humanoids can highly emulate those of real human beings. Such humanoid robots can also act like human beings, have the same expression, and make corresponding reactions when encountering issues. The reason why humanoid robots can act like humans and have human behavior is that they have a central system constructed by sensors, which controls and directs the behavior of the robot in a way similar to that of the brain. To achieve such a function, various parts of humanoids are equipped with a variety of sensors, including optical sensors, which enable them to see surrounding objects and distinguish their sizes and colors; sound sensors, which enable the robots to hear surrounding sounds; and touch sensors, which give humanoids a tactile sense similar to that in human beings[1],[2]. Some humanoids are also equipped with ultrasonic sensors, so that they can hear ultrasonic waves that cannot be heard by human ears[3],[4]. However, in order to realize these complex skills, corresponding powerful network support is inevitably needed to carry the extensive amount of communication generated between thousands or even tens of thousands of sensors all over the body of the humanoids. In this paper, we propose the in-robot network (IRN), which is intended to support the extensive amount of data communication generated between the sensors, processors, and actuators in humanoids. We will focus our research on the communication network issues rather than social functionalities such as voice communication and vision abilities. These issues include the network architecture to ensure reliable data transmission between communication elements with different network requirements for different functionalities. Although social functions are one of the indispensable capabilities of humanoid robots, the social-level information processing in the application layer is not included in the scope of this paper. However, we incorporated its data when studying the required amount of data and transmission speed, such as the bit rates of the audio streams and the data packet sizes of the actuator control commands sent by the processors when performing body movements. Similar to the neural network of the human body, the sensors in the humanoids play the role of sensory neurons and collect the temperature, humidity, pressure and other environmental factors of the external environment. These environmental factors are transmitted through the IRN to the central procession unit (CPU), which serves as the robot’s brain. The processor analyzes these data and generates further commands to control the humanoids’ actions. The actuators play the role of motor neurons, similar to the muscle tissue of the human body, enabling the humanoids to perform various complex motion functions similarly to humans. In previous studies, we analyzed the complex perception of the human body from various perspectives such as temperature, pressure, vision, and hearing[5]. By investigating literature in the areas of human biology, we discussed the number of various sensory spots, sensitivities, and abilities to identify environmental factors of the human body. Based on the discussion, we suggest the distributions of the number of sensors and the sensitivities of the sensors in the sensor network for the humanoids. We first estimated the required data size for various sensors in the networks and the minimum communication delay requirements. We used these to calculate the network bandwidth requirements that need to be realized in the humanoid IRN. In a similar way, we then estimated the data size of the packets received by the actuators that act as human motor organs, data transmission speed, and communication delay requirements. In this paper, we refer the concept of in-vehicle network (IVN) and apply it into IRN. Our goal is to design a set of IRN architecture forward-looking and apply it to the humanoid industry in the future. When the robot industry level in the future can restore human perception to a high degree, the IRN architecture we proposed can be directly applied to it to carry the huge network communication traffic and meet the basic communication requirements. We not only refer to the bandwidth and delay requirements estimated in previous studies but also propose three near-optimum humanoid IRN architectures through the viewpoints of the weight, cost, and wiring length of the IRN. These architectures under different requirements are evaluated through comparative analysis. To reduce the traffic loads of the backbone networks in these architectures and prevent data congestion, we divide the architectures into several different domains. The partitioning of the domains can be changed according to the different requirements of the robot function. We found that the existing research on IRNs is only at the basic ethernet and control area network (CAN) level and does not solve the large-scale communication network issues we proposed.[1],[6],[7]Therefore, we examined the IVN and found that in order to provide the required security level, time sensitivity, and communication speed for different network nodes, the IVN divides the entire vehicle network into several domains and assigns different network communication protocols. Therefore, we try to incorporate the concept of the IVN into and the IRN and propose a new architecture for IRNs that is different from that of IVNs. Then, we used the OMNeT++tool to simulate the three IRN architectures that we proposed through two kinds of scenarios to compare the performances of the three IRN architectures in fully loaded communication environments. The end-to-end delay was used as a measure of performance to compare the different network architectures. We tested the average propagation delay from sensors to the CPU and from the CPU to actuators. The organization of this paper is as follows.Section IIidentifies and explains problems in IRNs of existing humanoids and proposes general requirements of humanoids from a biological perspective such as the numbers of sensors and actuators and required bandwidths.Section IIIintroduces, explains and discusses the general ideas of the three IRN architectures we proposed. In this section, the possible weights, costs, and wire lengths of IRNs with the proposed architectures are also discussed.Section IVsorts out and compares the end-to-end delays for the different architectures. Finally,Section Vconcludes this paper.<Background and Related Work>The IRNs of humanoids are generally divided into sensor networks, actuator networks, and the backbone network that carries all communication categories. Investigations show that existing humanoids are not yet able to realize all the functions of human beings[8]–​[11]. Instead, a limited number of sensors and actuators are employed to realize part of the functions. Therefore, it is necessary to design an efficient IRN architecture to support the very large amount of traffic between increasing numbers of sensors and actuators. At the same time, it is also necessary to find the proper bandwidths, traffic engineering, and architectures to guarantee the minimum transmission delay requirements. In this section, we first introduce the functions, degrees of freedoms, and sensor distribution of existing humanoid robots and show that they do not have enough sensors and actuators. Therefore, in the second part of this section, the number of elements and minimum bandwidth requirements of sensor networks and actuator networks are introduced, which may serve as an important basis for the designs of the IRN architectures in this paper. Humanoid Nadine, jointly developed in 2015 by Kokoro Japan and Nanyang Technological University, is a social robot that can communicate with people. Nadine has a human appearance with natural skin and hair. Nadine can have a continuous dialogue with humans by recognizing facial expressions and dialogue content. Nonetheless, a temperature sensor that senses the ambient temperature and a pressure sensor that achieves tactile ability are not included in order to achieve these social functions. Therefore, Nadine still lacks the ability of human skin to perceive the outside world. Nadine has 27 degrees of freedom, which supports only facial expressions and upper limb movements[8]. Sophia is a social humanoid robot developed in 2016 by the Hong Kong-based company Hanson Robotics. The camera in Sophia’s eyes is combined with computer algorithms to enable her to see. She can follow faces, maintain eye contact, and identify individuals. In addition, Sophia has the ability to imitate more than 60 facial expressions[9]. However, as Sophia is a social robot similar to Nadine, the lack of action actuators makes it impossible to fully restore human motion functions. The humanoid ASIMO developed in 2011 by Honda can talk to multiple people at the same time. When it encounters other people in action, it will predict the direction and speed of the opponent and precalculate alternative routes to avoid collisions. The exercise capacity and range of motion of the legs enable not only walking, running, and walking backwards but also jumping on one foot and two feet, changing directions while jumping, and walking on slightly uneven ground[10]. ASIMO 2011 has a walking speed of 0.75 m/s, a running speed of 2.5 m/s, and a total of 57 degrees of freedom. Atlas, developed in 2013 by the American-based robotics company Boston Dynamics, is specially designed for mobile operation. It is very good at walking on a wide range of terrains, including snow, and can perform backflip and rollover maneuvers. The whole body contains 28 joints that are actuated hydraulically[11]. In addition, it can adjust the dynamic interaction between the whole body and the external environment through algorithms for motion planning. In the in-vehicle network (IVN), the entire network structure is divided into four or five domains according to the differences in traffic information and functions, including the infotainment, body, power train (PT)/chassis, and advanced driving assistant system (ADAS) domains[12]. The IVN connects the various electronic control units by means of different communication media, so that the information of the sensors and actuators of each electronic control system is shared among the various units through multiplex transmission technology. In the IRN, different body parts have sensors with different accuracy and sensitivity levels. Therefore, it is necessary to allocate different communication protocols in a way similar to that in the IVN in order to reduce communication costs while providing ideal data transmission capabilities. Similarly, referring to the IVN, we divide IRN architectures into several different domains according to different functional requirements and physical location factors. This can not only divide network devices to meet similar bandwidth and delay requirements but also effectively reduce the complexity of network wiring and at the same time reduce the weight and economic costs of the entire structure. In addition, in the IVN, according to the distinction between functions and safety requirements, respective priority principles are formulated for different nodes in each network domain to obtain the timely response required in a vehicle collision accident. In the IRN, network components also need to be divided in a similar way. For example, the actuators on the torso and upper limbs of a humanoid robot are distinguished from those on the lower limbs in terms of function and use frequency. Moreover, in situations where humanoid robots may lose their balance, lower limbs often require more precise movement control than upper limbs. Therefore, in certain scenarios, the data transmission process generated to control the movement of the lower limbs often generates more traffic and requires a higher priority and less transmission delay. Therefore, for different domains, it is necessary to match the adapted network protocol to the requirements for data transmission rate, bandwidth, network priority judgment, and time sensitivity abilities. The specific network protocol division can refer to the in-vehicle network. In the IVN, different types of nodes are respectively connected by multiple buses of different speeds, and gateway services are used to realize the information sharing and network management of the entire vehicle. Among them, equipment such as windows, seats, and lighting systems use the low-speed network connection of the local interconnect network (LIN) protocol[13]. This type of equipment has low requirements for network transmission rates, generally less than 10 kbps. For fault diagnosis, air conditioners and instrument panels require a higher transmission rate but do not require high real-time performance, so most of them use low-speed CAN protocol networks for connection[14]. For engine control, anti-lock brake systems (ABSs), electronic stability programs (ESPs), and suspension control, a high-speed CAN protocol and FlexRay protocol with a transmission rate of 125~1000 kbps are used between devices that have high real-time requirements and directly affect driving safety. Technologies such as media oriented systems transport (MOST), Ethernet, and Bluetooth are used in multimedia and navigation systems that require high transmission rates[15]–​[17]. In addition, the IEEE P802.3cg Single Pair Ethernet Task Force proposed by the 802.3 WG-Ethernet Working Group in 2019 can support data transmission and power supply at the same time with a single pair of cables[18]. The common Ethernet before these requires two pairs of cables and separate cables for the power supply. It can also greatly reduce costs and reduce the weight of the equipment while providing 10 Mbps of data signaling. The transmission rates of 100, 200, and 400 Gbps provided by IEEE P802.3ck can be applied to the network used by the camera equipment that generates a large amount of data transmission in humanoid robots[19]. In addition, when building the IRN of humanoid robots, not only are the bandwidth and delay of the network important indicators for measuring network performance but also the actual physical weight and cost of the entire network equipment are factors that cannot be ignored. Additionally,$\alpha _{1} + \alpha _{2} + \alpha _{3}= 1$.<IRN Architecture Concept>Based on the numbers of different sensors and actuators and bit rates for an ideal humanoid generated during the communication process provided, we analyze network load situations and divide the networks into several domains as in the concept of humanoid domains. This section introduces three IRN architectures designed to meet the requirements for different communication scenarios.<Simulation Result Analysis>Due to the huge scale of our simulation models, we choose OMNeT++, which is relatively stable and can flexibly track and debug network parameters, as our simulation experiment tool. At the same time, we used and extended the network protocols provided in the open-source model library INET Framework in OMNeT++. The simulation experiment of the IRN of the three humanoid robots is carried out using OMNeT++. Taking the IRN architecture of a balanced bandwidth distribution robot as an example, the simulation props are first divided into four domains and connected in a star topology through the switch on the backbone network, as shown inFigure 4.Figure 5(a)shows the internal structure of the head domain, which contains the camera, mic, smell sensor and multiple actuators located in the head. These nodes are connected to the CPU through the switch located in the head domain.Figure 5(b)shows the skin domain of the IRN. The temperature and pressure sensors all over the robot are connected to the switch in the skin domain.Figure 6shows the arm and hand domain and leg and foot domain containing the body part actuators of the IRN. We tested the average end-to-end propagation delay in three different network architecture simulations under the condition of a full network load. The end-to-end propagation delay we tested is divided into two types, where one is the delay generated when the information collected by the sensor is sent to the CPU. When sending data packets from the sensor to the CPU, we check the corresponding timestamps when the data are sent to the network link and when the data are received. The average propagation delay result can be calculated through these.Equation 7shows the definition of the average end-to-end propagation delay,\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{t}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{m=0}^{N_{t}-1} \left [T_{r}^{t}\left ({m }\right)-T_{s}^{t}(m) \right ]}{N_{t}},\tag{7}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{t}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{m=0}^{N_{t}-1} \left [T_{r}^{t}\left ({m }\right)-T_{s}^{t}(m) \right ]}{N_{t}},\tag{7}\end{equation*}where$T_{s}^{t}(m)$is the timestamp reading which indicates the timing of data packets sent from the mthtemperature sensor. and$T_{r}^{t}\left ({m }\right)$is the timestamp result that indicates the timing of data packets sent from the mthtemperature sensor received by the CPU. The range of$m$is from 0 to$N_{t}-1$. Similarly, the average end-to-end propagation delay of the pressure sensor to the CPU can be obtained by the following equation:\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{p}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{n=0}^{N_{p}-1} {[T_{r}^{p}\left ({n }\right)-T_{s}^{p}\left ({n }\right)] }}{N_{p}},\tag{8}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{p}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{n=0}^{N_{p}-1} {[T_{r}^{p}\left ({n }\right)-T_{s}^{p}\left ({n }\right)] }}{N_{p}},\tag{8}\end{equation*}where$T_{s}^{p}\left ({n }\right)$is the timestamp reading at the time when data packets are sent from the nthpressure sensor.$T_{r}^{p}\left ({n }\right)$is the timestamp reading that indicates the time when data packets sent from the nthpressure sensor are received by the CPU. The range of n is from 0 to$N_{p}-1$. The other end-to-end propagation delay is generated when the central processing unit sends a command to the actuator. The average end-to-end delay can be obtained in a similar way as shown inequation 9.\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{a}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{k=0}^{N_{a}-1} {[T_{r}^{a}\left ({k }\right)-T_{s}^{a}\left ({k }\right)] }}{N_{a}},\tag{9}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} D_{p}^{a}=\frac {\sum \nolimits _{k=0}^{N_{a}-1} {[T_{r}^{a}\left ({k }\right)-T_{s}^{a}\left ({k }\right)] }}{N_{a}},\tag{9}\end{equation*}where$T_{s}^{a}\left ({k }\right)$represents the timestamp reading of actuator control data sent by the CPU to the kthactuator.$T_{r}^{a}\left ({k }\right)$is the timestamp reading that indicates the time when actuator control data packets are received by the kthactuator. In addition,$N_{a}$is the total number of actuators distributed in the head domain, arm and hand domain, and leg and foot domain.\begin{equation*} N_{a}={N_{a}^{H}+N}_{a}^{AH}+N_{a}^{LF},\tag{10}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} N_{a}={N_{a}^{H}+N}_{a}^{AH}+N_{a}^{LF},\tag{10}\end{equation*} We have established two kinds of communication scenarios. In the first scenario, we tested the end-to-end delay performance of the three network architectures when the humanoid is in different environments and the sensor data changes to different degrees due to changes in environmental parameters. First, the network remains fully loaded, and the size of the data packet generated by the sensor is stable. This scenario means that the temperature and pressure of the humanoid’s environment have not changed significantly. In this scenario, we set the median value of the temperature data generated by all temperature sensors to 25 degrees Celsius, and the amount of random fluctuation is controlled within ±0.4 degrees Celsius. The median value of the random number generated by the pressure sensor is set to 1 kPa, and the amount of change is controlled under ±10 Pa. Subsequently, in order to reflect the impact of sudden changes in surrounding environmental factors on the communication volume of the sensor network. We do not change the median value of the random number generated by all sensors but increase the range of change for some sensor values to 5 times the original value, with the intention of restoring a large data change in some sensors. We define that when the difference between the data value generated by the temperature or pressure sensor and the average value in a period of time reaches 1 degree Celsius or 50 Pa, the values of the two kinds of sensors reach the excited threshold and the related sensors are in the excited state, and vice versa call it stable state. In excited state, sensor data management will have to forward the data collected by these sensors to the CPU that acts the brain functionality. We first adjust the proportion of sensors in the excited state to 20% of the total number of sensors. Therefore, since the value change generated by these 20% of the sensors exceeds the threshold of sensor data management filtering data, it will generate a greater communication volume than the first solution. Then, we adjusted the sensor values of this solution to 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% to compare the impacts of varying degrees of change in environmental factors on the average end-to-end delay of the entire network. Figure 7shows the average sensor to CPU end-to-end propagation delay results collected during the communication process of the three network architectures under different conditions of varying degrees of environmental factors. It can be found that since sensor data management is not used to filter the generated signals, the end-to-end propagation delay results of architecture 1 and architecture 2 in different environments are basically stable. The end-to-end propagation delay of architecture 1 has been maintained at approximately 70.5 ms, and since architecture 2 contains more switches than architecture 1, which reduces the congestion of the network, the end-to-end propagation delay is stable at approximately 67.6 ms. The results of architecture 3 show that the end-to-end propagation delay is 49.3 ms in a stable state where the environmental factor change is 0, which is quite different from the results for the other two architectures. The result of architecture 3 tends to move closer to the result of architecture 1 as the degree of change in environmental factors increases. When the proportion of sensors whose data change exceeds the threshold is 100%, the result is basically the same as that for architecture 1. Figure 8shows the average CPU to actuator end-to-end propagation delay results of the three network architectures when the degree of environmental factor change is different. Similar to the sensor to CPU end-to-end, the delays in the results of architecture 1 and architecture 2 remain stable under different conditions, at approximately 11.7 ms and 11.0 ms, respectively. The result for architecture 3 increases with the change in the proportion of sensors whose data changes exceed the threshold, from 7.5 ms to 12.5 ms. In the second scenario, we tested the average end-to-end delay changes generated by the three network architectures when reducing the bandwidth of the backbone network to compare the performances of the three architectures. In this scenario, the initial bandwidth of the backbone given to the three network architectures is consistent with scenario 1. At the same time, in order to compare the impacts of the number of sensors in the excited state on the network performance in this scenario, we conducted two sets of tests. The first test set keeps the data value content in the stable state. The other test set assumes that all the sensors are in the excited state. Based on the required backbone bandwidth, we reduced the bandwidth by 5% increments and performed several tests until the bandwidth was reduced to 70%. InFigure 9, all the sensors of three architectures are in the stable state. On the other hand, all the sensors are in the excited state inFigure 10. This is to compare the performances in the two extreme cases. In architecture 3, compared to the other two architectures, due to the use of sensor data management, both the sensor-to-CPU and CPU-to-actuator delay are low. Because architectures 1 and 3 have the same network structure except for the sensor data management, as the bandwidth decreases, the delays show similar rising curves. Compared with architecture 2, the other two architectures show a larger upward trend when the bandwidth is reduced to 80%. InFigure 10, architectures 1 and 3 both start from a similar starting point, and the end-to-end delays show similar rising curves as the bandwidth decreases. Due to the multiple switches are used in architecture 2, the test result shows a smaller rising trend than the other two architectures.<Conclusion>In this paper, efficient IRN architectures for humanoid robots are proposed and analyzed with simulations. To achieve equivalent human perception and motor capabilities, large numbers of sensors and actuators need to be implemented in a humanoid robot. To maintain good data transmission conditions between sensors, actuators and processors, a complex and reliable network architecture is essential. Considering the differences in physical locations and functions of sensors and actuators as the starting point, the IRN is first divided into several domains. Each domain contains a large number of network nodes and switches with similar functionalities and capabilities. The switches connect the nodes to the backbone network. In addition, according to the differences in the bandwidth requirements of the different domains, 10 Mbps, 200 Mbps and 10 Gbps Ethernet network links are assumed. In addition, this paper proposes three IRN network architectures and verifies their communication delays in several cases including fully loaded network environments. The results show that in such environments, although the three architectures can maintain the delay within an acceptable range when sufficient bandwidth is allocated, due to the differences in network architecture design, there are significant differences in the test results of the three architectures under different communication conditions. Therefore, from a biological point of view, these delays obtained through simulation are similar to the propagation speed of electrical signals in the human nervous system. In architecture 2, the number of switches is greater than that in the other architectures. Although the increase in the number of switches would increase the physical weight of the network components to a certain extent, the network congestion may be reduced accordingly. In architecture 3, the sensor data management device may effectively reduce the repeated transmission of redundant signals sent by the sensor in a stable environment. The reduction in the amount of data brought about by the filtering of either repetitive or nonessential data may greatly reduce the transmission delay and the backbone network traffics. In future research, a set of new network communication protocols and standards that cope with the network architecture requirements may be studied. For example, network protocols may address the physical weights of communication devices and traffic engineering such as priorities, credit-based shaping, bypassing, and preemption. Additionally, partial failures and survivability of networks should be considered.

title: Humanoid Motion Control by Compliance Optimization Explicitly Considering its Positive Definiteness
abstract: This article discusses a compliance optimization approach that satisfies positive definiteness. Physical human–robot interactions are an important topic in robotics, for which force or compliance control is a key technology. Operational space control (OSC) is one of the most common approaches for robot force control with redundant degrees of freedom. By linearizing OSC, we can derive joint stiffness and viscosity matrices equivalent to the OSC. For an appropriate control, it is important that these matrices are positive definite. However, the stiffness matrix equivalent to the OSC is not always positive definite. In this case, a high kinetic energy is required, which is a problem in terms of the control performance. Therefore, the control performance can be improved by explicitly considering the positive definiteness of the stiffness or compliance. In this article, the authors derive a dynamically consistent compliance formulation and propose a compliance optimization that satisfies positive definiteness. The space of the symmetric positive definite matrix is a Riemannian manifold. We show that minimizing the Riemaniann geodesic distance results in a better performance compared with using OSC. The proposed method is validated via forward dynamics simulations and experiments using a hydrostatically driven humanoid Hydra.
