title: A Novel Algebraic Inverse Kinematics Based Approach to Gaze Control in Humanoid Robots
abstract: The vision system of humanoid robots is one of the essential components that allow them to do complex activities. This has led to numerous studies on artificial gaze stabilization, many of which are based on biological vision system reflexes. The gaze stabilization solution includes image capture and processing, inverse kinematics, and feedback control to achieve the desired gaze behavior. Generally, the multi-solution problem of finding the desired gaze direction and the inverse kinematics problem of finding the desired joints are solved by using cost functions and numerical solvers. This results in disadvantages that include long processing time, uncertain number of iterations, and risk of numerical instability. In this work, an alternative algebraic method is introduced by exploiting the cascading structure of the neck and eye. By using direct equations instead of numerical solving, the multi-solution and inverse kinematics problems are solved utilizing the geometrical structure and the proposed virtual configurations. Moreover, a sliding mode controller is designed to move the neck-eye joints to their desired positions. The developed scheme is simulated in the MATLAB/SIMULINK environment. Results for various scenarios show that the system can effectively gaze at different stationary and moving targets, showing human-like gaze behavior. In terms of timing, the desired gaze direction is quickly achieved and stabilized, whereas the neck-eye system dynamics stay longer. For one of the simulation cases presented, it took 0.3 seconds to achieve the desired gaze direction for the dynamics of more than 1 second.
text: <title>A Novel Algebraic Inverse Kinematics Based Approach to Gaze Control in Humanoid Robots<abstract>Abstract:The vision system of humanoid robots is one of the essential components that allow them to do complex activities. This has led to numerous studies on artificial gaze stabilization, many of which are based on biological vision system reflexes. The gaze stabilization solution includes image capture and processing, inverse kinematics, and feedback control to achieve the desired gaze behavior. Generally, the multi-solution problem of finding the desired gaze direction and the inverse kinematics problem of finding the desired joints are solved by using cost functions and numerical solvers. This results in disadvantages that include long processing time, uncertain number of iterations, and risk of numerical instability. In this work, an alternative algebraic method is introduced by exploiting the cascading structure of the neck and eye. By using direct equations instead of numerical solving, the multi-solution and inverse kinematics problems are solved utilizing the geometrical structure and the proposed virtual configurations. Moreover, a sliding mode controller is designed to move the neck-eye joints to their desired positions. The developed scheme is simulated in the MATLAB/SIMULINK environment. Results for various scenarios show that the system can effectively gaze at different stationary and moving targets, showing human-like gaze behavior. In terms of timing, the desired gaze direction is quickly achieved and stabilized, whereas the neck-eye system dynamics stay longer. For one of the simulation cases presented, it took 0.3 seconds to achieve the desired gaze direction for the dynamics of more than 1 second.<Introduction>Image-dependent applications are increasing with the emergence of artificial intelligence and robots. This visual dependency is very high in humanoid robots as they are required to perform complicated tasks, mimicking normal human behavior. By Digital Image Stabilization (DIS) and Optical Image Stabilization (OIS), the visual input is stabilized to get the most information. Although DIS is responsible for processing the image, the information contained in an image is governed by the mechanism of getting it, which is the responsibility of OIS. In this work, the neck and eyes of a humanoid robot form the responsible vision system. Through coordinated motion between the neck and eyes, gaze stabilization can be achieved. However, the humanoid vision system should resemble the normal Human Vision System (HVS) to some extent. HVS performs gaze stabilization by exploiting complicated biological techniques called reflexes. Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR) is the reflex responsible for keeping the gaze stabilized at the current gaze point in space, whereas Optokinetic Reflex (OKR) is the reflex responsible for keeping the gaze on track with the target[1]. Many researches have developed gazing techniques based on HVS to make the robot exhibit a gazing behavior similar to human gaze behavior[2]. It should be noted that gaze control, generally, includes image capturing, image processing, and system control[3]. Gaze stabilization is done in the system control stage by considering the information of the target and elements of the vision system[4]. On the other hand, image stabilization is done in the image processing stage to reduce the blur problem[5]. An eyeball or camera serves as the vision sensor that feeds the system with visual input. Research in the field goes back to the previous century, such as research on eye motion, gaze stabilization, and humanoid vision systems[1],[6],[7],[8],[9],[10]. One of the common problems addressed in the field is compensating for vibrations affecting the captured image. This problem was addressed in[11]by designing a compensating electromagnetic actuator, called 3 Degree of Freedom Electromagnetic Actuator for Image Stabilization (3D-EAIS), on artificial eyeballs that could isolate them from vibrations of body frame. Modelling and control of 3D-EAIS were done in[12], whereas experimenting on a fabricated model is shown in[13]. Approaching the same problem differently in[14], stabilization of bionic eyes was done mechanically to compensate for vibrations and gravity. The system considered has 3 degrees of freedom (DOF) for the neck and 2 DOF for each eye. Researches also considered motion and rotation behaviors during performing tasks. In[15], an analysis of gaze stability was conducted on patients with vestibular loss and healthy people by observing the visual acuity during a gaze shift for standing, rotating the head, and walking cases. Furthermore, movements of human head were emulated and analyzed in[16]. Position variables were obtained by using geometric relationships instead of fixed reference methods. In addition, kinematic models for coordinated movements of eye-head were derived in[17]for a general model of two-eye humanoid head with 6 DOF. Another work, in[18], has addressed the problem of keeping a distance by gaze and motion stabilization. Model reference adaptive control was used with adaptive feedforward gains and visual information as feedback. Several studies have been extended to research animal vision systems. Some experiments were conducted on mice to monitor their eye movements[19]. A technique for stabilizing the gaze of a robobee during a maneuver was developed and inspired by some insects’ techniques[20]. However, studies on HVS have resulted in a huge impact on the improvement of the humanoid vision system by taking inspirations from stabilization techniques such as VOR and OKR. For example, VOR has been analyzed by OpenGL visualization for camera movements to evaluate image stabilization[21]. Moreover, the visual stimulus has been analyzed during a car drive to develop a model based on VOR and OKR[22]. Discussion of researches on the topic that address used models, problems and solutions, designs of robots, control methods, and system behavior can be seen in comprehensive reviews, such as[2]and[23]. Many solutions have been proposed and developed for the control problem of humanoid gaze stabilization throughout the literature. For ARMAR-III humanoid robot, a method using saliency maps was developed in[24]to have the gaze fully automated with a combination of gaze stabilization and view selection to achieve required tasks. On the same robot model, another method has been developed to be more robust by including more sources of disturbances, namely, visual, proprioceptive, vestibular, and inertial information[25]. A different approach was taken by considering the problem of tracking the fixation point of the eyes on iCub humanoid robot by developing a passive gaze stabilization with VOR and saccadic motion[26]. In the literature, deep learning methods were also used in the gazing problem to address unmodeled nonlinearities[27]. In addition, it is used to estimate the gaze, as discussed in[28], for various applications. One of the applications is gaze gesture-based control, such as controlling a wheelchair or a robotic car by reading the eye movements[29],[30]. Another application is Human-Robot Collaboration, where people and robots cooperate to accomplish specific goals[31]. Similarly in the medical field, deep learning approaches have been used to develop gaze-controlled surgical robots[32]. Additional to gaze estimation, the learning process has been used to develop a learned gaze control humanoids such as iCub[33]. Humanoid robots also use deep learning to form Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) behaviors by learning gaze expressions[34]. HRI research has also used fuzzy logic to develop humanoid robot behavior in various aspects. For instance, a fuzzy logic controller with seven criteria was developed to control the gazing behavior of a humanoid and make it more natural[35]. In addition, fuzzy logic was utilized in developing interactive emotion expressions[36]. Also, gaze-based control has been approached by fuzzy logic through reading of gaze and siliency maps[37]. Overall, the gaze system is controlled to be utilized in different areas with various approaches that must address two main problems. The first one is the redundant solution problem, which is the result of possible different actions to reach an ultimate goal. The second problem is the inverse kinematics (IK) problem, which translates desired actions into desired joint positions. These are usually solved by cost functions and numerical solvers[38]. Even though many different numerical methods are found in the literature such as Newton-Raphson and Levenberg-Marquardt methods, finding a numerical solution also includes problems such as numerical instability risks, uncertain number of iterations depending on the initial guess, and the need of performing a time-consuming process[39]. Therefore, different approaches are being developed to avoid related problems. In[40], the fruit fly optimization algorithm was used to optimize the parameters of the back propagation neural network in order to solve the inverse kinematics problem. Another study introduces an adaptive part to the particle swarm optimization to achieve more efficient and accurate solutions of IK[38]. On the other hand, in[41], it was proposed to use direct calculations rather than solvers by developing a 3D triangulation approach. In this work, the gaze control problem of a humanoid robot is addressed by developing an algebraic method to avoid the problems related to the numerical solution. It is based on the system cascading structure, that can be used to find the joints’ configuration of the desired state. In addition, the multi-gaze solution problem is tackled by introducing virtual components considering the geometrical structure. The developed method is simulated in MATLAB/SIMULINK environment using a developed sliding mode controller for smooth response. A comparison of the different features of existing and proposed approaches is presented inTable 1. The most suitable research papers were considered as only a little research has a comprehensive presentation discussing the system, inverse kinematics, controller, and dynamics.<Methods>The system considered in this article is the neck and eyes of a humanoid robot, as it represents the vision system. The neck-eye system is modeled based on iCub model which has its information available in multiple sources such as[42],[43], and[44]. It consists of 3 joints for the neck and 2 joints for the eye, with 5 DOF in total. Only one eye was considered as the work is extendable to the second eye.<Results>Before discussing the simulation results, some important notes should be considered. It is assumed that the camera focus is of the same distance from the camera to the target. In addition, the zero configuration of gaze and face directions has a direction towards the negative y-axis. Furthermore, millimeters and radians are used for distance and angle, respectively. Moreover, the joints are restricted by the data ofTable 2. Lastly, Multiple tests have been performed with different values of lambda and k in order to get the desired response. It also includes running the eye controller twice as fast as the neck controller, which is achieved by doubling the k and lambda values for the eye controller. The parameters of each controller are tuned to be$\lambda = 3.5$and$k = 15$for the neck controller, and$\lambda = 7$and$k = 30$for the eye controller. So, considering all of the above, the first test case is shown inFig. 8, which has a target of [1200 -100 1700] for the first 2 seconds and then [1200 -1000 1100]. The gaze direction can be followed by observing the gaze point change to the first and second targets, which does not show any abnormality. This can be further discussed by looking at the joint response shown inFig. 9. The first thing to notice is the fast reaction of eye joints EJ1 and EJ2 compared to the neck joints NJ1, NJ2, and NJ3, which is because of the faster controller that controls the eye joints. In addition, eye joints angles begin by increasing, then quickly decreasing to be steady at some point. The increasing part represents the quick eye motion that tries to reach the desired gaze direction as quickly as possible. However, at approximately 0.3 seconds, the desired direction is reached. So, after that point, the eye joints angles begin to decrease to compensate for the neck joints motion to stabilize the gaze at the target point. The eye joints reach a steady state when the neck joints reach their steady state, meaning the face is directed towards the target in normal cases. Therefore, the eye joints angles should normally reach zero at steady state but, in the shown case, eye joints angles reach a non-zero steady state for the first desired target. This is because the neck joints, specifically NJ2 and NJ3, have reached their limit angles resulting in the inability to direct the face towards the target. So, the non-zero steady state of eye joints represents continuous compensation for that inability. On the other hand, the second target case shows a zero steady state of eye joints at 2.5 seconds, meaning that the face direction has been reached. This shows that the reaction of the eye joint to neck motion resembles the VOR reflex of HVS. Another view of the same problem can be seen by considering the gaze point coordinates. InFig. 10, it can be observed that the gaze point smoothly reaches the target point at around 0.3 seconds. This shows that the eye joints have succeeded in quickly reaching the target point and stabilizing it during the neck motion. The quick eye motion, resembling saccadic motion, shifts the eye towards the target point, while the eye joints compensation, resembling VOR, keeps the gaze stabilized at it. The error presented inFig. 11confirms that the desired gaze point has been reached as it is of zero error. Similarly, the gaze direction can be viewed by using the spherical coordinates as shown inFig. 12. Both angles reach the desired, meaning the direction of the gaze is also reached. There is no observation of an error in the steady state as presented inFig. 13. Other cases should be tested to ensure the validity of the work. One case is object tracking as shown inFig. 14. The target moves with constant motion of around [$300-100\,\,100$] mm/s during the first interval of 2 seconds. In the second interval, the direction and speed change to [$- 600- 100-100$] mm/s. The gaze shows a smooth pursuit motion tracking the moving target, resembling the OKR reflex. In this case, if the neck joints can keep up with the movements of the target, the eye joints will not do much work. However, in the case of a faster motion, the eye will follow the target until the face direction keeps up with the target motion. Another case is tracking a circular motion as shown inFig. 15. The target follows a circular path with an amplitude of 75 mm and a frequency of$\pi $Hz. The eye joints quickly take the gaze towards the circular path, stabilize it at the target, and compensate for neck motion as the face is also directed towards the circling target.<Conclusion>Addressing the humanoid gaze, a humanoid neck and eye were modeled based on iCub. Additional to the gaze direction task, a face direction subgoal is introduced to have a more natural gaze. An IK was developed for the eye to achieve the desired gaze direction. Similarly, the desired face direction was achieved by developing an IK for the neck. By suggesting an algebraic approach, the developed scheme has avoided the problems related to numerical approach such as the processing time of uncertain number of iterations, and the numerical instability risks. The multiple solutions problem was adderessed by using virtual states with direct equations instead of using constraints, cost functions, or solvers. In addition, the desired joints were obtained analytically instead of using numerical solvers. Simulation results show that the gaze rejects undesirable neck motion and tracks targets, exhibiting VOR and OKR reflexes, respectively. Moreover, a gaze change from one target to another is quickly made, resembling saccadic motion. Overall, the gaze has been controlled, showing human-like gazing behavior. For future work, recommendations are given in the following: Generalization of the developed IK method.The developed IK method can be generalized by considering the rotation plane of humanoid joints and their normals.The number of DOF may vary between systems, but the method should be able to achieve the desired result by decomposing the problem into subproblems with certain objectives.Although any subproblem should be composed based on the related system itself, position and direction are the ultimate goals for each one.Therefore, by decomposing the main objective into enough subobjectives and using all the system’s DOF, the method should result in a unique analytical solution. The developed IK method can be generalized by considering the rotation plane of humanoid joints and their normals. The number of DOF may vary between systems, but the method should be able to achieve the desired result by decomposing the problem into subproblems with certain objectives. Although any subproblem should be composed based on the related system itself, position and direction are the ultimate goals for each one. Therefore, by decomposing the main objective into enough subobjectives and using all the system’s DOF, the method should result in a unique analytical solution. Controlling the gazing behavior by introducing a gaze path objective in the controller.Although neck and eye coordination affects the gazing behavior, the path taken towards the desired directions should also be considered.One way is to define a maximum proportional deviation from the actual gaze with fixed or adaptive ratios for each joint so that a desired behavior will be followed.Another way is to include a machine learning algorithm by making it learn certain gaze features in order to impose them on the gaze control.Ultimately, by defining different gaze styles with certain features, multiple algorithms can be developed to follow a particular behavior. Although neck and eye coordination affects the gazing behavior, the path taken towards the desired directions should also be considered. One way is to define a maximum proportional deviation from the actual gaze with fixed or adaptive ratios for each joint so that a desired behavior will be followed. Another way is to include a machine learning algorithm by making it learn certain gaze features in order to impose them on the gaze control. Ultimately, by defining different gaze styles with certain features, multiple algorithms can be developed to follow a particular behavior. For cases like stationary target, small change in target position, huge change in target position, slow moving target, etc., theÂ fuzzification method can be utilized to provide more appropriate control actions for each defined case. In general, learning algorithms and artificial intelligence can also be utilized to provide high-level decisions.

title: Improving Perception Accuracy of Flexible Capacitive Stretchable Sensors Using Piecewise Power-Law Model
abstract: Flexible capacitive stretchable sensors have a promising prospect in humanoid and soft robots. However, flexible sensors are difficult to be extensively deployed due to their low accuracy caused by intrinsic nonlinearity. The nonlinearity is mainly from the hysteresis of the material of the sensors. In this article, a piecewise power-law (PPL) model is proposed to improve the perception accuracy of a flexible capacitive stretchable sensor. The kernel of the model is the hysteretic operator generated from the PPL function. Benefiting from the design, the proposed model can better describe the asymmetric dynamic behavior of the flexible sensor than some hysteresis models. Its capability to characterize hysteresis in the flexible sensor is demonstrated by comparing the predicted data of the model and the real captured data from the flexible sensor. Then, the proposed model is used to compensate for the hysteresis of the sensor to promote its perception accuracy. The accuracy performance of the proposed method is also compared with the other three different methods. The flexible sensor is deployed in a homemade humanoid knee and a tensile test platform to be tested involving the bending motion and the linear motion, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate that the maximum absolute error (MAE) of the proposed method is significantly smaller than other methods.

title: YAREN: Humanoid Torso Robot Platform for Research, Social Interaction, and Educational Applications
abstract: In the pursuit of maximum efficiency and performance, robots are often designed with complex functionalities and mechanisms customized for specific applications. These designs are frequently proprietary, limiting their adoption by the research community for experimentation. This work introduces YAREN, an open-source humanoid torso robot for social and educational applications. We modeled YAREN’s anatomy based on anthropometric measurements, considering dimensions and mobility limitations, to promote more friendly and natural interactions with its end-users. YAREN has 12 degrees of freedom which allows it to perform a wide variety of movements, generating more realistic and dynamic interactions. Executing broader and more expressive poses enables more efficient and meaningful social communication with users. The electronic components were selected for availability and robustness, ensuring the robot’s structure moves without complications. Relatively low-cost components were selected to provide a high-quality product that remains accessible to multiple laboratories, even in resource-limited contexts. YAREN’s software is based on the Robot Operating System (ROS) to facilitate expansion and scalability. We also provide the kinematic model and tuning of the PID controller for the motors to control each joint precisely and optimize movement without compromising user safety. Based on our proposed open-source design, YAREN can be expanded to perform diverse interactive functions for social and educational purposes, promoting the research and development of humanoid robots. We hope our design can be replicated by researchers worldwide to support multiple projects and help grow more laboratories.
text: <title>YAREN: Humanoid Torso Robot Platform for Research, Social Interaction, and Educational Applications<abstract>Abstract:In the pursuit of maximum efficiency and performance, robots are often designed with complex functionalities and mechanisms customized for specific applications. These designs are frequently proprietary, limiting their adoption by the research community for experimentation. This work introduces YAREN, an open-source humanoid torso robot for social and educational applications. We modeled YAREN’s anatomy based on anthropometric measurements, considering dimensions and mobility limitations, to promote more friendly and natural interactions with its end-users. YAREN has 12 degrees of freedom which allows it to perform a wide variety of movements, generating more realistic and dynamic interactions. Executing broader and more expressive poses enables more efficient and meaningful social communication with users. The electronic components were selected for availability and robustness, ensuring the robot’s structure moves without complications. Relatively low-cost components were selected to provide a high-quality product that remains accessible to multiple laboratories, even in resource-limited contexts. YAREN’s software is based on the Robot Operating System (ROS) to facilitate expansion and scalability. We also provide the kinematic model and tuning of the PID controller for the motors to control each joint precisely and optimize movement without compromising user safety. Based on our proposed open-source design, YAREN can be expanded to perform diverse interactive functions for social and educational purposes, promoting the research and development of humanoid robots. We hope our design can be replicated by researchers worldwide to support multiple projects and help grow more laboratories.<Introduction>With technological advances, social robots are becoming more sophisticated. Researchers are integrating artificial intelligence, machine learning, and natural language processing algorithms to produce more human-like interactions. Most social robots have a human-like appearance and belong to the humanoid robots category. Their structure’s links are based on the human skeleton, while their movable joints emulate human articulations. These robots can make movements increasingly similar to those performed by humans[1]. For most social tasks, one of the most relevant aspects is the emotional expression the robot conveys towards the person it interacts with. Emotional expression is a major factor affecting the user’s perception and acceptance of the robot’s behavior. The ability to mimic human body language facilitates communication and increases familiarity during human-robot interactions[2]. A trend is emerging where the “faces” of humanoid robots are equipped with screens to reproduce facial expressions. Doing so increases the anthropomorphism of the social robot, allowing it to convey more emotional responses. In this way, greater confidence, trustworthiness, and comfort are provided to the user[3]. The state-of-the-art applications for social robots include advanced natural language processing and machine learning algorithms to enable more human-like interactions. These robots can recognize emotions, understand and respond to complex verbal and non-verbal cues, and adapt their behavior to the individual they are interacting with[4]. Other advanced applications include using social robots in collaborative work environments, in high-risk physical tasks, and integrating augmented reality technologies to enhance the user experience[5]. Currently, humanoid robots are used often for research purposes. The NAO robot is one of the most popular in this area[6]. It is a bipedal humanoid robot developed by Aldebaran Robotics. This robot is often used in research to implement IoT projects and to improve its locomotion with functions such as object detection. NAO’s main field of application is in research laboratories and mass markets[7]. It is also widely used as a companion robot, for example, for neurodivergent children[8],[9]or as an assistant in medical contexts[10]. Other research focuses on improving the humanoid robots’ social interaction and learning capabilities. iCub is a well-known example within this context. This humanoid has the appearance of a young child. Users can familiarize themselves with it and interact by trying to teach new skills. For example, iCub trials consisted of a person giving it instructions to build an object. Human-robot interactions occur verbally and through gestures or eye contact[11]. Currently, social robots are used in diverse fields. For example, in education, they are utilized to facilitate language learning and teach children with autism[12]. An example of this last application is the low-cost robot KASPAR. It has a minimally expressive face capable of representing four facial expressions: neutral, small, medium, and large smiles. Additionally, it can move its arms to interact with toys and perform gestures. Despite having lower limbs, it is a stationary robot, meaning it remains seated with its legs bent (like young children), unable to stand up or move by itself. Children of different ages have interacted positively with KASPAR. The simplicity of its design prevents children with autism from feeling overwhelmed[13]. At the same time, the robot’s ability to respond and interact sparks a greater interest in children than using conventional toys. This allows them to expand their social skills by practicing communication and feeling confident[14]. The Pepper robot developed by SoftBank Robotics is a humanoid robot that replaces its lower limbs with a mobile base equipped with omnidirectional wheels for mobility. This robot has been deployed in diverse environments. For instance, in education, it assists teachers during classes by reading, explaining topics, proposing exercises or interactive games, and giving feedback on quizzes, among other activities[15]. Another context where this robot has been used is in medicine. Field studies conducted in Japan analyzed the effectiveness of this robot in accompanying patients with schizophrenia during their rehabilitation. The results demonstrated that patients could interact positively with the robot, engaging in simple conversations. However, researchers concluded that further research was needed to ensure the feasibility of the robot interacting for extended periods of time[16]. In healthcare, social robots enhance the patient experience due to friendly interactions. They are used to educate the patients about their condition and medication. Also, they assist healthcare professionals with delivering supplies and monitoring patients, reducing the healthcare professionals’ workload[17]. Cody is a humanoid robot assistant capable of performing bed baths and other patient hygiene tasks. It has the appropriate configuration to control the movements of its arms and the force applied during the wiping motion. Other social robots with a higher load capacity are often used when a patient needs to be lifted and transferred. Examples include RIBA, which has a giant teddy bear appearance, and the Robotic Nursing Assistant, which features a humanoid upper torso. Both robots are capable of performing the described task. They incorporate tactile sensors to identify contact with the patient and can hold them with the necessary balance between strength and gentleness[18]. Furthermore, social robots can also provide emotional support to patients. Many children in hospitals experience anxiety, loneliness, and stress, which can negatively impact their recovery. Robots can offer companionship, helping to reduce their feelings of isolation[19]. An example is PARO the seal (known as Nuka in Spanish-speaking countries). This is a medical robot shaped like an animal, designed to simulate being a pet for patients. It has sensors to recognize user interactions and responds to them as a pet would (purring, opening and closing its eyes, etc.). PARO has shown positive results, especially with children and the elderly, helping to reduce feelings of loneliness and improve patients’ cognitive abilities[20]. For these reasons, this paper presents YAREN, a half-torso robot designed for social applications (Figure 1). YAREN can interact by moving its torso, upper limbs, and head. It features a variety of audio and facial expressions communicated using a screen as its face, enabling it to respond emotionally to its interlocutor. In the following sections, we describe the main dimensions of the robot, the characteristics of the selected actuators, and other electronic components. YAREN’s mobility is determined by the DH parameters of its kinematic chains and the constraints of each joint. Also, we illustrate the different reachable postures and workspace. The motor settings, along with the programming of their controllers, allow for smooth mobility resembling human movements. Human-like movements enable YAREN to interact naturally and convey comfort to users. Moreover, all CAD files of YAREN’s parts and assembly are stored in a GitHub repository and include information about its electronic system and the necessary code for programming it. To summarize, the main contribution of this article is: The explanation and analysis of the design decisions made allow readers to replicate this methodology and adapt it to their specific application needs. This includes describing the criteria for selecting the robot’s dimensions, degrees of freedom, motor types used, and more. An exhaustive review of the state of the art, along with a comparison of Yaren’s advantages over other social robots currently available in the market. The range of motion of YAREN is justified, and the advantages this brings to its potential applications are discussed. We demonstrate that it is a friendly, cost-effective design with high potential for diverse uses. We provide a simulation of the system using the Robotics Operating System (ROS) software, allowing other researchers to interact with the system, conduct experiments, and test various customizations according to their interests before physically implementing the robot. An open-source repository containing all the necessary information for the implementation of Yaren. This includes CAD files for building the robot, a detailed description of its electronic system and connections, as well as all the programming required to control the movements and interactions that Yaren can perform. We strongly believe YAREN is a valuable contribution to the robotics research community, especially as an open-source platform. Until 2022, only 3% of humanoid robots were open-source, and just 25% of all humanoid robots (both open-source and proprietary) were commercially available[21]. This highlights the need for further contributions to this area of development. Thus, YAREN aims to be an open-source platform that can be adopted by laboratories around the world as a tool for their applications. The goal is to reduce the economic barrier that often limits research in this field. Currently, robots available on the market tend to be very expensive. Moreover, their design, configuration, and programming are often protected by intellectual property, which prevents or restricts the adaptations researchers can make. This forces researchers to either adapt their ideas to the available hardware or invest in designing and building their own tools. With YAREN, we address this issue by providing a low-cost robot with a high level of expressiveness and functionality, capable of adapting to a wide range of contexts. Our modular system and fully available documentation allow users to replicate, expand, and modify the design to suit their specific needs. In this way, we enable worldwide collaboration, including laboratories of all scales. This also promotes the integration of robotics into more frugal contexts such as developing countries, low-resource schools, public hospitals, community centers, nursing homes, and other settings where technology can have a significant impact but its use has been delayed due to budgetary constraints.<Design Concept>The robot showcased in this paper, YAREN, features a humanoid design. The dimensions of each part were determined based on the anthropometric proportions of the human body.Figure 2shows the main measurements of the robot. The robotic torso has a total height of 500mm, resembling the dimensions of a child. The robot’s body is divided into 10 sections: lower torso, upper torso, right shoulder, left shoulder, right arm, left arm, right forearm-hand, left forearm-hand, neck, and head. The experience of other designers has shown that it is preferable to maintain a simple yet robust design. For this reason, YAREN was designed with an appropriate number of parts to ensure easy construction while maintaining acceptable mobility. The selected size, slightly smaller than the torso of a small child, makes the robot more approachable for users of all ages. Studies have shown that larger designs with more elaborate shapes can sometimes intimidate users, leading to rejection or discomfort. Additionally, this compact size makes the robot lightweight and easy to move, allowing it to be placed in a wide range of settings for its use in multiple context and applications. For instance, it can be positioned on a study desk, on a chair facing the user, or next to a hospital bed, making it easy to situate the robot in the optimal spot for clear communication, full visibility of its gestures and body language, and effective eye contact with the user. Another important aspect was to avoid the “uncanny valley” effect. This phenomenon occurs when a non-human object has features that are too close to human characteristics, causing discomfort in users[22]. Simpler designs, like the one presented in this paper, successfully avoid this issue. The upper torso is the widest section, with a width of 215mm and a height of 180mm. It was designed to house the main electronic components that energize and control the actuators. Additionally, it can accommodate extra components depending on possible applications for YAREN, which led to the determination of a depth of 90mm for this section. The upper limbs are divided into three parts: the shoulder, upper arm, and lower arm. The total length of the upper limbs is 300mm. Moreover, when the arms are fully extended to the side, they reach a total length of 335mm. The shoulders, which connect the entire arm to the upper torso, contain a motor inside to enable motion, and measure$75\times 65\times 55$mm. The upper arm, with a length of 80mm, is mounted onto the motor shaft of the shoulder and houses the actuator responsible for elbow movement. Lastly, this joint connects to the lower arm, which includes the forearm, wrist, and hand, and has a length of 190mm. The lower torso, or base, was dimensioned to also serve as the structure’s counterweight. Its mass and a diameter of 175mm were chosen to lower the center of gravity, ensuring that the center of mass is always projected within the support surface to enhance the robot’s stability. This section is connected to the torso via the hip. From a frontal view, the hip is much narrower than the upper torso and the base to mimic a human-like waist appearance, with dimensions of$70\times 50$mm. Its depth of 85mm is consistent with other parts of the robot, allowing for greater stability and proper accommodation of the required motors. The robot’s head is approximately rectangular in shape, with dimensions of$160\times 145$mm. It houses a screen that displays the robot’s face, featuring facial expressions such as eyes, eyebrows, and mouth. The size of the display was carefully chosen to ensure that gestures and expressions are easily recognizable, thereby enhancing expressiveness. The head has a depth of only 80mm, which allows it to be stable and lightweight while maintaining a pleasing design aesthetic. Additionally, a camera is located above the robot’s face, enabling it to interact with and make decisions based on image recognition. The head is attached to the rest of the body via the neck. The neck is the smallest part, measuring 50mm in width and 40mm in height. With a depth of only 20mm, it offers improved flexibility for the head while keeping the weight low. However, this also makes the neck the most fragile part of the assembly. Therefore, its geometry was designed to consider the points of critical stress and reinforce those areas, ensuring safe movement and support for the head. The articulations, represented by revolute joints, are configured to mimic natural human movements. Parts attached to motors are modeled to accommodate the actuators within them. Additionally, the orientations of the motor axes define the types of motion performed. The parts include perforations to facilitate wire routing, ensuring that the wires do not interfere with or obstruct movement and prevent damage to the wires during motion. The connections made and their degrees of freedom are specified in Table??. It can be observed how many degrees of freedom each joint has and how it was constructed, that is, how many motors were required to achieve the corresponding mobility. Note that the connections between torso-shoulder, shoulder-arm, and arm-forearm appear only once in the table for visual simplification. However, the number of degrees of freedom and motors corresponding to these joints must be doubled, due to the symmetry between the robot’s two upper limbs. YAREN is a half-torso robot with the possibility of expanding its design to a full-body robot. However, it is projected to be used as a companion robot for emotional support. Therefore, YAREN’s ability to move is not considered a priority. Instead, as explained, the mobility decisions were based on enabling YAREN to adopt more expressive postures. At the same time, the design was kept simple, with a limited number of joints. It has been demonstrated that there is a trend towards reducing the degrees of freedom in social robots to simplify their design and control while also lowering manufacturing costs[21]. YAREN’s overall design features 12 degrees of freedom, enabling a level of mobility and expressiveness that closely resembles human movement. This is particularly important for social robots, as it facilitates more natural interactions and enhances user acceptance. Achieving this degree of mobility within the proposed dimensions was challenging due to the limited space available for actuator placement. To address this, our prototype introduces a novel shoulder and neck design using double joint motors. These actuators integrate two orthogonal axes within a single motor, providing two degrees of freedom with just one component. This significantly reduces the robot’s weight, cost, and size. As a result, the design becomes more aesthetically pleasing while maintaining excellent mobility and expressiveness. Additionally, we conducted tests to ensure proper load distribution throughout the system. However, this double joint technique was not applied to the hip joint. On the other hand, the two degrees of freedom in the hip articulation are achieved using two separate single-axis motors. This latter configuration was determined because the hip needs to support and move almost all of YAREN’s structure, requiring high torques in comparison to those in the arms or head articulations. Regarding the neck joint, an offset in its design was considered to allow the head to make a wider twist around the neck’s horizontal axis. Body language is one of the most relevant communicative tools in humans. Thus, the robot was designed to be capable of adopting poses and movements that resemble human behavior. A significant part of this expressiveness is obtained through the arms, each designed with four degrees of freedom, as shown inFigure 3. This design allows the robot to perform wide movements with its arms. The elbow and shoulder joints allow the arms to extend along the coronal plane and facilitate hand positioning in supination and sideways, as seen inFigure 3a. The rotation limits of these joints are imposed by the geometry of the pieces themselves to prevent collisions between them. Additionally, the joint between the torso and the shoulder allows extending the hands forward and backward, as seen inFigure 3b. These postures enable YAREN to perform actions such as shaking hands with its user, pointing, greeting, and even holding objects in its palms or applying pressure to hold something between both hands. The arms can also be raised to reach points above the head’s height, predominately in front of the robot’s body. However, it is not possible to lift the arms behind the head, which mirrors the natural restrictions in human movement; despite having greater flexibility, humans also cannot perform 360° rotations in all their joints. The robot is also capable of rotating its hip, as shown inFigure 3c. By rotating around the sagittal axis, greater expressiveness and dynamism are achieved in the robot’s movements[23]. This also allows the hands to reach further and lower positions. The rotation angle at this joint is limited, given that the robot’s stability is constrained by keeping the projection of the robot’s center of mass within the base area. Furthermore, the robot’s hip rotates around the longitudinal axis, allowing the robot to turn around, face different directions, and revolve the arms’ workspace. As a result, the robot has a greater range of interaction and is capable of recognizing and registering most of its surroundings through a camera. Finally, the head’s joints are primarily intended to allow more natural interactions. Their displacement range is depicted inFigure 3d. The head’s upward and downward twists, combined with the facial expressions on the screen, achieve appropriate body language. Additionally, by turning its head right or left, the robot can provide greater familiarity during communication and look at different points or users without needing to move its entire body.<Yaren’s Control System and Prototype>Given that the robot will be employed in interactive environments, it is essential to design a robust control system. Therefore, this section describes the robot’s control system. First, a kinematic analysis is conducted to determine the Denavit-Hartenberg parameters for each of the robot’s kinematic chains. Then, the design procedure for each joint’s controller is detailed. Finally, the robot’s ROS software architecture is described, with an emphasis on how it controls the robot’s actuators and electronic devices.<Test and Results>A large set of actions was performed to validate that the design of the PID controllers met the desired requirements.Figure 9portrays an example of a step response (joint position through time) for each of the motor models located at different joints throughout the structure.Figure 9adescribes the step response of a 2XC430-W250 motor (joint 8).Figure 9bportrays the step response of a XC430-W240 motor (joint 5). Finally,Figure 9cdescribes the step response of a MX-106R motor (joint 1). The step responses indicate acceptable overshoots, lower than 20%, and stabilization times of at most 3 seconds. Also, their rise times of less than a second suggest that joints’ velocities are moderate. These values are considered appropriate for the rigor required in the potential applications for YAREN. A broad range of joint displacements were considered, as well as a variable number of joints that moved simultaneously. Hence, testing was carried out considering the structure’s several parts and the actuators were under different loads in each scenario. Several actions, as depicted inFigure 10, allowed to analyze the robot’s behavior and evaluate if further tuning for the PID controllers was required. This way, it was shown how YAREN is capable of performing the different poses described in the Design section. The limits of the different joints were tested, and movements were made to cover the entire workspace defined for the robot. The experiments were successful as the robot was able to maintain stability and smoothness throughout the whole motion. Each action was associated with a face displayed on a screen and an audio emitted through the speaker, based on whether or not the camera recorded a person. Several movement sequences were implemented and allowed to evaluate the robot’s interactive ability by testing it in front of infants. YAREN’s main characteristics are listed inTable 4. As seen, YAREN is capable of generating a wide variety of poses and expressions, conveying a broad range of emotions and reactions. Unlike most robots, which are limited to basic expressions such as “happy,” “sad,” “angry,” or “neutral,” YAREN combines facial features and body movements to express more nuanced reactions such as being thoughtful, surprised, embarrassed, etc. It can even portray the same emotion at different intensity levels by varying its poses. For example, it can show laughter in different ways: by raising its arms, by touching its abdomen or head, or by bending its torso. This ability to react differently even in similar contexts gives YAREN a more natural and engaging communication style. It was important to reach this behavior since repeating the same pose for the same intention might otherwise become dull or tiresome for the user. Such expressiveness was made possible through YAREN’s wide range of motion of all its parts, which results from a carefully engineered mechanical design, appropriate load distribution, and the use of actuators that maintain both aesthetic and compact form. YAREN’s casing was fully manufactured using 3D printing with Polylactic acid (PLA) material. This approach provided several advantages, including the low cost of the printing technology and the versatility of the material. The lightweight PLA contributed to YAREN’s total weight being just 3.45 kg (including all electronic components). The reduced weight lowers the robot’s energy consumption for movement, extending the battery life. This is beneficial in multiple companion functions, for example, to help alleviate patient stress during clinical procedures that may last several hours. Additionally, this improves the robot’s safety, as it minimizes potential harm to users in the event of collisions or accidents[25]. Due to its dimensions, YAREN is classified as a child-size robot. As mentioned in early sections, this size makes it suitable for friendly interactions with all target audiences from children to elderly people. To better understand YAREN’s position compared to its competitors, a comparison was made with seven of the most renowned robots in this category. As a social robot designed for children and the elderly, YAREN’s ability to convey emotions is one of its most crucial attributes. For this reason, the main variables considered were expressiveness (Y-axis) and cost (X-axis), as shown inFigure 11. To assess expressiveness, several parameters were evaluated. The three robots with the lowest expressiveness were rated as such because they have static faces, unable to represent any facial gestures. Notably, nearly 30% of robots on the market share this limitation[21]. Robots like Pepper, NAO, and iCub offer slightly more expressive gestures using lights or eye movements[24],[26]. However, the most common, economic, and effective method for expressing emotions is through a facial display screen, which allows for a wide variety of facial expressions. Coupled with the robot’s ability to execute poses that enhance body language, this creates better social interaction[21]. Based on these criteria, YAREN was considered more expressive than the aforementioned robots, surpassed only by Poppy, which can display a greater variety of gestures and poses due to its higher degrees of freedom. However, YAREN remains well-positioned as it offers a significantly more affordable alternative. With a cost of 3650, YAREN is approximately half the price of its main competitor. Therefore, YAREN proves to be a highly attractive option, offering a much more empathetic service and warmer companionship to users at a fraction of the cost of other commercial alternatives.<Conclusion and Future Work>YAREN’s design, an open-source humanoid torso robot, has been presented in this paper. We proposed a humanoid appearance for more natural interactions with people, as well as a design of parts with scaled-down dimensions and anthropometric proportions to facilitate the user’s approval and comfort while interacting. Furthermore, the location and number of joints were determined in order to obtain the desired robot’s workspace and humanoid behavior. This was enabled by selecting double joint motors, which allowed us to achieve a more aesthetic and compact design while enhancing the robot’s mobility. We implemented a control system for the motors located at each of the robot’s joints by designing and tuning PID controllers after performing a kinematic analysis. We presented a hardware and software design comprised of electronic components and a system’s architecture developed in ROS that provided the system with scalability to incorporate audio and video-related functionalities for research, social, and educational applications. Finally, the robot was tested in real time, demonstrating its diverse and smooth movements. It was shown how YAREN is capable of performing multiple postures and gestures to transmit emotions. More importantly, YAREN features a design and functionality that makes it suitable for a wide range of applications. Its level of expressiveness, higher than most of its competitors, helps earn users’ trust and enables it to connect even with sensitive audiences such as children, elderly individuals, and neurodivergent patients. As future work, several applications regarding computer vision and speech recognition could be developed with the proposed hardware components. Sentiment analysis of the input data could be performed to adapt the robot’s behavior to its user’s mood. Large language models could be utilized for an enhanced interactive experience by processing what the user says and generating a response that the robot would speak to him. Also, other complex control methodologies could be explored to obtain more precise actuator responses. YAREN successfully incorporates the most essential characteristics of other social robots on the market—at a significantly lower cost—while maintaining a high degree of expressiveness. This makes it useful in countless scenarios, including but not limited to: hospital companionship, reducing feelings of anxiety or loneliness, and supporting the learning process for children and adolescents, including those with conditions such as autism and ADHD. We hope that small- and medium-scale laboratories will take advantage of this platform, using the provided repository to build their own versions of the robot. Our team is committed to open-source technology, as we believe it is essential for empowering and supporting fellow researchers around the world. By keeping the prototype affordable and featuring a modular, easy-to-implement design, YAREN has the potential to become a multidisciplinary tool that enables engineers from various backgrounds to adapt and expand their ideas across different contexts and research fields.
authors: D. Sánchez-Orozco; R. Valdez; Y. Uchuari; M. Fajardo-Pruna; L. C. Quero; R. Algabri; E. Q. Yumbla; F. Yumbla

title: XBG: End-to-End Imitation Learning for Autonomous Behaviour in Human-Robot Interaction and Collaboration
abstract: This letter presents XBG (eXteroceptive Behaviour Generation), a multimodal end-to-end Imitation Learning (IL) system for whole-body autonomous humanoid robots used in real-world Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) scenarios. The main contribution is an architecture for learning HRI behaviours using a data-driven approach. A diverse dataset is collected via teleoperation, covering multiple HRI scenarios, such as handshaking, handwaving, payload reception, walking, and walking with a payload. After synchronizing, filtering, and transforming the data, we show how to train the presented Deep Neural Networks (DNN), integrating exteroceptive and proprioceptive information to help the robot understand both its environment and its actions. The robot takes in sequences of images (RGB and depth) and joints state information to react accordingly. By fusing multimodal signals over time, the model enables autonomous capabilities in a robotic platform. The models are evaluated based on the success rates in the mentioned HRI scenarios and they are deployed on the ergoCub humanoid robot. XBG achieves success rates between 60% and 100% even when tested in unseen environments.

title: End-Effectors Changer Design for Humanoids
abstract: Almost all (not to say all) existing humanoids have not been designed with the ability to change their end-effectors (head, feet and hands) on-the-fly. Inspired by the tool-changing mechanisms in robotics automation and manufacturing, we propose an end-effectors changer mechanism suitable to humanoids. This letter explains why enabling humanoids with such a technology is important and why existing tool-changer mechanisms are not adapted. The proposed changer mechanism is not actuated. Yet, it does not require human intervention to assist the change of end-effectors. We assess our mechanism through a comparative study with existing tool-changers and demonstrations with the HRP-4 humanoid. We claim that our idea could be a new turn in the design of future humanoids and open perspective to modular sizing of robots. The proposed mechanism can possibly apply to animaloids to some extent.

title: A 65-nm Humanoid Robot System-on-Chip Using Time-Domain 3-D Footstep Planning and Mixed-Signal ZMP Gait Scheduler With Inverse Kinematics
abstract: This work presents a footstep planning chip for humanoid robot. It integrates a time-domain graph search engine for high-level 3-D footstep planning and a mixed-signal zero moment point (ZMP) gait scheduler with neural inverse kinematics, enabling efficient low-level motion control. The key contributions of this work include a time-domain graph search engine for 3-D footstep planning, featuring 3-D search capabilities, $D^{\ast } $ replanning for real-time adjustments, redundant path blocking, and efficient result readout. In addition, it introduces an energy-efficient mixed-signal ZMP gait scheduler for maintaining robot balance, along with a time-domain neural-network-based inverse kinematics module for controlling robot joints. This work is demonstrated in situ on a fully assembled robot using the 65-nm system-on-chip (SoC), achieving $2.7\times $ energy savings for graph search and an $18.4\times $ improvement in energy efficiency for motion control compared with prior works.
text: <title>A 65-nm Humanoid Robot System-on-Chip Using Time-Domain 3-D Footstep Planning and Mixed-Signal ZMP Gait Scheduler With Inverse Kinematics<abstract>Abstract:This work presents a footstep planning chip for humanoid robot. It integrates a time-domain graph search engine for high-level 3-D footstep planning and a mixed-signal zero moment point (ZMP) gait scheduler with neural inverse kinematics, enabling efficient low-level motion control. The key contributions of this work include a time-domain graph search engine for 3-D footstep planning, featuring 3-D search capabilities,D∗replanning for real-time adjustments, redundant path blocking, and efficient result readout. In addition, it introduces an energy-efficient mixed-signal ZMP gait scheduler for maintaining robot balance, along with a time-domain neural-network-based inverse kinematics module for controlling robot joints. This work is demonstrated in situ on a fully assembled robot using the 65-nm system-on-chip (SoC), achieving2.7×energy savings for graph search and an18.4×improvement in energy efficiency for motion control compared with prior works.
authors: Q. Cao; J. Chuen Oh; J. Gu

title: Reinforcement Learning of Contact Preferability in Multi-Contact Locomotion Planning for Humanoids
abstract: In this letter, we propose the multi-contact locomotion planning framework for humanoid robots that leverages the target contact selection considering its long-term preferability by reinforcement learning (RL) in optimization-based motion generation with feasibility constraints. It is difficult to predict how the next target contact will affect the motion of the robot over the future in multi-contact locomotion, where humanoid robots are required to perform complex motions with kinematic constraints and static equilibrium. To solve this problem, we evaluate the preferability of the motion planned by the optimization-based motion planner to reach the target contact, which we define as contact preferability, as the reward for RL. This idea enabled us to train the policy to provide a contact with the large future preferability without explicitly designing its future promise by ourselves. We also propose the design of action space for RL based on the robot's reachability. We construct sets of feasible joint angles for each limb of the robot as successors and use them as the action space instead of directly managing contact poses. By defining the deterministic mapping from the successor to the target contact, the proposed framework can manage acyclic multi-contact motion where the number of contacts can be changed. We evaluate the proposed framework in three scenarios and prove that it can plan a preferable contact sequence for multi-contact locomotion with a high success rate and short computational time.
keywords: multi-contact whole-body motion planning and control
