title: Optimization of Pelvic Rotation Walking Pattern Considering Future States Using Model Predictive Control to Increase the Step Length
abstract: Pelvic rotation, which is observed in human gait, is used to increase a robot’s step length in the humanoid robot walking. Existing methods empirically or experimentally generate the pelvic-rotation angle offline using predetermined pelvis and foot trajectories. Therefore, these methods are difficult to be used with the method to generate the center of mass (CoM) trajectory in real time using techniques such as preview control or model predictive model control. In this study, we propose a method that generates a pelvic-rotation trajectory that can be used with a real-time CoM generation method while reflecting the future state of the robot. The step length increased due to pelvic rotation was kinematically analyzed and compared with the step length increased by the proposed method. Upper body motion to compensate for yaw angular momentum generated by lower body movement during walking using pelvic rotation was optimized using centroial dynamics. The waist yaw joint for pelvic rotation, leg joint for the walking, and upper body joint for arm swing were optimized using separate optimal controllers. Energy efficiency, increase in step length, and decrease in the possibility of singularity occurrence of pelvic rotation walking were analyzed and compared in simulations. The proposed method was experimentally verified using humanoid robot Dyros-Jet.
text: <title>Optimization of Pelvic Rotation Walking Pattern Considering Future States Using Model Predictive Control to Increase the Step Length<abstract>Abstract:Pelvic rotation, which is observed in human gait, is used to increase a robot’s step length in the humanoid robot walking. Existing methods empirically or experimentally generate the pelvic-rotation angle offline using predetermined pelvis and foot trajectories. Therefore, these methods are difficult to be used with the method to generate the center of mass (CoM) trajectory in real time using techniques such as preview control or model predictive model control. In this study, we propose a method that generates a pelvic-rotation trajectory that can be used with a real-time CoM generation method while reflecting the future state of the robot. The step length increased due to pelvic rotation was kinematically analyzed and compared with the step length increased by the proposed method. Upper body motion to compensate for yaw angular momentum generated by lower body movement during walking using pelvic rotation was optimized using centroial dynamics. The waist yaw joint for pelvic rotation, leg joint for the walking, and upper body joint for arm swing were optimized using separate optimal controllers. Energy efficiency, increase in step length, and decrease in the possibility of singularity occurrence of pelvic rotation walking were analyzed and compared in simulations. The proposed method was experimentally verified using humanoid robot Dyros-Jet.<Introduction>Humanoid robots have been studied for the purpose of being applied to human work environments. However, the low walking speed of humanoid robots limits their usability. Methods that enable long strides are required to improve the walking velocity of humanoid robots. Humanoid walking using pelvic rotation has been studied to increase step length. Pelvic rotation during walking causes the hip of the swing leg to move forward as the swinging foot moves. This movement increases the landing distance with respect to the pelvis length. A human gait analysis showed that pelvic rotation is also present in the human gait[1],[2]. The angular momentum generated during walking may weaken the stability of a robot because a longer the stride increases the yaw angular momentum generated by the swing of the leg. Biomechanics studies have revealed that humans use arm swings to compensate for the yaw angular momentum[3],[4] The application of pelvic rotation to robot walking has been attempted to increase step length. In pelvic rotation walking, as the pelvis rotates, the hip of the swinging leg moves further forward than the hip of the supporting leg, and the step length can be increased. The yaw joint trajectory used for the pelvic rotation was determined offline using the previously generated pelvis and foot trajectories.A method used to generate the pelvic trajectory utilizes a sine function such that the pelvis can rotate according to the swing of the leg[2]. The pelvic rotation angle was experimentally determined to be proportional to the distance between the supporting and the swinging feet[5]. Additionally, the pelvic rotation angle was determined with respect to the velocity of the swinging foot[6]. Human walking motion data measured by a motion-capture device were used to optimize the pelvic rotation walking pattern[7]to reduce the error between the robot and motion-capture date. A genetic algorithm was also used to optimize the pelvis and foot trajectories[8]. The aforementioned methods to determine the pelvic rotation angle are limited because both the pelvis and foot trajectories must be generated in advance. Therefore, the pelvic-rotation trajectory is not generated in real time. However, preview control or model predictive control (MPC), which is often used in humanoid robot walking research, generates a center of mass (CoM) trajectory in real time[9]–​[12], which is difficult to combine with the method of generating the pelvic rotation trajectory introduced above. In a position-controlled robot, inverse kinematics (IK) was used to generate the angle of the leg joints using the positions and rotation trajectories of the pelvis and foot. To use IK, the pelvis and foot trajectories should be expressed in the same frame. For computational convenience, pelvis and foot trajectories that are expressed based on the pelvis frame are typically used for IK. Therefore, if the orientation of the pelvic-rotation trajectory is non-zero, the foot trajectory is generated by considering the rotation of the pelvis. A method using the torso was proposed to compensate the yaw angular momentum of humanoid robot walking[13]–​[16]. Using a simplified model of the robot’s upper body generates the waist yaw joint trajectory required to rotate the torso. When the waist yaw joint is used to rotate the torso of the robot to compensate for the angular momentum, it cannot be used to increase the step length because the pelvic rotation is fixed. When walking using pelvic rotation, angular momentum cannot be compensated using the waist yaw joint; therefore, the robot arm should be used. To compensate for the yaw angular momentum using the robot’s arm, a more accurate model than the simplified model of the robot’s upper body is required. Centroidal dynamics, which calculate the momentum in the CoM frame, is used to generate the arm-swing motion of the robot[17],[18]. Centroidal dynamics can calculate the momentum generated by the movement of each joint of the robot; therefore, it can calculate momentum more accurately than a simplified model. Centroidal dynamics was used as the whole body controllers for balancing. Centroidal dynamics has also been used to generate upper-body movements to compensate angular momentum during walking[18]–​[20]. Our previous study proposed a whole-body walking pattern generation method for the long step lengths. In the proposed method, the pelvic rotation trajectory was generated using the redundancy, and the method could be used with the real-time CoM trajectory generation method[21]. The lower body of the robot consisted of a waist yaw joint and both leg joints; therefore, it could be considered a redundant system. In addition, using the quadratic programming-based IK (QP-based IK) eliminated the process of changing the reference frame of the foot trajectory by reflecting the rotation of the pelvis. However, the future states of the foot and pelvis were not reflected; only the current states were reflected. Therefore, the waist yaw joint rotated only when the foot swung, and the angular velocity of the waist yaw joint increased rapidly as the step length increased. This sharp increase in the angular velocity of the waist joint may weaken the walking stability. In this study, we propose a method to optimize the pelvic-rotation trajectory for a long step length by reflecting the future state of the robot. The MPC scheme optimizes the pelvic-rotation trajectory using the predicted future CoM positions and the pre-determined foot trajectory in advance. Using a redundant kinematic structure, in which the waist yaw joint is included in the lower body, the angles of the lower-body joints are obtained using the QP-based IK. By using a redundant lower body, it is unnecessary to change the frame of the foot trajectory to account for pelvic rotation. The effect of pelvic rotation on the increase in step length was kinematically analyzed and comparatively verified in simulations. In addition, the waist yaw joint cannot be used to compensate for the yaw angular momentum; therefore, an arm swing motion that compensates for the yaw angular momentum was generated using centroidal dynamics. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.Section IIanalyzes the effect of pelvic rotation on the increase in step length. The structure of the proposed system is explained inSection III.Section IVexplains the concept of walking pattern generation.Section Vdescribes the process of optimizing the walking pattern, including the pelvic rotation trajectory, using an MPC scheme. InSection VI, the results of the simulation and experiments are discussed, andSection VIIconcludes the paper.<Kinematic Analysis>This section kinematically analyzes the extent to which pelvic rotation walking can increase step length.Fig. 1shows the maximum step length with and without pelvic rotation. For the kinematic analysis of the increase in step length, it is assumed that the robot’s left and right legs are outstretched, and the center of the pelvis is between the feet, as shown inFig. 1. If the length of the leg when the knee is extended is$l_{leg}$and the height from the ankle to the hip joint is$z_{0}$, the maximum step length during walking without pelvic rotation,$l^{pelvic-fixed} _{step max}$is as follows:\begin{equation*} l^{pelvic-fixed}_{step max} = 2\sqrt {l^{2}_{leg}-z^{2}_{0}}.\tag{1}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} l^{pelvic-fixed}_{step max} = 2\sqrt {l^{2}_{leg}-z^{2}_{0}}.\tag{1}\end{equation*} When the pelvis rotates around the hip joint of the supporting leg by$\theta _{pel}$, the forward distance in the sagittal plane between both hip joints,$\delta d_{hip}$, increases proportionalyy to the width of the pelvis and$\theta _{pel}$:\begin{equation*} \Delta d_{hip} = l_{pel}\cdot sin \theta _{pel}.\tag{2}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} \Delta d_{hip} = l_{pel}\cdot sin \theta _{pel}.\tag{2}\end{equation*} The kinematically possible maximum step length during walking using pelvic rotation is when the line passing through both hip joints coincides with the line passing through the ankles of feet, and can be calculated using the length of the pelvis and the width between the feet.\begin{equation*} l^{pelvic-rotation}_{step max} = \sqrt {(l^{step}_{max}+l_{pel})^{2}-w_{step}^{2}}\tag{3}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} l^{pelvic-rotation}_{step max} = \sqrt {(l^{step}_{max}+l_{pel})^{2}-w_{step}^{2}}\tag{3}\end{equation*} For kinematic analysis, it is assumed that the robot stands while the center of the pelvis is located between the feet with both legs extended. However, when the pelvis moves toward the front foot during the double support phase (DSP), a singularity occurs in the hind leg. Therefore,$l^{pelvic-rotation}_{step max}$cannot be regarded as a possible step length for humanoid robot walking. As a simple example, an increase in the step length owing to the pelvic rotation during static walking is shown inFig. 2. During the single support phase (SSP), if it is assumed that the center of the pelvis is at the center of the supporting foot, and the robot does not fall, even during the leg swing. At this time, the maximum step length when walking without pelvic rotation is the distance from the hip to the ankle of the robot when the foot lands on the ground, and the knee of the swinging leg is fully extended.\begin{equation*} l^{*pelvic-fixed}_{step max} = \sqrt {l^{2}_{leg} - z^{2}_{0}},\tag{4}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} l^{*pelvic-fixed}_{step max} = \sqrt {l^{2}_{leg} - z^{2}_{0}},\tag{4}\end{equation*} Walking using pelvic rotation increased the step length in accordance with the angle of the pelvic rotation.\begin{equation*} l^{*pelvic-rotation}_{step max} = \sqrt {l^{2}_{leg}-z^{2}_{0}} + \Delta d^{*}_{hc},\tag{5}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} l^{*pelvic-rotation}_{step max} = \sqrt {l^{2}_{leg}-z^{2}_{0}} + \Delta d^{*}_{hc},\tag{5}\end{equation*}where$\Delta d^{*}_{hc}$is the length from the left hip joint to the center of the pelvis in the$x$direction, ($\Delta d^{*}_{hc} = 0.5*l_{pel}\cdot sin \theta _{pel}$). The humanoid robot used in this study, Dyros-Jet, had$l_{leg}$of 0.75 m,$z_{0}$of 0.68 m,$l_{pel}$of 0.21 m, and$w_{step}$of 0.243 m. For the pelvic rotation angle, it is assumed that the hip joint of the right leg is sufficiently rotated to be in the same position as the ankle joint in the x direction. At this time, the pelvic rotation angle,$\theta _{pel} = 45^{\circ }$, and the maximum step length with pelvic rotation is 0.42 m. The step length increased by 35% compared with the maximum step length of 0.31 m when walking without pelvic rotation.<Walking Pattern Generation>This section describes the generation of the walking patterns. The CoM, pelvis, and foot trajectory are generated based on the supporting foot frame and are used after changing to the pelvis frame. In addition, the lower-body Jacobian that is expressed based on the pelvis frame is used in the structure of the robot system.<Proposed Method for Optimizing Pelvic Rotation Trajectory>This section describes the proposed method for optimizing the pelvic-rotation trajectory using the predicted future state of the CoM in the MPC scheme. With the predicted CoM states and the foot trajectory, which is generated in advance, the angular velocity of the the waist yaw joint is optimized using the MPC. The optimized waist yaw joint is used as the constraint for the QP-based IK to track the desired foot velocity. Centroidal dynamics is used to generate the arm-swing motion to compensate for the yaw angular momentum.<Conclusion>This study proposed a method to optimize pelvic-rotation walking using MPC in multilayered optimal control. The multilayered optimal control proposed herein consisted of three layers that optimized the waist yaw joint, leg joints, and upper joints, respectively. The waist yaw joint was optimized using MPC for pelvic-rotation walking. Moreover, the reference pelvis angle used for the MPC was determined using the predicted future positions of the pelvis and foot of the robot. In successive optimal control layers, the leg and upper body joints were optimized to track the desired foot trajectory and compensate the angular momentum. The proposed method was analyzed via a simulation. Walking using pelvic rotation increased the step length by approximately 33% compared to walking without pelvic rotation. In addition, the pelvic-rotation trajectory generated by reflecting the future state of the robot using MPC was more stable than that generated by reflecting only the robot state at every control time using the redundancy of the robot. The energy consumption of the different walking methods was compared and analyzed in the simulation. Walking using the proposed method consumes the least energy, except for a specific step length. In addition, a comparison of condition numbers showed that walking using pelvic rotation reduces the possibility of a singularity occurrence. The experiment verified the proposed algorithm and demonstrated that the arm swing compensated the yaw angular momentum. In future, we intend to study the utilization of pelvic rotation when changing the position of the foot or changing the CoM trajectory to balance against disturbances. This study considered only the yaw rotation of the pelvis; therefore, we will study the roll and pitch orientation of the pelvis to the robot and analyze its effect. In addition, we will apply the heel-strike and toe-off motions to the robot walking motion to increase the step length by avoiding the singularity that occurs in the hind leg while the robot moves forward during the DSP.
authors: B. Park; J. Park

title: MPC-Based Walking Stability Control for Bipedal Robots on Uneven Terrain
abstract: This paper proposes an algorithm capable of regenerating gait patterns online. The algorithm is designed using the Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, with the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model as the basis of the predictive model. For bipedal robot walking, it divides ZMP (Zero Moment Point) constraints into single-leg support, double-leg support, and start-end phases, reformulating them into a complete quadratic programming problem. This approach allows for adjustments to both the foot placement and the timing of steps to maintain dynamic stability during walking. To address the limited contact force sensing capability between the robot and the ground in the gait generator, pressure sensors on both feet of the robot are used to monitor pressure distribution, adjusting the allocation of pressure between the feet accordingly. Finally, simulation and experimental results demonstrate the performance of the proposed method. The controller maintains dynamic stability for the bipedal robot when walking on either soft artificial grass or hard wooden boards.
text: <title>MPC-Based Walking Stability Control for Bipedal Robots on Uneven Terrain<abstract>Abstract:This paper proposes an algorithm capable of regenerating gait patterns online. The algorithm is designed using the Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, with the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model as the basis of the predictive model. For bipedal robot walking, it divides ZMP (Zero Moment Point) constraints into single-leg support, double-leg support, and start-end phases, reformulating them into a complete quadratic programming problem. This approach allows for adjustments to both the foot placement and the timing of steps to maintain dynamic stability during walking. To address the limited contact force sensing capability between the robot and the ground in the gait generator, pressure sensors on both feet of the robot are used to monitor pressure distribution, adjusting the allocation of pressure between the feet accordingly. Finally, simulation and experimental results demonstrate the performance of the proposed method. The controller maintains dynamic stability for the bipedal robot when walking on either soft artificial grass or hard wooden boards.<Introduction>After years of research, many robots are now deployed in practical applications, with most being stationary robots[1]and wheeled robots. Due to their structural design, these robots are limited to specific environments, such as factories and warehouses. For instance, the wheeled robot Stretch, developed by Boston Dynamics[2], demonstrates excellent load-carrying capacity and maneuverability, even with the ability to handle up to 800 boxes per hour. However, its structural limitations restrict its operation to flat environments. To navigate complex terrains encountered in real life, alternative forms of mobility beyond wheeled robots are required. One such option is humanoid robots. For example, the Cassie bipedal robot developed by Agility Robotics[3]can effortlessly traverse stairs, sidewalks, and rural roads—everyday environments commonly seen in schools, factories, and apartment complexes. Cassie can even reach a walking speed of up to 5 km/h, which is comparable to that of an average adult male. Although continuous research and improvements are necessary for humanoid robots, their excellent adaptability to various terrains underscores their potential for future development. The stability of humanoid robots during walking is typically determined by whether the Zero Moment Point (ZMP)[4]remains within the robot’s support polygon. As such, ZMP is an important control variable in bipedal walking. Many studies have examined methods to control ZMP, with model-based approaches focusing heavily on mathematical models for humanoid robots. Among the most popular models is the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM)[5], which, when expanded, can take the center of mass (CoM) acceleration[6]or ZMP velocity[7]as input variables, ensuring ZMP stability by calculating the input accordingly. This paper employs the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model because the dynamics of humanoid robots are complex, and overly complicated calculations may lead to control delays. Using the linearized inverted pendulum model ensures a certain level of stability while reducing computation. Controllers that calculate model inputs are referred to as gait generators. Early approaches commonly used polynomial[8]calculations for model inputs; however, due to the complexity of humanoid motion, polynomials cannot account for numerous influencing factors. In recent years, the field of humanoid robotics has increasingly turned to optimization[9]to solve robotic challenges, with Model Predictive Control (MPC)[10],[11],[12]emerging as a popular method. MPC’s advantages include its ability to perform optimization over a finite time horizon and maintain iterative calculations, often used in speed control and gait generation for humanoid walking. However, since MPC requires iterative calculations, it demands significant processing power, making it challenging for typical embedded development boards. Consequently, much research has focused on reducing the complexity of optimization problems. Modern gait generators are mostly designed with closed-loop feedback, offering a certain level of disturbance rejection. However, to minimize computational load, gait generators often limit control variables. Disturbances not considered by the gait generator are typically compensated for using stabilizers[6],[13]. Common research topics in this area include Push Recovery[14]and balance control on uneven terrain[15],[16]. Humanoid robots are classified as floating base, subject to various disturbances during movement. This makes state estimation challenging compared to stationary robots. Accurate state estimation directly impacts controller or compensator performance, making it a highly relevant topic in humanoid robotics. To overcome measurement errors caused by disturbances, many studies employ fusion algorithms, with algorithms that fuse IMU information and kinematics being widely used. These typically require only a single IMU sensor placed on the waist, a simple and reliable approach especially suited to small humanoid robots where additional components cannot be installed. Depending on specific functions and goals, other sensors such as cameras[17], pressure sensors[18], and LIDAR[19]are also used for data fusion.<System Architecture>The primary objectives of the humanoid robot’s walking control in this paper are twofold: first, to use its mathematical model to pre-plan motion trajectories, and second, to utilize a stabilizer to compensate for any inadequacies in the motion trajectory. Ideally, bipedal walking can be achieved by planning the desired gait trajectory for the humanoid robot. However, in real-world conditions, it is impossible to achieve stable bipedal walking with open-loop control alone, as any disturbance could cause the robot to topple. Therefore, feedback on the robot’s state is needed to adjust its motion trajectory. The walking gait control framework used by the humanoid robot in this paper is shown inFig. 1. The system is implemented using Model Predictive Control (MPC) as the core technology, with a feedback-based gait pattern generator. The cruise parameters guide the gait generator to produce either straight walking or turning gaits. The gait generator then instantly generates the CoM (Center of Mass) trajectory$p_{c}^{d}$and bipedal foot trajectories$p_{L}^{d}$and$p_{R}^{d}$required for bipedal walking based on the robot’s CoM position$p_{c}$and velocity$\dot {p}_{c}$. Subsequently, the gait trajectory undergoes further adjustments by the bipedal pressure controller to modify the foot trajectories$p_{L}^{d^{\ast } } $and$p_{R}^{d^{\ast } }$. This adjustment is necessary because the gait generator is designed under the assumption that the robot is walking on flat ground. When disturbances occur or the robot encounters uneven terrain, additional compensation is required to maintain stability. To calculate the ZMP position, eight single-degree-of-freedom (1 DOF) pressure sensors are installed on the soles of the humanoid robot’s feet, allowing the measurement of the vertical ground reaction force. The Center of Mass (CoM) observer, used in this paper, estimates the CoM position$p_{c}$and velocity$\dot {p}_{c}$of the humanoid robot during motion, providing the robot states required by the gait generator. This observer is based on Kalman filtering as the core technology. The measurements are obtained using the IMU to capture the tilt angles of the robot’s upper body, combined with a fixed-point strategy to estimate the CoM position. The predictive model is a discretized Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM), which is used to derive the predicted state estimation. Finally, through iterative calculations, the optimal state estimation is obtained. The humanoid robot used in this paper is a custom-developed small humanoid robot, shown inFig. 2. It is height 59 cm, a weight of 5.4 kg, and is designed with 6 DOF in each leg, 1 DOF in the waist, 4 DOF in each arm, and 2 DOF in the head, for a total of 23 DOF. For the human-machine interface and process control, a PICO-APL3 industrial computer with a Pentium N4200 2.4 GHz processor is used. Motion control and the MPC framework are implemented on a DE10-Nano SoC embedded development board with a dual-core ARM Cortex-A9 800 MHz processor. The MPC framework is written in C++ and operates in real-time, utilizing the Eigen library for matrix operations, the eiquadprog library (modified with the dual method) for solving quadratic programming problems, and an eigenvector method for matrix exponential calculations. The control frequency of the MPC framework is set to 16.66 Hz (sampling time). According to the experimental results of this paper, the humanoid robot can walk on a combined terrain of soft and hard surfaces, thereby meeting the control requirements.<Gait Pattern Generator>This paper designs a feedback-based gait pattern generator implemented using Model Predictive Control (MPC) as the core technology. This module generates the gait trajectories required for bipedal walking based on gait commands provided by either the user or the humanoid robot itself. The control framework is shown inFig. 3. The footstep generator is the first component of the gait pattern generator, planning the positions of the humanoid robot’s foot soles on the ground$p_{f}$based on user-defined cruising parameters. Then, using the predictive model and ZMP constraints, MPC is designed to generate the CoM (Center of Mass) trajectory$p_{c}^{d}$and the ZMP trajectory$p_{f}^{d}$based on feedback from the robot’s CoM state. Finally, the swing foot trajectory generator produces the trajectories of the robot’s feet while swinging in the air.<Bipedal Pressure Controller>This paper designs a controller to adjust the vertical pressure$(f_{Lz},f_{Rz})$between both feet during the Double Support Phase (DSP).\begin{equation*} z_{ctrl} =A_{fz} [(f_{Lz}^{d} -f_{Rz}^{d})-(f_{Lz} -f_{Rz})] \tag {32}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} z_{ctrl} =A_{fz} [(f_{Lz}^{d} -f_{Rz}^{d})-(f_{Lz} -f_{Rz})] \tag {32}\end{equation*}According to this control law, the height of both feet will be adjusted through this control method. The error$f_{Lz}^{d} -f_{Rz}^{d}$of the reference force$(f_{Lz}^{d},f_{Rz}^{d})$output by the ZMP distributor is used as the reference input. The error$(f_{Lz}^{d} -f_{Rz}^{d})-(f_{Lz} -f_{Rz})$, when multiplied by the admittance gain$A_{fz}$, produces the controller output$z_{ctrl}$. The height of both feet will then be modified through$z_{ctrl}$to achieve the control objective$f_{Lz}^{d} -f_{Rz}^{d}$. The modification of the foot heights is implemented using the following equation:\begin{align*} p_{Rz}^{d^{\ast }}& =p_{Rz}^{d} +0.5z_{ctrl} \tag {33}\\ p_{Lz}^{d^{\ast }}& =p_{Lz}^{d} -0.5z_{ctrl} \tag {34}\end{align*}View Source\begin{align*} p_{Rz}^{d^{\ast }}& =p_{Rz}^{d} +0.5z_{ctrl} \tag {33}\\ p_{Lz}^{d^{\ast }}& =p_{Lz}^{d} -0.5z_{ctrl} \tag {34}\end{align*}Here,$p_{Rz}^{d},p_{Lz}^{d}$represents the foot sole position planned by the gait generator, and$p_{Rz}^{d^{\ast } },p_{Lz}^{d^{\ast } }$represents the corrected position after adjustments.<Conclusion>We proposed a method capable of regenerating gait patterns by utilizing Model Predictive Control (MPC) to achieve gait generation with tracking control. The process begins by planning a series of footstep positions based on the walking direction. Then, using the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM) as the predictive model foundation, the formulation of the cost function and ZMP constraints is rewritten into a complete quadratic programming problem to generate the robot’s CoM trajectory. The foot force difference controller mitigates the impact of reaction forces when the robot’s feet contact the ground. Simulation and experimental results of the robot’s walking validate the proposed method, demonstrating that the bipedal robot can stably walk on surfaces under various conditions. The MPC parameters proposed in this paper can be adjusted according to different humanoid robot structures, such as variations in mass and center of mass position. Although the method used in this paper enables stable walking for humanoid robots, implementing MPC on lower-performance hardware and ultra-low-power devices remains a challenge.
authors: C. -C. Liu; Y. -C. Lin; C. -S. Li

title: Time-Efficient Contact Consistent Whole-Body Control Framework via Reduced-Dimension Dynamics Construction
abstract: Whole-body control frameworks for highly redundant, floating-base robots like humanoids are challenging due to the increased computational complexity arising from their high degrees of freedom. In this paper, the concept of reduced-dimension dynamics previously applied to whole-body control frameworks is extended by integrating it into the operational space formulation. The reduced-dimension dynamics simplifies the dimension of the dynamic model of humanoid robots by partitioning the kinematic chain into constrained and unconstrained chains. The unconstrained chain is reduced using centroidal dynamics, enabling efficient computational modeling in the operational space. By applying the reduced-dimension dynamics to operational space whole-body control, the computational burden caused by the high degrees of freedom in the whole-body dynamics is reduced, leading to shorter computation times. Unlike existing methods that utilize full-dimensional whole-body dynamics, the proposed method constructs a more efficient framework by performing optimization on reduced-dimensional dynamics, combined with operational space formulation. Comparative simulation results demonstrate a significant reduction in computation time, specifically a 41% decrease compared to existing methods, which provides a new approach to contact-consistent control in humanoid robots.
text: <title>Time-Efficient Contact Consistent Whole-Body Control Framework via Reduced-Dimension Dynamics Construction<abstract>Abstract:Whole-body control frameworks for highly redundant, floating-base robots like humanoids are challenging due to the increased computational complexity arising from their high degrees of freedom. In this paper, the concept of reduced-dimension dynamics previously applied to whole-body control frameworks is extended by integrating it into the operational space formulation. The reduced-dimension dynamics simplifies the dimension of the dynamic model of humanoid robots by partitioning the kinematic chain into constrained and unconstrained chains. The unconstrained chain is reduced using centroidal dynamics, enabling efficient computational modeling in the operational space. By applying the reduced-dimension dynamics to operational space whole-body control, the computational burden caused by the high degrees of freedom in the whole-body dynamics is reduced, leading to shorter computation times. Unlike existing methods that utilize full-dimensional whole-body dynamics, the proposed method constructs a more efficient framework by performing optimization on reduced-dimensional dynamics, combined with operational space formulation. Comparative simulation results demonstrate a significant reduction in computation time, specifically a 41% decrease compared to existing methods, which provides a new approach to contact-consistent control in humanoid robots.<Introduction>Humanoid robots have achieved remarkable advancements in recent years, primarily driven by the growing need for machines capable of operating seamlessly within human-centric environments. A central challenge in this domain is the real-time control of robots with high degrees of freedom (DOF), especially when they engage in complex and dynamic interactions with their surroundings. Whole-body control (WBC) has emerged as a pivotal solution to this problem, enabling robots to perform multiple tasks simultaneously at the torque level while accounting for essential constraints such as contact forces and the robot’s intricate dynamics[1],[2]. Following these developments, significant progress and successful applications of WBC in tasks like balancing, motion stabilization, and reactive walking have continued[3],[4],[5]. However, these methods involved calculating control inputs analytically, by projecting the whole-body dynamics to the operational spaces, and could not consider inequality constraints such as contact requirements or torque limits. To address this limitation, Quadratic Programming (QP)-based controllers were developed[6],[7],[8],[9]. Subsequently, to maintain an explicit hierarchy of tasks and constraints, several studies have utilized Lexicographic Quadratic Programming (LQP), also known as Hierarchical Quadratic Programming (HQP)[10],[11]. Despite these advancements, controlling high-DOF humanoid robots in real time remains a formidable challenge. The inherent computational complexity of such systems often leads to latency, which can critically undermine control stability’a concern highlighted in prior studies[12],[13]. One major contributor to this computational burden is the necessity to model humanoid robots as floating-base systems. This modeling approach requires the introduction of virtual joints to represent the robot’s free-floating movements in space, effectively increasing the DOF and adding unactuated variables that must be compensated for by the actuated joints. Moreover, continuous contact interactions and the high DOF themselves further exacerbate the computational burden. To achieve computational efficiency greater than the previous research, this paper extends the application of Reduced-Dimension Dynamics[14]to the Operational Space Formulation based HQP (OSF-based HQP)[15], as seen ifFig. 1. The reduced-dimension dynamics is partial-simplification method of dynamics. Unlike other methods, this method maintains the dynamics properties in perspective of constraints and interaction of robot to the environment. OSF-based HQP is a framework that combines OS-WBC with HQP, thereby showing the significant enhancement to computational efficiency. This paper aims at combining these two efficient previous methods, reduced-dimension dynamics and OSF-based HQP, creating an exceptionally efficient control framework that leverages existing research in the field. The contributions of this paper are threefold: By combining the existing methods of reduced-dimension dynamics and the OS-WBC framework, significant computational efficiency was achieved compared to traditional approaches. Extending this framework to incorporate HQP, enhancing the control system’s capability to handle multiple tasks with a clear hierarchy. Establishing a highly efficient control framework that not only reduces computational load but also maintains the accuracy and stability of the control system. To elucidate these contributions, the paper is structured as follows:Section IIprovides a related work to the computational efficiency of the WBC.Section IIIintroduces the fundamentals of WBC and OS-WBC, OSF-based HQP and reduced-dimension dynamics.Section IVintroduces the application of reduced dimension dynamics to OS-WBC framework for constructing efficient dynamics and integrating them into an HQP formulation. InSection V, the proposed framework is validated through simulations, demonstrating its computational efficiency and effectiveness. Finally,Section VIconcludes the paper with a discussion of the findings and potential avenues for future research.<Related Work>The high computational cost due to the high DOF and the complexity of the frameworks are always the concern in humanoid research[16],[17]. To mitigate this issue, various methods have been proposed to enhance computational efficiency. Herzog et al.[11]proposed the LQP method, and reduced computational cost by decomposing the optimization variables, especially constraints arising from whole-body dynamics. De Lasa et al.[18]focused on developing solvers to reduce the computational load of LQP. Additionally, dedicated solvers have been developed[19],[20]that achieve significant computational improvements. Despite the development of dedicated solvers for LQP, many WBC approaches still rely on off-the-shelf optimization solvers due to the difficulty of building custom solvers[21],[22],[23]. From this perspective, Sathya et al.[24]formulated the LQP problem using a weighted method and linear problem method, demonstrating performance improvements even with off-the-shelf optimization solvers. Previous related works were focused on the formulation or solving method of the optimization problem. Unlike these methods, Lee et al.[15],[25]tried another approach, utilizing the OSF to the WBC optimization problem, constructing OSF-based HQP framework. This method enables optimization formulation in the operational space and results in an efficient optimization framework. However, the OSF-based framework had the drawback that constructing the OSF required significantly more time as the robot’s DOF increased. To address the persistent issue of high computational cost in WBC formulations, another novel method, the reduced-dimension dynamics was introduced in previous work[14]for constructing reduced-dimension rigid body dynamics. This state-of-the-art approach involves partitioning the robot’s kinematic chain into constrained and unconstrained segments based on contact constraints. By projecting the dynamics of the unconstrained joints into a centroidal space, informed by their centroidal dynamics, the overall dynamics are effectively simplified without compromising the accuracy of the control inputs. Leveraging the dynamic properties of the unconstrained chain allows for more efficient management of computational loads and a significant reduction in computational time. This study also demonstrated that by applying reduced-dimension dynamics to LQP, computation time can be significantly reduced even when using off-the-shelf QP solvers.<Background on the Whole-Body Control Framework of Humanoid Robots>The proposed method combines reduced-dimension dynamics with the OSF-based HQP framework. Therefore, this section explains the background of the OSF-based HQP framework and reduced-dimension dynamics. Additionally, since the OSF-based HQP relies on the OSF, an explanation of OSF will also be provided.<Proposed Method>The proposed method combines reduced-dimension dynamics with OSF-based HQP. To achieve this, it first constructs the OSF using reduced-dimension dynamics and develops a method for calculating the control torques accordingly. Then, an HQP control framework is built utilizing the OSF constructed through reduced-dimension dynamics. In this section, the method for constructing the OSF based on existing task classifications (CP tasks and IP tasks) is explained, followed by a description of how to formulate the HQP framework using this reduced-dimension dynamics OSF. The proposed method extends the reduced-dimension dynamics to OSF, then apply the reduced-dimension OSF to the HQP framework. When calculating control torques using the reduced-dimension OSF, it is essential to project the task spaces from the original model into the reduced model. Tasks are classified based on how they are affected by this projection process.<Verification>The proposed method combines two efficient previous methods: OSF-based HQP and reduced-dimension dynamics. To demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method, computational time is compared to that of the conventional OSF-based HQP method. Additionally, since previous research has shown that reduced-dimension dynamics improve computational efficiency in LQP formulations of whole-body control, the computational time of the LQP formulation utilizing reduced-dimension dynamics is also compared with that of the proposed method. Since the proposed method focuses on computational efficiency, the simulation calculations are compared to evaluate its performance.<Conclusion>In this paper, a new computationally efficient framework has been developed by combining reduced-dimension dynamics with OSF-based HQP. Both methods represent a departure from previous approaches that sought to enhance computational efficiency through solver-based or constraint-based techniques. Reduced-dimension dynamics reduces the dimensionality of the dynamics itself, while OSF-based HQP precomputes the optimization formulation using OSF. By integrating these two efficient methods into a unified framework, a significant reduction in computation time compared to existing frameworks has achieved. Specifically, in the double-support scenario, the computation time of the proposed framework decreased by approximately 41% when compared to conventional OSF-based HQP. Compared to the conventional LQP, we observed a 92% reduction, and compared to the LQP with reduced-dimension dynamics applied, a 76% reduction in computation time. Additionally, the control results were identical to those obtained with the conventional OSF-based HQP, indicating that the proposed method maintains dynamic characteristics while solely reducing computation time, unlike other simplification techniques. Simulations also showed that the framework becomes more efficient with fewer contact DOFs and a greater number of unconstrained chain tasks. This application not only proves the practicality of the reduced-dimension dynamics method in the context of OS-WBC but also introduces a new perspective on calculating control torques for high-DOF humanoid robots. By effectively reducing the computational burden associated with traditional WBC methods, the approach addresses a critical challenge in the real-time control of humanoid robots. This reduction in computation time results in decreased control latency, which can lead to an increased phase margin, thereby enhancing control stability. to enhanced control stability. Additionally, the lower computational cost may not only improve control stability but also reduce processor expenses and increase power efficiency in computers. The successful implementation of reduced-dimension dynamics opens avenues for further research and development. Future work will explore applying these principles to develop faster computational models for Model Predictive Control (MPC), aiming to surpass the speed of conventional whole-body MPC approaches. Additionally, integrating the OS-WBC framework with learning-based control methods represents another promising direction. These advancements aim to harness the computational efficiencies detailed in this study to enhance the responsiveness and adaptability of control systems, paving the way for more dynamic and efficient robotic applications.<Appendix Average Spatial Velocity>Theaverage spatial velocityof the multi-body robots as inFig. 2can be interpreted through centroidal dynamics[32]. The centroidal momentum vector can be obtained as follows.\begin{equation*} \mathbf {h}_{G} = \mathbf {A}_{G}(\mathbf {q}){\dot {\mathbf q}} \tag {36}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} \mathbf {h}_{G} = \mathbf {A}_{G}(\mathbf {q}){\dot {\mathbf q}} \tag {36}\end{equation*}where$\mathbf {h}_{G} \in \mathbb {R}^{6 \times 1}$is a centroidal momentum vector.$\mathbf {A}_{G}(q) \in \mathbb {R}^{6\times n} $is a centroidal momentum matrix, which can be obtained easily using the inertia matrix of the robot[33]. With this centroidal momentum vector, the average spatial velocity$\mathbf {v}_{G}$of the robot can be calculated:\begin{equation*} \mathbf {v}_{G} = (\mathbf {I}_{G})^{-1}\mathbf {h}_{G}, \tag {37}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} \mathbf {v}_{G} = (\mathbf {I}_{G})^{-1}\mathbf {h}_{G}, \tag {37}\end{equation*}where$\mathbf {I}_{G} \in \mathbb {R}^{6 \times 6} $is a inertial matrix containing mass and inertia tensor. From this average spatial velocity$\mathbf {v}_{G}$, the centroidal inertial Jacobian can be obtained as\begin{equation*} \mathbf {J}_{G} = (\mathbf {I}_{G})^{-1} \mathbf {A}_{G}(\mathbf {q}). \tag {38}\end{equation*}View Source\begin{equation*} \mathbf {J}_{G} = (\mathbf {I}_{G})^{-1} \mathbf {A}_{G}(\mathbf {q}). \tag {38}\end{equation*}With this centroidal inertial Jacobian$\mathbf {J}_{G}$, the relationship between the joint velocity of a multi-body system and the average spatial velocity can be calculated.

title: Learning Humanoid Arm Motion via Centroidal Momentum Regularized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Humans naturally swing their arms during locomotion to regulate whole-body dynamics, reduce angular momentum, and help maintain balance. Inspired by this principle, we present a limb-level multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) framework that enables coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots through emergent arm motion. Our approach employs separate actor-critic structures for the arms and legs, trained with centralized critics but decentralized actors that share only base states and centroidal angular momentum (CAM) observations, allowing each agent to specialize in task-relevant behaviors through modular reward design. The arm agent guided by CAM tracking and damping rewards promotes arm motions that reduce overall angular momentum and vertical ground reaction moments, contributing to improved balance during locomotion or under external perturbations. Comparative studies with single-agent and alternative multi-agent baselines further validate the effectiveness of our approach. Finally, we deploy the learned policy on the MIT Humanoid, achieving robust performance across diverse locomotion tasks, including flat-ground walking, rough terrain traversal, and stair climbing.

title: A Hybrid Motion Optimization Framework for the Humanoid Upper-Body Robot: Safe and Dexterous Object Carrying
abstract: In this letter, a novel hybrid motion optimization framework is proposed for a humanoid upper-body robot with two 7-DOF arms and a 2-DOF waist, to flexibly and safely carry objects in constrained and dynamic environments. The framework consists of trilayer interconnected optimization, which is dedicated to planning the optimal carrying configuration, waist-arm motion trajectory, and dual-arm nullspace trajectory, respectively. The top layer finds the most dexterous waist-arm carrying configuration that satisfies environmental constraints, which is achieved by the effective integration of the multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (EA), the proposed optimal manipulation index, and the parameterization method. The middle layer applies a non-linear optimization method to plan collision-free trajectory that connects the initial and optimal carrying configuration. The bottom layer is achieved by equipping the top layer with elite reproduction operator strategy and adaptive evolution space strategy, generating dual-arm nullspace trajectory in real-time for dynamic obstacle avoidance. The various carrying experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Optimized Design and Calibration of a Human-Eye-Sized Active Binocular Vision System Based on Spherical Parallel Mechanism
abstract: The Active Binocular Vision System (ABVS), resembling the human eye, demonstrates potential for improving visual perception in robotic systems, especially in dynamic and complex environments. In this letter, we present an optimized design of a three degree-of-freedom (DoF) Active Monocular Vision System (AMVS) based on a Spherical Parallel Manipulator (SPM). By combining two identical AMVS units, we form an ABVS, which has been successfully integrated into a humanoid robotic head. Due to the highly nonlinear kinematics of SPM and complex error coupling in its multi-link structure, traditional end-to-end neural network training methods are insufficient in accuracy and require large datasets. To address these challenges, we propose a two-branch optimization network that significantly improves calibration accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a four-branch fine-tuning strategy that enables accurate kinematic models to be obtained with only a small amount of data from new AMVS devices. Experimental results demonstrate that the two-branch optimization network reduces rotational prediction error by 16% and translational error by 5% compared to a single-branch network. Furthermore, the four-branch fine-tuning network achieves comparable accuracy to a fully trained single-branch network using only 343 data points. Finally, our ABVS shows the capability to perform 3D visual tasks, such as stereo reconstruction during movement.

title: Fast Autolearning for Multimodal Walking in Humanoid Robots With Variability of Experience
abstract: Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) and humanoid robotics are rapidly addressing the challenge of adapting to complex, dynamic environments in real time. This letter introduces a novel approach that integrates two key concepts: experience variability (a criterion for detecting changes in loco-manipulation) and experience accumulation (an efficient method for storing acquired experiences based on a selection criterion). These elements are incorporated into the development of RL agents and humanoid robots, with an emphasis on stability. This focus enhances adaptability and efficiency in unpredictable environments. Our approach enables more sophisticated modeling of such environments, significantly improving the system's ability to adapt to real-world complexities. By combining this method with advanced RL techniques, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), and incorporating self-learning driven by stability, we improve the system's generalization capabilities. This facilitates rapid learning from novel and previously unseen scenarios. We validate our algorithm through both simulations and real-world experiments on the HRP-4 humanoid robot, utilizing an intrinsically stable model predictive controller.
keywords: deep learning methods and reinforcement learning

title: Maximising Tolerance to Disturbances via Combined Control-Actuation Optimisation for Robust Humanoid Robot Walking
abstract: Combined optimisation of various robot subsystems as a co-design problem has been shown to identify performant robots. However, classical optimisation methods result in point-optimum solutions that may not ensure robust performance and physical feasibility, i.e., the existence of components with specifications matching the computed optimum value. To address this problem, we present a set-based robust co-design optimisation strategy to maximise disturbance tolerance. Instead of identifying a single point-optimum solution, a so-called solution space evaluates the combination of the largest design space that delivers the necessary performance while being robust to the largest set of disturbances. The utility of the proposed approach is demonstrated via a computational design study of the ergoCub robot. This study focuses on the robots' walking performance, illustrating (1) improvement in task success considering at least 3 times larger magnitudes of disturbances, (2) identifying a set instead of a point-solution in the design-disturbances space, and (3) improving standardisation of the joint actuation design.
keywords: methods and tools for robot system design
text: <title>Maximising Tolerance to Disturbances via Combined Control-Actuation Optimisation for Robust Humanoid Robot Walking<abstract>Abstract:Combined optimisation of various robot subsystems as a co-design problem has been shown to identify performant robots. However, classical optimisation methods result in point-optimum solutions that may not ensure robust performance and physical feasibility, i.e., the existence of components with specifications matching the computed optimum value. To address this problem, we present a set-based robust co-design optimisation strategy to maximise disturbance tolerance. Instead of identifying a single point-optimum solution, a so-called solution space evaluates the combination of the largest design space that delivers the necessary performance while being robust to the largest set of disturbances. The utility of the proposed approach is demonstrated via a computational design study of the ergoCub robot. This study focuses on the robots' walking performance, illustrating (1) improvement in task success considering at least 3 times larger magnitudes of disturbances, (2) identifying a set instead of a point-solution in the design-disturbances space, and (3) improving standardisation of the joint actuation design.<Introduction>Optimisation-driven automatic gain-tuning (GT) is often used to tune the controller parameters to obtain the required output performance of a robot[1]. Alternatively, concurrent optimisation of various subsystems like mechanical, actuation, and control of a robotic system, as a co-design (CD) problem, has been shown to identify not only better-performing designs[2]but also novel designs with a non-intuitive trade-off between the subsystems[3]. However, GT and CD strategies lie on the two ends of the development spectrum concerning cost and time. A compromise of optimising a limited number of subsystems can still improve the system's performance, as shown in[4],[5]. Similarly, this work presents the co-optimisation of the controller and actuation subsystems. In such a case, the computed optimum corresponds to the modifications to the robots' joint actuation system comprising the motor, gearbox, and controller design variables (DVs). Compared to a full-scale CD, resulting in the development of an entirely new robot, modifications to the joint actuation subsystem result in a relatively smaller set of changes. When employed to solve CD problems, conventional optimisation methods result in point-optimum solutions in the subsystems' combined design space. Such point-optimum solutions may consist of physically infeasible values, i.e., a physical component with the exact computed specifications may not be possible to manufacture or purchase off-the-shelf. Moreover, deviating from the computed optimum may result in non-intuitive trade-offs in the multidisciplinary coupled space of the CD problem. Alternatively, constructing a so-calledsolution spaceresults in maximising the permissible ranges of the DVs of the various subsystems for the given constraints and quantities of interest (QoI), leading to the identification of the largest set of feasible designs[6]. Such set-based optimisation methods have also been successfully used for manipulator design[7]and collision-free motion planning[8]. Additionally, the tolerance to disturbances of the computed solutions resulting from both point-based (PB) and set-based optimisations may not be guaranteed, and any disturbance encountered by the robot may cause it to deviate from planned execution, resulting in a loss in performance. Robust optimisation techniques offer a way to deal with such variation in task conditions[9],[10]. However, the computational burden associated with the increased number of DVs limits its applicability to high-dimensional problems. The current work presents the optimisation of solution space with disturbance tolerance (SSDT), a robust CD optimisation approach. It augments the existing PB-CD optimisation techniques to identify a set of feasible designs instead of a single point-optimum while ensuring robustness to disturbances. This results in a two-step optimisation problem illustrated in Fig.2. The first step involves solving a conventional CD problem to identify a point-optimum solution, followed by SSDT step to identify the maximum permissible ranges of the DV values robust to the largest set of disturbances as shown in Fig.1. Unlike PB solutions, the proposed set-based optimisation formulation enables the trade-off between the subsystem DV value ranges and the system-level tolerance to disturbances which can be visualised as modifying the edges of a high-dimensional box as shown in Fig.1. Moreover, by identifying overlapping solution ranges of similar DVs, the computed intersecting regions may enable the standardisation of subsystem components. For example, the same motor or gearbox variant can be used for the joint actuation subsystem of two different joints. The implementation details and the videos illustrating the robots behavior are available in the accompanying git repository1. The proposed method is employed for a computational design study of the ergoCub humanoid robot[12]. The motivation for the task and the interest in improving its tolerance to disturbances stems from the study of the iCub3 avatar system[11], developed for the All Nippon Airways (ANA) Avatar XPrize competition. As shown in Fig.3, during the competition, the iCub3 avatar system experiences an unaccounted external contact, resulting in the robot's fall, preventing it from completing the tasks ahead. As an investigation into such scenarios, an identical walking task is considered with two external disturbances: (1) stepping on rubble modelled as a small spherical collision object and (2) encountering lateral contact with a wall modelled as a rectangular box. Other sources of noise in the environment are also modelled as disturbances, elaborated in detail in SectionIV. The robots' behaviour in such scenarios can be improved by better planning[13], responsive torque control[14]and synthesising recovery strategies[15]. However, such strategies are limited to optimising the controller architecture and assume immutable hardware subsystems. The scope of the present work is to investigate the limits of the current joint actuation-controller combination in improving the performance, while keeping the existing control architecture intact. The core contributions of the paper are summarised below: The modelling and robust co-design optimisation of the actuation-controller subsystems of a humanoid robot. The optimisation of solution space with disturbance tolerance (SSDT) formulation, improving the robustness and physical feasibility of point-optimum solutions. Generation of the least number of unique motor and gearbox component variants necessary, improving standardisation of the joint actuation system.<Related Work>This section summarises the relevant literature within the scope of the current work.<Background>Consider a conventional CD problem involving the optimisation of the controller and joint actuation subsystems denoted by the variables$\boldsymbol{x} _{K}$and$\boldsymbol{x} _{A}$respectively, shown as the first of the two optimisation steps depicted in Fig.2. $\boldsymbol{x} _{K}$$\in \mathbb {R} ^{N_{C}}$includes the controller gains of different joints and tasks, as explained in[23]and shown in Fig.4. Details of the controller are presented in SectionIV. $\boldsymbol{x} _{A}$$=\,[{\boldsymbol{x}}_{N}^\top,\,{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\tau }^\top ]^\top \in \mathbb {R} ^{N_{A}}$represents the robot joint actuation subsystem consisting of the gearbox and the motor components parametrised by the gear ratio${\boldsymbol{x}}_{N}$and the peak torque${\boldsymbol{x}}_{\tau }$respectively. A conventional CD optimisation problem is formulated as,\begin{align*} \min _{\boldsymbol{x}}\,&L(\boldsymbol{x}), \\ \text {subject to,}\quad & \boldsymbol{h} (\boldsymbol{x}) = 0, \\ & \boldsymbol{g} (\boldsymbol{x}) \leq 0, \\ & {\boldsymbol{x}}_{l} \leq \boldsymbol{x} \leq {\boldsymbol{x}}_{u}, \tag{1} \end{align*}View Source\begin{align*} \min _{\boldsymbol{x}}\,&L(\boldsymbol{x}), \\ \text {subject to,}\quad & \boldsymbol{h} (\boldsymbol{x}) = 0, \\ & \boldsymbol{g} (\boldsymbol{x}) \leq 0, \\ & {\boldsymbol{x}}_{l} \leq \boldsymbol{x} \leq {\boldsymbol{x}}_{u}, \tag{1} \end{align*}where$\boldsymbol{x}$is the set of all the DVs,$[ {{\boldsymbol{x}}_{K} }^\top, {{\boldsymbol{x}}_{A} }^\top ]^\top$and${\boldsymbol{x}}_{l}$and${\boldsymbol{x}}_{u}$are the lower and upper bounds of the design space respectively. Further,$L$represents the objective function. The rigid body equations of the robot along with the prescribed initial and final states are imposed as equality constraints$\boldsymbol{h} $. Finally,$\boldsymbol{g} $represents the constraint on task completion enforced as the minimum fraction of the task successfully simulated before failing. Additionally, the objective function in(1)is the total energy loss associated with task, as used in[24]which results in a point-optimum solution${\boldsymbol{x}}_{CD}^{*}$in the combined space of the various subsystems. Note that the computed point-optimum has a certain range of tolerance to disturbances, shown within blue lines in Fig.1but provides no flexibility in design since the range of solutions is limited to just${\boldsymbol{x}}_{CD}^{*}$.<Methodology>This section summarises the proposed algorithm's scope and mathematical formulation. As depicted in Fig.2, the two optimisation steps are decoupled, enabling the latter step SSDT to augment existing PB-CD formulations, highlighting the versatility of the proposed approach. The authors would like to thank Eduardo Rodrigues Della Noce and Nicola Barthelmes for their thoughtful discussions.<Results>The proposed methodology is employed for the computational design study of the ergoCub robot. Details regarding the robots' morphology and a discussion on the design of its joints are presented in[12]and[28], respectively. It is observed that the gains tuned using expert knowledge fail at the task in the presence of the introduced disturbances necessitating the GT optimisation. Initially, the results of the conventional PB optimisation formulation in(1)for both the GT and CD cases are presented. Although the result from the CD optimisation improves robustness, as discussed earlier, the optimum may not be physically feasible. Therefore, SSDT optimisation step is later employed for the CD case. The resulting improvement in the size of the feasible design space and the tolerance to disturbances between different strategies is investigated.<Conclusion>We present a robust co-design optimisation of a humanoid robot for a given walking task, improving its tolerance to disturbances. Additionally, SSDT enables the computation of the largest permissible bounds of the DV values resulting in the identification of a set of designs robust to a range of disturbances. Moreover, overlapping regions of the computed DV ranges are exploited to identify the smallest necessary set of unique component variants, resulting in the standardisation of the joint actuation subsystem components. The proposed SSDT can augment existing co-design approaches such as[37], improving their translation from sim-to-real and alleviating the need for non-intuitive trade-offs associated with point-optimum solutions. The constructed volume metric corresponds only to a Cartesian approximation in the DV space. Such a set only represents a fraction of the complete set of feasible designs depicted as a green hull in Fig.1. Further work is needed to develop a richer approximation to prevent such loss of volume of feasible designs. Additionally, the results of a CD problem are influenced by the chosen set of tasks. Therefore, the results corresponding to the motor torque and gearbox DV values that are not influenced by the task or the disturbances may be incorrectly sized. However, this can be alleviated by incorporating several relevant scenarios as presented in[12]at the cost of increased function evaluation time.

title: Hierarchical Control for Robust Standing Stability and Fall Recovery of Task-Performing Humanoid Robots
abstract: Maintaining robust standing stability is critical for humanoid robots performing precision manipulation tasks, where traditional balance strategies (e.g., stepping) can disrupt task execution. Designing a controller that ensures both stability and effective disturbance rejection is challenging, as these goals impose conflicting requirements on body sway and stepping behavior. To address this, we propose a hierarchical control framework that decouples these objectives into three parts: 1) a Task-Oriented Standing Policy trained via reinforcement learning with strict penalties on stepping and body sway, specialized for non-stepping disturbance rejection; 2) Ankle Strategy Modulation embedded within the standing policy, which dynamically adjusts the Zero-Moment Point (ZMP) to eliminate Divergent Component of Motion (DCM) errors, thereby accelerating recovery from disturbances; and 3) a fall prediction and recovery mechanism that triggers a transition to a robust stepping policy when disturbances exceed the stability threshold. Extensive experiments on a Q-series humanoid robot, in both simulation and hardware, validate the controller’s effectiveness. We achieved a 100% task success rate over 100 trials in practical scenarios including robot archery and part grasping/placement. Note to Practitioners—This study addresses a critical challenge in deploying humanoid robots for manipulation tasks: maintaining operational continuity during frequent upper-body movements, where traditional balance strategies—such as stepping—can disrupt workflow. We propose a hierarchical control framework that resolves the inherent conflict between non-stepping stability and fall recovery through three integrated components: a reinforcement learning-based standing policy enforcing minimal body sway and zero foot movement, ankle-based Zero-Moment Point (ZMP) modulation for real-time Dynamic Capture Model (DCM) error correction, and a fall prediction mechanism that triggers stepping recovery when necessary. This architecture enables separate training of non-stepping and stepping strategies, improving both stability and disturbance resilience. Experimental validation demonstrates 100% task success over 100 trials across realistic tasks, such as archery and part manipulation. Limitations include simplified sensory, and disturbance models and the decoupled control of upper and lower body motions, which constrain whole-body coordination. Future work will focus on improving multimodal perception and implementing whole-body cooperative control for more complex tasks.
