title: Human–Robot Interaction Video Sequencing Task (HRIVST) for Robot's Behavior Legibility
abstract: People's acceptance and trust in robots are a direct consequence of people's ability to infer and predict the robot's behavior. However, there is no clear consensus on how the legibility of a robot's behavior and explanations should be assessed. In this work, the construct of the Theory of Mind (i.e., the ability to attribute mental states to others) is taken into account and a computerized version of the theory of mind picture sequencing task is presented. Our tool, called the human–robot interaction (HRI) video sequencing task (HRIVST), evaluates the legibility of a robot's behavior toward humans by asking them to order short videos to form a logical sequence of the robot's actions. To validate the proposed metrics, we recruited a sample of 86 healthy subjects. Results showed that the HRIVST has good psychometric properties and is a valuable tool for assessing the legibility of robot behaviors. We also evaluated the effects of symbolic explanations, the presence of a person during the interaction, and the humanoid appearance. Results showed that the interaction condition had no effect on the legibility of the robot's behavior. In contrast, the combination of humanoid robots and explanations seems to result in a better performance of the task.
text: <title>Human–Robot Interaction Video Sequencing Task (HRIVST) for Robot's Behavior Legibility<abstract>Abstract:People's acceptance and trust in robots are a direct consequence of people's ability to infer and predict the robot's behavior. However, there is no clear consensus on how the legibility of a robot's behavior and explanations should be assessed. In this work, the construct of the Theory of Mind (i.e., the ability to attribute mental states to others) is taken into account and a computerized version of the theory of mind picture sequencing task is presented. Our tool, called the human–robot interaction (HRI) video sequencing task (HRIVST), evaluates the legibility of a robot's behavior toward humans by asking them to order short videos to form a logical sequence of the robot's actions. To validate the proposed metrics, we recruited a sample of 86 healthy subjects. Results showed that the HRIVST has good psychometric properties and is a valuable tool for assessing the legibility of robot behaviors. We also evaluated the effects of symbolic explanations, the presence of a person during the interaction, and the humanoid appearance. Results showed that the interaction condition had no effect on the legibility of the robot's behavior. In contrast, the combination of humanoid robots and explanations seems to result in a better performance of the task.<Introduction>The increasing use of robots in different fields of human activities requires that people accept the robots' presence and trust that they are able to complete critical tasks and look for people's well-being. In such scenarios, robots need to adapt their behaviors to overcome the possible negative attitudes of people toward them (e.g., fear and anxiety), which may negatively affect people's trust in robots[1]. To address these issues, the relatively new research area called explainable robotics began to study explainability in human–robot interaction (HRI)[2]. This field investigates how to make a robot's behavior legible ([3],[4]) by providing explanations of its actions and recommendations. Existing works on explanation evaluation in AI usually break down the problem into the evaluation of narrower aspects of an explanation, such as its intelligibility, accuracy, precision, completeness, and consistency (see[5],[6]for a survey on the state of the art). These criteria are generally context-dependent and hard to assess in a general way. They typically do not consider the role of physical actions and the effects of human–robot collaborations on the robot's behavior legibility. Our purpose, instead, is to design context-independent evaluation metrics starting from the assumption that one of the main drives to generate explanations and develop legible behavior in HRI is to easily communicate the robot's goal or “intent” independently of the specific application scenario[7]. We also believe that the correct attribution of a robot's goal-directed behaviors depends on its ability to perform actions that are readable, and to provide the correct explanations when it is needed. The ability to attribute mental states, such as beliefs, goals, and intentions different from one's own[8], and the ability to understand and predict the behaviors of others[9], are indispensable processes to effective social interactions, that are known as Theory of Mind (ToM). Is mind attribution necessary to correctly understand robots' behavior? Do people need to think that a robot can have a rational intention to be able to predict what the robot is going to do?According to some authors ([10],[11]), the answer to these questions may be “yes.” The influence of people's mental representations of robots in predicting their behaviors seems to be shown by[11], who observed people forming a mental model of the robot's knowledge based on their own knowledge and on the information about the robot's origin and language. Huang et al.[10]highlighted the inadequacy of goal understanding to effectively predict a robot's future behavior, and emphasize the importance of having a good mental model of the robot's decision mechanism. According to the authors, people need to have an implicit representation of what drives the robot's behavior (i.e., a qualitative understanding of the tradeoffs the robot makes to achieve a certain goal). A similar distinction can be found also in Dragan et al.[12]that differentiates legibility, which is defined as the ability to correctly infer the goal and predictability, which is defined as the ability to predict the specific action that will achieve that goal. Hellström and Bensch[13]instead introduced the term “understandability” defined as having sufficient knowledge of the robot's state of mind in order to successfully interact with it. A similar definition of legibility is provided by Takayama et al.[14]according to which the robot behavior is legible if people can figure out what the robot is doing, and reasonably predict what the robot will do next, and ultimately effectively interact with the robot. These definitions show a partial overlapping between legibility, as defined in human–robot interaction, and ToM, as defined in human–human interaction. In this direction, we believe that a comprehensive definition of legibility is well provided by Lichtenthaler and Kirsch[15], and it is defined through two factors: 1) understandability of intentions (an umbrella term including predictable action, predictable motion trajectory, and predictable goal); and 2) the matching between the behavior of the robot and the expectations of the human observer or interactor. In this regard, the aims of the present study are: 1) to create a valid measurement tool that assesses the ability of humans to attribute a goal-oriented behavior to robots and to correctly read their behaviors in different contexts (e.g., both in the case of humanoid and nonhumanoid robots or if they are interacting with a user or performing actions on their own); and 2) to start assessing the role of symbolic explanations in improving human prediction of robots' behavior. We created a variation of the theory of mind picture sequencing task, which could be applied to social cognition in human–robot interaction. The resulting tool, called the human–robot interaction video sequencing task (HRIVST) involves watching a randomly ordered video sequence of actions while trying to put them in the correct logical order. The test is accompanied by two open-ended questions assessing the understanding of the intentions of the robots. We recruited a sample of 86 healthy subjects. Results showed that the HRIVST has good psychometric properties and could be a valuable tool for assessing the legibility of the robot's behavior in terms of the human ability to solve the task and attribute a goal-oriented behavior to the robot. Results also showed that the interaction condition has no effect on the legibility of the robot's behavior, while better performances were obtained in videos presenting humanoid robots and no explanations.<Background and Related Works>In this work, we start from the hypothesis that the need for legibility and explainability of a robot's behavior is a direct consequence of the need to understand what the robot is doing or is going to do. Since the ToM has been assumed to be a unitary process supporting different functions depending on which kind of judgments are made (on intentions, emotions, beliefs, etc.), there is a wide variety of measurements to assess this ability ([16],[17]). The measurements are different for test formats (verbal, visual, audiovisual, or scale) and aims.<Human–Robot Interaction Video Sequencing Task>On the basis of the background and related works so far explored, we designed a tool to assess the legibility of a robot's behavior by evaluating the human's ability to properly interpret the intentions of the robotic agent, and therefore of its final goal, by looking at a sequence of goal-oriented actions. To evaluate this, we proposed a new version of the well-known TPST test that could be applied to the evaluation of social cognition in HRI. Our solution differentiates from the TPST in the use of video clips instead of pictures that the subject has to order correctly to create a logical sequence of events. We believe that watching video clips of a robot performing actions may contribute to greater ecological validity. To apply the metrics to the evaluation of a robot's behavior, such behavior has to be recorded in a video. The video showing a goal-directed behavior has to be divided into several video clips, one for each single, purpose-directed, robot action so that humans could have temporal projections to create a logical sequence. Indeed, cognitive psychology showed that people perform their actions based on intended consequences[40], and they tend to perform mental simulations through mirror neurons to understand the final outcome[41]. Then, the test consists of asking the participants to order the video clips to form a sequence of logical sense in the shortest time possible. As in TPST, we measure people's sequencing ability using the scoring method of Langdon et al.[35]. Therefore, we assign two points each for both the first and the last video clips, while we assign two points divided by the number of remaining clips if people correctly order the remaining clips. For example, in the case of a video composed of four clips, four points are assigned for the first and last video clip, and one point is assigned for correctly positioning each of the central clips within the sequence. Thus, for each correct sequence, the subject can obtain a maximum score of six points. To measure whether people are able to recognize the robot's actions as intelligible and understandable, participants underwent a semistructured questionnaire that had a twofold task. We used it to investigate what was objectively the action that the robot was performing (“What is the intention of the robot?”) and, similarly to the TPST, we wanted to measure the robot's predictability (“What do you expect the robot to do next?”). This first phase of the questionnaire allowed us to investigate the correct understanding of the robot's intentions and the attribution of mental states. We assigned a one-point score for each correct answer. A high and low score indicate respectively a good and bad understanding of the intentions of the robots. We then assessed the subject' perceived confidence in correct intentionality attribution (“How difficult was it for you to attribute intention to the robot?”) using a Likert scale [from 1 to 5]. Thus, the total score of our measuring instrument is given by the sum of the score obtained from the logical sequence task (i.e., 0 to 6) and the score of correct answers given to the questionnaire (i.e., 0 to 2), so that the total ranges from 0 to 8, for each video.<HRIVST Validation>The task validation consisted of three phases: 1) video selection; 2) video clip creation; and 3) testing. Moreover, we decided to address the effect of some factors on human understanding of the robot's behavior, with specific reference to: the humanoid appearance of the robot; the presence of symbolic explanations. We also investigated whether the presence of a human agent involved in the robot's actions may influence the capacity to predict its behavior.<Results>The mean values and SD obtained for each video of the questionnaire are reported in TableIII.<Discussion>The results of this study showed that the HRIVST test has good psychometric properties, in terms of reliability and construct validity (both convergent and discriminant), providing a valuable metric for future investigations. The correlation between the HRIVST and the TPST scores indicated a fair convergent validity, and, therefore, suggests that our test is able to assess people's ability to attribute mental states. The HRIVST also has good internal consistency, with a Cronbach's$\alpha$value of 0.97. Observing that participants had similar HRIVST scores for each video, this result leads us to believe that the difference in the video average results is linked to the legibility of the robot's behaviors across different tasks. The low and not significant correlation between the HRIVST score and cognitive tasks scores (MMSE and RPCM) indicated good discriminant validity, meaning that the considered tasks assess different constructs. Building on these preliminary data based on healthy participants, we highlight the need for future studies to investigate the effect of different age groups of adults on the ability to attribute mental states to robots. In particular, the results of our study highlighted that: a) Individual participants' scores significantly differ depending on each video:The comparison of the mean scores for each video showed some remarkable patterns: The worst scores were obtained in Video 2 and Video 8, while the best score was obtained in Video 7. In Video 2 participants showed significantly worse scoring than all videos except for Video 4 and Video 12. Indeed, Video 2 presented all the conditions resulting in lower scores, such as the presence of explanations, the longest sequence, and the presence of a nonhumanoid robot. In Video 2, deficient performances may also be due to the used characteristics for creating the video, such as viewpoint, lighting, and frame resolution. These seem to have worsened the resulting scores in the nonhumanoid, the long sequence, and the explanation conditions. In Video 8, participants may have scored lower in the nonhumanoid condition than in the humanoid condition for similar reasons. Indeed, action recognition through video may be difficult when the video's recording quality does not provide a full overview of the scenario[49]. In a complex sequence of actions where the single movements cannot always be clearly distinguished, the detection of objects may help to a better understanding of the ongoing event, providing useful information[50]. This may not be the case in Video 8, in which a robot opens a drawer, grasps a toy car from one of the shelves, puts the car in the drawer, closes it and opens another drawer. In this video, multiple cars are visible, and this may have led the participants to confuse the opening and closing actions of the drawer. As a result, the sequence and the robot's goal could have been more difficult to discern, resulting in the worst scores. On the contrary, Video 7 resulted in having the highest score with no explanation, a short length of time, and a humanoid robot. In summary, we found that the significant differences in participant scores for each video are consistent with the existing literature about the methods to achieve legible robot behaviors[15]. In particular, to generate legible robot behaviors, the following variables were proposed: human-like behavior ([51],[52]); stereotypical motions of everyday activities (e.g., reaching for an object) ([51],[53]); the addition of complementary gestures to clarify intentions (e.g., gaze, pointing) ([54],[55]); and the greatest possible visibility of the robot motion ([56],[57]). We agree that these variables reported may have played a role in the scores. For example, the visibility of the robot motion may have been reduced by the video's recording features; the activities which are not carried out in daily life (e.g., grasping a tool to assemble an object in an industrial-like environment, like in Video 2) may have been responsible for reduced scores to our questionnaire. b) No significant difference was found between participants' scores in the interaction condition:Independently of the presence or absence of another agent, we believe that the absence of a significant effect of the interaction condition may suggest that watching a robot performing a sequence of goal-oriented actions elicits in a human observer an intention attribution that is influenced more by the robot's goal than by the context. This is supported by Gazzola et al.[23]who showed that the goal of action might be more important for the activation of the mirror neuron system, which plays a role more in the understanding of the actions than the completion modality of the action[17]. For a better understanding of our results, with particular reference to section a) and section b), we believed that greater focus should be given to the similarities and differences characterizing the task's videos and to what we mean by “context.” Our idea was to create a measure that could be used in different scenarios and not be limited to assessing the legibility of a robot's behavior in the restricted context of a specific task. For this reason, we wanted to explore how the readability of a robot's behavior may vary in different situations. Specifically, we decided to first investigate how an HRI scenario may affect this variable, compared to a scenario with a robot alone. In the selection phase, we chose six videos presenting a human–robot interaction scenario and six videos presenting a robot in a solitary setting. Of the first six videos, three of them presented a humanoid robot, while the other three presented a nonhumanoid robot. The same distinction was maintained for the other six videos. Despite this subdivision, the videos still have in common the presence of a robot performing a goal-oriented action (e.g., a behavior driven by an expectation that it is likely to bring about a desired outcome)[58]. Most of the videos also include a manipulation task (e.g., grasping an object, or folding laundry). This similarity may account for the absence of an interaction effect, meaning that despite the presence of a human–robot interaction or not, what makes a behavior readable is the comprehension of the goal itself. Therefore, physical features such as the presence of an object and whether it is visible, may have a leading role in the capacity to infer on robot's actions in different scenarios as features that are closely related to the target. c) Participants performed better in videos showing humanoid robots than nonhumanoid robots:Our results also showed that people find it easier to understand the behavior of a human-like robot rather than a nonhumanoid robot. This is in line with the existing literature that highlights the role of human-like appearance in facilitating mind attribution ([18],[21],[22]). Our finding can also be considered in line with the “complementary gesture” assumption, according to which the use of complementary motions made by the robot could improve legibility (e.g., during an arm motion looking at the object)[59]. This might be the case in humanoid robot videos shown in our measure's validation, where the robot's head faced and followed the object of interest in goal-oriented actions. This robot's behavior is a forethought cue that makes the robot's behavior more readable. For example, in Video 7, the robot turns its head toward origami before grasping it. d) Participants performed better in videos without explanations than with explanations:Contrary to our expectations, symbolic explanations seem to worsen the scores (i.e., making the robot's actions less readable). However, we observed that in videos featuring a nonhumanoid robot, explanations may have a facilitating effect, although not significant. Indeed, participants scored higher on videos with explanations and a nonhumanoid robot than on videos with explanations and a humanoid robot. The legibility and predictability of the robot's actions increase in the scenario with a nonhumanoid robot providing explanations. We believe that, in this case, since participants were not able to attribute a mental model similar to humans, people were able to predict the robot's behaviors with the help of verbal descriptions. In the case of humanoid robots, textual explanations were a distracting or annoying factor for the participants, which is in line with recent studies exploring the effect of the timing of explanations on people's perception of a robot and its behavior. Indeed, Han et al.[42]found that approximately half of the participants who watched videos of robots performing action-oriented movements wanted the robot to explain unexpected events as they happened, and only a small percentage of participants preferred the explanations from the robot before these happened. Another study also found that providing explanations of a robot's behavior before its execution rather than afterward makes the robot's behavior perceived as less desirable[60]. e) Participants performed better in the videos presenting short sequences rather than long and medium-long sequences:We hypothesized that participants were able to attribute intentions to the robot's action better when shown in short sequences rather than in medium or long sequences because sequencing tasks with a larger number of video clips may require a higher cognitive workload.<Limitations and Future Work>Our current work presents some limitations that will guide future research. First, while some studies highlighted comparable results for assessing users' evaluation of robots' behavior using both video-based and in-person interaction studies[61], other studies suggest that people do not necessarily respond in the same way to robots in videos and physical scenarios[62]. Specifically, video scenarios presenting an interaction between a robot and a human were more effective in increasing users' perceptions of a robot's ease of use and adaptability (i.e., how well the robot completed its tasks) compared to a live interaction scenario, probably due to the fluency with which the video presented the interaction[62]. For a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of explanations, we will explore different modalities for providing explanations considering different information provided as well as different ways to provide them (oral or written). Finally, we intend to assess whether the individuals' characteristics (e.g., age) influence the legibility of the robot's behavior. Thus, we will focus on the extension of a diverse sample of participants to provide useful insights for enhancing human–robot interaction in different contexts.<Conclusion>In this work, we were interested in developing evaluation metrics for the legibility of the robot's behavior starting from the assessment of the ability of humans to attribute intentions to robots in different contexts. To these extents, we asked healthy subjects to evaluate the intentions of humanoid and nonhumanoid robots performing goal-oriented actions in videos with or without labels describing such actions. We evaluated their perceptions and the robot's legibility and predictability by a new measurement, HRIVST, here presented. Our results show that HRIVST is a reliable tool for assessing the legibility of a robot's behavior by evaluating the human ability to correctly interpret its intentions. Our results also showed that people find the behaviors of a human-like robot more comprehensible than those of a nonhumanoid robot. This is also in line with the existing literature that underlies the role of human-like appearance in facilitating mind attribution. Moreover, our results have shed some light on the role of symbolic explanations in enhancing people's understanding of a robot's intentions, as assessed through video scenarios. Our results suggest a facilitating, although not significant, effect on the legibility of the intentions when the video included nonhumanoid robotic behaviors. The finding of this study will be used to investigate further both the effects of individual characteristics and the role of subjective perception of the effectiveness of explanations in determining the legibility of a robot's behaviors.
authors: S. Rossi; A. Coppola; M. Gaita; A. Rossi

title: A Biologically Inspired Program-Level Imitation Approach for Robots
abstract: Robots may learn new skills from humans to better assist us with everyday tasks. We propose a novel, biologically inspired imitation approach to enable robots to understand and perform complex actions using high-level programs that incorporate sequential regularities between sub-goals a robot can recognize and physically achieve. To learn a new task, human-provided demonstrations—obtained by a robot through different modalities such as kinesthetic teaching or behavioural observation—are processed by an algorithm to discover multiple possible arrangements of sub-goals that achieve the task goal. When performing the task, the robot first evaluates the available sequences in the program based on user-defined criteria, through mental simulation of the real task, to find the optimal sequence of actions. The selected sequence is then executed using the hierarchical structure of actions embedded in the program. We implemented the proposed learning architecture on an iCub humanoid robot and evaluated the effectiveness of the system in multiple scenarios. Our approach accommodates variations in human teaching styles and is expected to help robots perform tasks with greater flexibility and efficiency, opening the way to more adaptable and intelligent robots.
text: <title>A Biologically Inspired Program-Level Imitation Approach for Robots<abstract>Abstract:Robots may learn new skills from humans to better assist us with everyday tasks. We propose a novel, biologically inspired imitation approach to enable robots to understand and perform complex actions using high-level programs that incorporate sequential regularities between sub-goals a robot can recognize and physically achieve. To learn a new task, human-provided demonstrations—obtained by a robot through different modalities such as kinesthetic teaching or behavioural observation—are processed by an algorithm to discover multiple possible arrangements of sub-goals that achieve the task goal. When performing the task, the robot first evaluates the available sequences in the program based on user-defined criteria, through mental simulation of the real task, to find the optimal sequence of actions. The selected sequence is then executed using the hierarchical structure of actions embedded in the program. We implemented the proposed learning architecture on an iCub humanoid robot and evaluated the effectiveness of the system in multiple scenarios. Our approach accommodates variations in human teaching styles and is expected to help robots perform tasks with greater flexibility and efficiency, opening the way to more adaptable and intelligent robots.<Introduction>Learning something new, for example, cooking an unfamiliar recipe or assembling a new piece of furniture, often involves only arranging skills we already have, such as mixing ingredients or screwing, into novel and complex sequences. Initially, we may exactly follow the given directions, but once we gain a better understanding of the sequence of stages and the structure of sub-goals, we may adapt to our unique situation to improve efficiency. For instance, based on how our own kitchen is organized, we may pick up a spice required later while grabbing a mixing bowl needed right now, thus avoiding repeated trips to the same cabinet. This high-level knowledge about achieving specific goals and how to structure events into discrete sub-goals is essential for successful task planning[1]. Humans and many other species of primates do not always merely copy the chain of observed events. Instead, they identify and use hierarchical action structures, which include sequential regularities, bimanual coordination, and possible arrangements of sub-goals[2],[3],[4]. Imitating overall task structure, rather than details of actions, is referred to as ‘Program-Level Imitation (PLI)’[3]. Efficient learning and adaptation methods are essential for robots to assist us in daily tasks[5]. A robot may observe people carrying out a similar task with varying orders of actions and motions of the hands and use objects with unique appearances. In such cases, as with humans and other primates, robots could identify and use the hierarchical structure of actions to know what sub-goals are needed and in what order, and how irrelevant information can be discarded[6]. Knowing possible ways of structuring sub-goals may make the robot’s actions more efficient. In this work, we propose a novel PLI architecture for robots. This approach enables robots to receive diverse task demonstrations from human teachers, identify possible sequences of known actions in the demonstrations, organize sub-goals into sequential structures, and apply this knowledge for effective task execution based on user-defined requirements in new situations. The robot in this study is assumed to have pre-existing low-level visuomotor control and sensing capabilities to perform specific sub-goals and detect the effects related to these sub-goals on objects within its view. To learn a new task, the PLI system analyzes the observed sequences of sub-goals and synthesizes feasible arrangements of robot primitives, along with useful relationships between the sub-goals, in the form of a ‘program.’ For task execution, the robot evaluates possible arrangements of sub-goals through mental simulation and selects the most suitable sequence of actions for the present situation and user preferences (e.g., prioritizing speed, safety, etc.). The robot then uses information contained in the program to accomplish sub-goals in the selected sequence to achieve the overall task goal. The present article outlines the core principles of PLI architecture (Section III), details its implementation on an iCub humanoid robot (Section IV), and then evaluates and discusses the robot’s performance when learning and executing two abstract real-world tasks (Sections VandVI) using both qualitative observations and quantitative measures. An early version of the PLI framework was previously introduced in[7]. The present work significantly extends that preliminary version by detailing an updated version of the PLI system capable of handling more complex relations between task sub-goals, using more advanced algorithms for program generation and execution, etc. Furthermore, the current study includes a considerably wider range of tests performed and discussed for system evaluation. With the proposed PLI system, learner robots may use inconsistencies among the demonstrations for their advantage and discover more ways of performing a task, given that people may have different styles in completing a particular task. Our PLI framework gives robots the potential to receive task demonstrations from humans through various modalities (e.g., kinesthetic teaching[8], behavioural observation, or verbal instruction), with or without errors, and allows for customization in task performance according to the current user’s expectations. A program may be used by different robots, each utilizing its own primitives to achieve the same sub-goals. By assessing sub-goals in real-time during task execution based on a program, robots can be interrupted and resume where they left off or recover from failed actions.<Background and Related Work>In this section, we introduce the concept of PLI and describe how it is achieved in primates and humans. We then review the previous work focused on enabling robots to learn structures of actions and situate our work within the existing literature.<Program-Level Imitation Architecture>This section describes our proposed PLI architecture for robots, which consists of modules illustrated inFigure 2. In summary, for learning a new task,demonstrations observerprocesses human-provided demonstrations and identifies the occurrence of sub-goals (explained inSection III-A).Program generatorthen analyzes the demonstrations to determine how different arrangements of sub-goals can lead to the task goal (explained inSection III-B). This module obtains a program that includes multiple possible sequences of sub-goals to complete the task and relations between them. When a user asks the robot to carry out a learned task,sequence selectorevaluates the available sequences based on user-selected functions that impose their expectations (described inSection III-D), considering the current task state obtained fromtask progress observer(outlined inSection III-C). The most suitable sequence in the program is then executed byaction planner(discussed inSection III-D).1 This architecture relies on a robot’s pre-programmed abilities to achieve certain basic ‘sub-goals’ with respect to objects and places, as well as the robot’s ability to detect the ‘effect’ associated with the completion of each known sub-goal in the environment. Only these basic actions, called ‘primitives’ of the robot, will be used for learning and performing new multi-step behaviours. Objects and places involved in each task need to be introduced to the robot before learning. In this work, given the abilities of an iCub robot[41], we programmed three primitives ofgrasping an object and putting it inside a box,pressing a button, andsliding a box to a different place. While the details of our robotic implementation are given inSection IV, the primitives will be referred to in this section to explain the architecture. We use the following notation to indicate the sub-goal associated with the achievement of each primitive, using IDs assigned to known objects and places: OX,Y: Grasping object X and putting it inside box Y BX: Pressing button X PX,Y: Sliding box X to place Y<Robotic Implementation>This section presents how we implemented the PLI architecture on an iCub humanoid robot[41]to evaluate the system and analyze the learning and execution of two abstract physical tasks, described inSection IV-A. An Intel RealSense camera[43]was mounted on the robot’s head for 3D localization when learning and performing tasks. An ArUco marker was attached to each known object or place in tasks, so that the RealSense camera could obtain 3D positions of the centre of each marker in the camera frame. Locations in the camera frame were then converted to locations in iCub’s base frame. The three primitives listed earlier inSection 2were incorporated into the system.3This section describes how the perception capabilities of the robot could be utilized to create ademonstrations observermodule that acquires demonstrations through remote observation. Atask progress observerwas also designed to evaluate the task state through remote observation. We also describe how the robot could act to achieve the sub-goals in a program, viaaction planner. Lastly, we define three examples of core optimization functions for thesequence selector.<System Validation>In this section, to evaluate the PLI system, we first describe examples of how a robot can generate programs based on multiple task demonstrations and improve its performance (Section V-A). We use task completion time and the estimated risk of robot failure as metrics to quantify the performance of the robot when learning tasks. Next, we evaluate the program generation when demonstrations contain errors by defining ‘success rate’ as a metric to evaluate sequences in the generated programs (Section V-B). We conclude by describing scenarios in which the robot uses the acquired programs for task execution (Section V-C).Appendix Cpresents an extra example related to learning Task 1.<Discussion>We introduced a novel imitation learning system for robots that enables them to understand the sequential structure of goal-directed actions. By learning from human demonstrations, the robot comes up with multiple possible sequences of sub-goals in the form of a program to perform tasks flexibly and to better adapt to contextual variations and different user preferences. We described how different modules in the proposed PLI framework work together, explained how such a system was implemented on an iCub robot, and evaluated the effectiveness of this approach in various cases. As a part of system evaluation inSection V-A, we presented examples of the learning and adaptation process of a robot to two physical abstract tasks. We explained how the system discovered more possibilities in achieving task goals and found more effective strategies for task performance, according to previously defined optimization functions and through mental simulation of the real tasks, when demonstrations that covered different situations were provided. In this work, optimization functions to reduce task completion time, lower the risk of robot failure, and more effectively arrange actions in a particular freezer organization task were employed. To use with our PLI system, robot designers can build many other optimization functions to give users a variety of options to customize robot behaviour for different scenarios and tasks. For example, a function may add to the total cost if an oven stays hot for some time before food is placed inside it, to reduce home energy consumption. A robot equipped with the present PLI system can be envisioned to record task demonstrations in two ways: when it is being explicitly taught by a human teacher (as was the case in this article) or when it is moving around and observes humans performing tasks, e.g., around a house. In both cases, the learning progress of the robot may be impacted by the recorded demonstrations. Diversity in the demonstrations will helpprogram generatorobserve different situations and therefore, obtain more information about sub-goals in a task to better discover possibilities in structuring the sub-goals. InSection V-B, we observed that when demonstrations contained five ‘random’ ways for task execution, less than 20 sequences were found on average for Task 1. Meanwhile, when a researcher carefully provided effective, diverse demonstrations of the same task (Example 1 inSection V-A), only four demonstrations were sufficient to obtain 30 sequences. Due to the importance of diversity in demonstrations, the full potential of the PLI system may not be realized in some situations, e.g., when only a few people teach a robot and they all tend to follow a specific general approach. Nevertheless, our approach can benefit robots by offering an effective way of accommodating variability in demonstrations, which is a challenge in learning from demonstration[5]. As outlined inSection III-B,program generatorcan be configured to group some sub-goals together in generated sequences. The ‘grouping’ strategy can reduce the search space for valid sequences and make programs easier to describe by forming ‘families’ of sequences. As humans, we may most of the time perform similar, repetitive actions altogether rather than holding some of the sub-goals in mind to come back and complete later. This has been shown to reduce cognitive and memory load in humans[44],[45]. For a robot, in contrast, considering the possibility of achieving some sub-goals in any place in sequences of actions only requires extra memory and calculations, which is not difficult for today’s modern robots. The proposed PLI system could allow various places for sub-goals to complete a task, even if some were always demonstrated together. Letting the sub-goals separate allows for more flexibility, which may lead to improved efficiency in new situations. Such a case was observed in Example 2 inSection V-A: while sub-goalsO6,3andO2,3were achieved one after another in all the demonstrations, they were not adjacent in all the generated sequences without the grouping strategy, and this could yield zero cost based on the optimization function that preferred picking objects in a form that reduces the risk of robot failure. In light of the above discussion, it would be better for a robot not to use grouping for sequence selection to enhance its performance, but to use grouping, when possible, for communicating programs to users. Grouping sub-goals according to the procedure noted inSection III-Bwill minimize the total number of groups. Nevertheless, more sophisticated strategies may be used to help the system decide whether or not to keep sub-goals in their existing groups. For example, pauses during task demonstrating after completing certain sub-goals have been shown to indicate the completion of end goals[46]. Such end goals may be considered to guide the PLI system to better group sub-goals. Throughout the main part of system evaluation inSection V-B, which focused on assessing the performance of the system by analyzing the generated programs, it was observed that by adjusting system parameters even in a limited manner and also employing the strategy of ‘filtering’, the system could learn multiple correct sub-goal sequences even if demonstrations contained errors. To obtain system parameters more accurately, a condition should be simulated that represents the average combination of errors that are expected to be in sets of demonstrations of different tasks in a real situation, i.e., when non-experts’ demonstrations are recorded by the robot. Despite the strategies in place for handling errors, the PLI system can greatly benefit if errors in sub-goal detection by thedemonstrations observerare reduced. As explained inSection IV-B,demonstrations observercan be designed to use multiple modalities of recording demonstrations at the same time. Combining different modalities may help the robot better identify sub-goals in the instances where a single modality fails to accurately detect sub-goals. In such cases, a system can be implemented such that if there is a conflict between learning modalities, the robot, e.g., verbally asks the teacher to repeat the last sub-goal. Then, only if the teacher does not repeat that part of the demonstration (it may be impossible because, e.g., the environment has changed inevitably) or the inconsistency persists, the sub-goal is recorded with missing information. With the PLI learning architecture, robots use their own primitives and this will allow the transfer of programs from one robot to another. A new embodiment can use different methods for detecting sub-goals and acting to achieve them, which can be pre-programmed by its designers. The correspondence problem[47]is not relevant here: as long as the robot can achieve the needed sub-goals, even in different ways, a program learned by another robot can be still useful. Furthermore, by allowing learned programs to be utilized as robot primitives in the PLI architecture, robot teaching can take place in a modular form, which may improve user experience. For example, in the abstract potato boiling task discussed in this article, a teacher may first teach a smaller task of ‘adding potatoes to the pot’ and then, after making sure the small task is properly learned, include it in the demonstration of the bigger task.<Limitations>The presented PLI system utilizes a robot’s pre-programmed capabilities for detecting effects associated with a set of known sub-goals and acting to achieve them. Implementing the PLI system on a new robot requires programming robot primitives in a way suitable for the new embodiment. Moreover, in a real-life context, decomposing tasks into sub-goals may be challenging[48]. In fact, tasks may consist of several sub-goals reached at the same time or in a continuous series of events. Human teachers may not always define sub-goals clearly. Furthermore, sub-goals may not always result in visible physical effects on the surroundings. Several studies in robot learning from demonstrations have focused on ‘learning’ to extract sub-goals in human demonstrations, e.g.,[23],[49],[50], and[51]. Future work can incorporate more effective, automated, and generalizable techniques for sub-goal detection in thedemonstration observermodule. Our proposed method is relatively simple in terms of how data is processed and decisions are made by the robot. While this minimalist approach can be particularly effective for learning tasks that consist of a small number of sub-goals, knowledge acquisition and performing tasks when many sub-goals are present may be computationally costly because of some large search spaces and high time complexity of the proposed algorithms, e.g., during greedy search inAlgorithm 1for program generation and during mental simulation of actions based on multiple sequences. There are also limitations when capturing statistical regularities used in programs. For instance, at least a few demonstrations that start from a reasonably small initial task state are required so that setsEandD(noted inTable 1) can be constructed. Another limitation of our approach is the simplistic strategy for sequence selection. At present, to find the optimal sequence for the robot’s actions,sequence selectoradds the costs associated with different aspects together and compares the total costs. Technical aspects of this work can be improved in future research. As an example, fuzzy logic may replace the simple technique for sequence selection[52]so that a user only defines certain ‘degrees of importance’, rather than numerical weights, for each criterion. Concerning the generalizability of the system, while the current implementation can learn tasks of different kinds, it does not allow for customization or substitution in the sub-goals, to generalize programs to cover other tasks which may have extra sub-goals compared to what was originally learned. Furthermore, the current system does not allow changes or replacements in the program in real-time when performing a task. A more effective approach forsequence selectorandaction plannermay allow dynamic sequence selection based on the task progress and current situation. The present work also discusses tuning of system parameters for learning new tasks in a limited setting. These generalizability limitations can be addressed with subsequent developments over time, which can be a challenge.<Future Directions>The present learning framework creates opportunities for realizing social learning of robots, i.e., learning through feedback and interaction with humans[53],[54]. One strategy for achieving this would be implementing a ‘learning from conversation’ modality as a part ofdemonstration observerto identify and record sub-goals in a task from verbal instructions. With such capabilities, a robot may even ask for clarifications from the human teacher in real-time during the conversation. In this area, LLMs may demonstrate great potential. Future work can employ LLMs to extract and record sub-goals from human-provided descriptions of tasks, possibly with the help of knowledge from other sources for widely known tasks, in a manner similar todemonstration observer. LLMs may also contribute to other aspects of our PLI architecture. For example, relations identified and used by theprogram generatormay be evaluated using an LLM according to the definition and purpose of each item, so that robot the robot asks for clarification or correction if needed. Our PLI approach opens up new possibilities for explainable learning systems. Here, generating programs is led by a limited number of sets and relations, each with a logical definition as noted inTable 1. Selecting a sequence is also driven by costs obtained via optimization functions that are defined for our physical world. Acting based on a sequence is also governed by relations that define why a particular sub-goal is being achieved, as described inAlgorithm 2. Future work can focus on developing a component that can express the system’s behaviour in any step of learning and performing tasks, to support explainability. LLMs may be useful in this context as well, by enabling the robot to explain its internal state, intents, goals, etc., through a natural conversation. Lastly, as an important future direction, the effectiveness of the present PLI approach should be tested in a broader range, including a variety of human-robot interaction scenarios. Having multiple human teachers, including novice robot users, demonstrate different tasks to teach the robot will help identify the strengths and weaknesses of the system, its effectiveness in addressing users’ preferences, challenges users may face, etc., and it is crucial to the future development of the system. The performance and effectiveness of the present approach should be quantitatively compared to other state-of-art robot learning techniques, e.g., LLM-based systems[38], by the perspective of non-expert robot users.<Conclusion>We presented a minimal biologically inspired PLI system for humanoid robots inspired by learning in primates. With this architecture, we illustrated how a robot can: Learn from people with different styles in doing a particular task and acquiring knowledge about task structure, Take into account a new user’s preferences and improve efficiency in a manner that a user may expect, Select a suitable sequence of actions among the multiple possible solutions for performing the task in a new setting, and Cope with interruptions and errors, which are very likely to occur in a domestic scenario[55].<Appendix AiCub Robot Sub-Goal Detection Strategies>In the present implementation, the iCub robot utilized the following strategies to detect the sub-goals related to each robot primitive in human demonstrations (viademonstrations observer) and in task state (viatask progress observer): Putting object X in box Y:During observational learning, the robot detects object X is moved into box Y if the object disappears for 3 seconds, as long as box Y was the closest box to where object X was last located, compared to other boxes, and this distance was shorter than a threshold. When evaluating the task state, in case there is only one box in the defined items, object X is considered as moved into box Y if it has disappeared for 3 seconds. If there is more than one box and the object is not visible in an area that defines a box, the target box remains unknown and the task state is reported as explained inSection IV-C. Pressing button X: In observational learning, the robot detects button X is pressed if thez-component of its location has been smaller than the average of this value in the past 2 seconds (indicating that the button has been moving downward) and the condition no longer holds (meaning the button is still). As part of evaluating the task state, the robot considers button X is pressed if thez-component of its location is below a certain value. Sliding box X to place Y: In observational learning, the robot detects movable box X is moved to place Y if they-component of its location stays within 2 cm of they-component of the location of place Y for 1 second. In the task state, the robot considers movable box X to be in place Y if they-component of its location is within 2 cm of they-component of the location of place Y.<Appendix BiCub Robot Action Strategies>The robot’s actions to achieve the sub-goals related to each primitive were programmed in the following manner: Putting object X in box Y:The robot finds the location of object X, approaches an adjusted location with its left hand and with fingers opened, moves its left hand closer, and finally closes the fingers. Then, it raises the left hand to the top of box Y and opens its fingers. In tests presented inSection V-A, iCub only used a single arm joints and therefore, due to its narrow dexterous space, if box Y was not reachable, the robot used its right hand to move the box within reach. Pressing button X: Assuming the button is horizontal, the robot finds the location of button X, moves its appropriate hand to 5 cm above the adjusted location with figures open, moves its hand without change of orientation 8 cm down and then backs up. Sliding box X to place Y: The robot moves its hand to a starting location, based on whether the box should be slid right or left, with its fingers open. It then starts moving that hand to an ending location, without changing the orientation, until box X reaches place Y, considering they-component of their locations.<Appendix CAnother Task Learning Example (Example 4)>In this example scenario, the PLI system could find a sequence to complete the task more efficiently than each individual task demonstration. A test in three parts was performed with the robot learning our abstract potato boiling task (Task 1), similar to Example 1 (Section V-A1), considering the empty initial task state (S1). title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Footstep Control for Humanoid Robots on Complex Terrain
abstract: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based footstep planning framework that enables a bipedal robot to achieve stable locomotion over challenging terrain. At its core, a learned step-following policy executes footstep commands with varying positions, orientations, and heights. These commands are generated by a heuristic planner that processes user-defined velocity and orientation inputs alongside a local height field to adaptively adjust step placement and height. By leveraging two-step foresight commands for each leg, the controller ensures safe and adaptive locomotion in dynamic environments. A comparative study of different foresight horizons (one-step, two-step, and three-step) demonstrates that the two-step controller provides the best trade-off between performance and complexity. Critically, our method plans footsteps without relying on dynamic models, making it simpler to implement and deploy. We show through comparisons with a model-based approach that it achieves competitive performance even without explicit dynamics information. To handle non-flat terrain, our method adopts a modular architecture that decouples perception from control, in contrast to end-to-end approaches that map perception inputs directly to motor commands. Perceptual information is processed into footstep commands, which are then provided to the controller. This design improves interpretability, simplifies debugging, and increases safety by ensuring the low-level policy consistently receives physically feasible commands. Trained in simulation to navigate environments with randomly placed obstacles, the resulting policy demonstrates robust locomotion across diverse terrains. The robot can overcome obstacles up to 50% of its leg length while accurately tracking speeds of up to 0.8 m/s, as validated in simulation on Bruce, a kid-sized humanoid robot platform.

The robot can overcome obstacles up to 50% of its leg length while accurately tracking speeds of up to 0.8 m/s, as validated in simulation on Bruce, a kid-sized humanoid robot platform.<Introduction>Achieving smooth and stable walking in bipedal robots remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. These robots aim to replicate human locomotion and are envisioned for use in diverse applications such as home assistance, healthcare, and exploration in hazardous environments. However, maintaining balance and stability across varying walking speeds and uneven terrain remains a difficult task due to the complex dynamics involved. In this work, we present a novel Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based controller designed for robust base-velocity tracking in dynamic environments (Fig. 2). Our approach enables the robot to adapt its footstep poses—as needed—including position, orientation, and height, in real time, allowing stable and precise locomotion over terrain with randomly distributed gaps, obstacles, and height variations (Fig. 1). In addition, robustness to external disturbances in the form of linear pushes applied to the robot’s base was evaluated, demonstrating that the policy achieves dynamic balance during walking. The proposed method aligns with classical navigation strategies in which a path is planned to guide the robot’s base position toward a target. By tracking the desired base velocity, the robot is able to follow this path. Simultaneously, our system allows the robot to adjust its foot placement to account for challenging terrain conditions, such as stairs, gaps, and uneven step heights. Unlike traditional model-based footstep planning approa ches, our method is model-free and relies on a heuristic-based step command estimator. This estimator interprets user-defined velocity and orientation commands and, when navigating uneven terrain, incorporates local height-field information, which in this work is obtained directly from the simulation environment. It predicts the next two footstep targets for each leg, along with smoothed base orientation and velocity trajectories. These high-level motion plans are then passed to the RL-based controller, which outputs the corresponding desired joint positions. The proposed framework adopts a modular architecture that explicitly separates perception and control. This design improves interpretability, facilitates deployment, and increases safety by ensuring the low-level policy consistently receives physically feasible commands. The key contributions of this work are as follows: Commanded Footstep Pose Tracking: We propose a model-free RL controller that explicitly tracks commanded footstep poses (position, orientation, height), enabling accurate path following and obstacle avoidance. Unlike prior model-based or fixed-step methods, our controller handles varying step lengths and demonstrates performance comparable to a model-based baseline. Two-Step Foresight Control: The controller anticipates future contacts using a two-step foresight strategy, improving balance on structured terrain such as gaps and discrete steps. A comparative study confirms that two-step foresight offers the best trade-off between complexity and the robot’s ability to accurately follow sequential step commands. Modular Perception-Control Architecture: A modular design separates perception from control, converting high-level inputs into footstep targets tracked by the policy. This structure improves interpretability, and ensures physically valid commands.<Learning Footstep-Constrained Gait Policies>Our control policy directly incorporates footstep poses as control commands, replacing conventional base velocity or gait-pattern inputs. This policy accepts explicit footstep targets, including position, orientation, and height for upcoming steps (seeFig. 2). This design necessitates a specialized reward function that emphasizes accurate tracking of footstep commands, prioritizing precise foot placement over periodicity in motion.<Simulation Results>In this section, we present the simulation results of applying our controller. We first trained the policy on flat terrain without any height information (the step height command is set to zero). Subsequently, the same policy was trained on terrain with randomly placed discrete steps. This training setup was chosen to ensure that the robot maintains its ability to walk effectively on flat terrain while simultaneously gaining experience in handling variations in ground height. The reader is referred to the accompanying submission video for demonstration results.<Conclusion and Future Work>In this work, we presented a learning-based step-following controller capable of tracking footstep positions and orientations while adaptively adjusting step height using terrain information. The approach demonstrated robust performance in simulation, successfully traversing complex terrains with gaps and obstacles up to 50% of the robot’s leg length and tracking speeds up to 0.8 m/s. By decoupling perception from control, the method improves interpretability, simplifies debugging, and ensures that the low-level policy always receives physically feasible commands. Several limitations remain. The robot’s arms are fixed, preventing the use of arm motions for balance. Evaluation is currently limited to simulation, and despite including domain randomization and noise in the height maps during training, sim-to-real transfer remains a significant challenge. In particular, the method relies on access to structured terrain height maps, which are difficult to obtain reliably in real-world environments with stairs, steps, or uneven ground. As noted in[12], integrating reliable perception with high-frequency control under such conditions is technically demanding, particularly on computationally constrained platforms. Future work will focus on developing robust perception pipelines, similar to those in[14], and extending the framework to real hardware. We also plan to integrate the controller into a hierarchical system, where a global planner such as the elastic band method[39]generates base paths while the local controller adapts footsteps. This combination of modularity, robustness, and safety provides a promising foundation for deploying bipedal locomotion in real-world environments.

title: Heteroscedastic Regression and Active Learning for Modeling Affordances in Humanoids
abstract: We investigate the learning of object and tool affordances in the iCub robot. We adopt the setup proposed in a previous experiment, using a Bayesian network (BN) in place of a least square support vector machine (LSSVM). The collected data, consisting of continuous and discrete variables, are used for learning the structure of the BN. Hence, the model is leveraged to: 1) identify a regression function for the prediction of the effects of actions on objects, calculated as the mean of the observed values; and 2) provide information on the reliability of the predicted values through the estimation of the variance for subsets of local observations. The information on the input-dependent variance is used to guide the learning algorithm in order to improve the performance of the robot, and hence to reduce the variance from the predicted values. The replacement of the LSSVM with the BN model provides a general probabilistic framework for dependencies among random variables; we perform conditional probability queries that enable the robot to choose the actions to perform on objects and select the most appropriate tool to obtain desired effects. The capability to make inference enables the robot to gather a better understanding of the world.

title: Brimory: Bringing Humanoid Memory Into Trajectory Prediction Model for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Predicting the future trajectories of moving agents serves as a pivotal endeavor in advancing safe autonomous driving forward within the context of the evolving Internet of Things technology. Despite significant progress driven by deep learning methods, a gap in predictive capability remains when compared to experienced human drivers, particularly in scenarios that demand heightened perception and broader situational understanding. In this study, we propose Brimory, a novel trajectory prediction approach inspired by human driving, designed to equip autonomous vehicles (AVs) with humanoid memory systems. The core concept of Brimory is to emulate human driving processes by enabling the model to deeply comprehend traffic scenes, establish working memory, and iteratively accumulate to form driving experience. Brimory first introduces the working memory generator, which processes multiple interactions between the scene elements in the driving environment. It is noted that unlike traditional models confined to the time domain, Brimory also extracts underlying dependencies in the frequency domain. The long-term memory builder module is then developed to adaptively retrieve information from working memory and gradually accumulate driving experience with the help of the designed iterative updating mechanism. To mitigate the impact of irrelevant components on long-term memory effectiveness, we devise a co-modulation strategy that retains meaningful representations in a learnable manner. Finally, the combined humanoid memories are leveraged by the multimodal trajectory predictor to forecast future motions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority, feasibility, and efficiency of Brimory. The results underscore the potential of humanoid memory frameworks in trajectory prediction, offering a promising path toward the realization of safer AVs.

title: TACT: Humanoid Whole-Body Contact Manipulation Through Deep Imitation Learning With Tactile Modality
abstract: Manipulation with whole-body contact by humanoid robots offers distinct advantages, including enhanced stability and reduced load. On the other hand, we need to address challenges such as the increased computational cost of motion generation and the difficulty of measuring broad-area contact. We therefore have developed a humanoid control system that allows a humanoid robot equipped with tactile sensors on its upper body to learn a policy for whole-body manipulation through imitation learning based on human teleoperation data. This policy, named tactile-modality extended ACT (TACT), has a feature to take multiple sensor modalities as input, including joint position, vision, and tactile measurements. Furthermore, by integrating this policy with retargeting and locomotion control based on a biped model, we demonstrate that the life-size humanoid robot RHP7 Kaleido is capable of achieving whole-body contact manipulation while maintaining balance and walking. Through detailed experimental verification, we show that inputting both vision and tactile modalities into the policy contributes to improving the robustness of manipulation involving broad and delicate contact.
keywords: deep learning in grasping and manipulation

title: Versatile Bipedal Locomotion and Walking-Running Transition: Coordinating Supervised Learning and Nonlinear Optimization
abstract: Online gait planning plays a crucial role for the locomotion of humanoid robots. While simplified models often fail to capture critical dynamic features of the robot’s motion, making online gait modifications with constrained nonlinear optimization in complex models is highly challenging with current computational power. This paper introduces a gait planning method that leverages supervised learning to expedite the gait planning and optimization process. Building upon our previous work, this paper extends a three-body model to the three-dimensional (3D) case. This model incorporates the angular momentum and height variation of body as well as the influence of leg motions, thus facilitating the generation of omnidirectional walking and running patterns. Due to the complexity of the model, an online gait planning modification is impractical. Therefore, supervised-learning is employed to train a policy derived from the model-based gait planning approach. This policy is then implemented online to produce versatile locomotion. Furthermore, the gradient of the trained neural network is utilized for nonlinear optimization of gait parameters, significantly improving the robot’s balance against external perturbations. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through a series of experiments conducted in simulation and on the real robot BHR-T, confirming its capability to generate adaptive walking and running motions in response to varying demands and disturbances. Note to Practitioners—The gait planning method presented in this paper addresses the practical challenge of real-time locomotion control in humanoid robots. This approach is beneficial for applications requiring quick adaptability to external disturbances and varying terrain. By integrating supervised learning with model-based nonlinear optimization, this method allows for the efficient generation and optimization of stable walking and running patterns. The trained neural network not only enhances the robot’s balance but also reduces the computational burden, making it feasible to implement in real-world scenarios. This method has been validated in both simulations and real-world tests, demonstrating its potential to improve the performance of humanoid robots in practical deployments.
